Transfer rule: If a concept requires public opposition to a potentially polluting or hazardous facility near homes, then exclude ordinary neighborhood-interest disputes lacking that risk element.
Error pattern: Success came from checking necessary defining features instead of matching on any nearby-resident opposition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes: public facility, perceived health/environmental risk, resident collective resistance; reject any option missing a required box.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about social effects, especially when several choices share protest, petitioning, or local conflict.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept definition is broad enough to include private projects or non-environmental inconveniences.

Transfer rule: If a rebuttal says costs are “ultimately paid by consumers,” then test whether the spending would occur anyway and is merely shifted across channels.
Error pattern: I accepted evidence that advertising is large/growing instead of checking the rebuttal’s hidden assumption about incidence and substitution.
Diagnostic check: Ask: holding firms’ total promo budgets fixed, would choosing this venue change consumers’ total burden, or only reallocate existing spend?
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions involving pass-through, advertising, subsidies, overhead, or claims that one group indirectly pays through product prices.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about short-run accounting facts, regulated pricing, or when total spending is clearly not fixed.

Transfer rule: If a claim says an action is the only cause or necessary for an outcome, then prefer evidence about the same subject showing the outcome without it or even better without it.
Error pattern: Chose a parallel-case alternative instead of testing the necessity claim on the original case.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option show, for the focal entity, the outcome would still occur, or occur more strongly, without the alleged sole cause?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions with words like only, must, can only, necessary, sole cause.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is merely correlational or comparative and does not assert exclusivity or necessity.

Transfer rule: If a broad quality conclusion is drawn from partial-year data, then test whether harmful cases are seasonally concentrated outside the sampled period.
Error pattern: Success came from checking representativeness over time instead of being distracted by cause-based or improvement-based statements.
Diagnostic check: Ask: would the conclusion still hold if the omitted months contain most negative events? If yes, weak challenge; if no, strong challenge.
Use when: Applies to arguments inferring overall status from first-half, recent, sampled, or otherwise incomplete time windows.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is explicitly limited to that same time window or when full-period coverage is already provided.

Transfer rule: If a definition centers on refusing to give up a specialized skill domain, then choose the case where career moves deepen that same technical/professional practice rather than shift to management, business, or exit.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking continuity of the core competence across choices, not surface prestige, hardship, or career advancement.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does the person keep doing the same specialized work as the central career identity after the change?
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching items about career anchors, motivations, or role continuity versus role change.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is about leadership, autonomy, security, lifestyle, or values unrelated to specialized expertise.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts stated beliefs with parents’ distracting behavior and uses a rhetorical twist, then choose a title capturing that irony, not just the broad topic.
Error pattern: I matched the majority factual theme while missing the author’s evaluative focus and contrast-driven headline style.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s final contrast, tone, and implied criticism; prefer the option reflecting all three.
Use when: This applies to title/main-idea questions with survey facts followed by a behavior contradiction or a punchline in the closing sentences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage is purely expository, neutral in tone, or asks for a summary rather than the best title.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires first economic application that creates a new production or supply function, then choose the option showing market-deployed recombination with commercial results, not mere technical advancement or technology import.
Error pattern: I matched on “advanced production technology” and ignored the stricter economic-innovation criteria of novelty in application, marketability, and system-level production change.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the example show commercialization, a new market-facing production/supply arrangement, and results beyond technical capability or adoption alone?
Use when: Relevant for definition questions separating economic innovation from invention, R&D strength, technical performance, or simple introduction of existing methods.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks only about scientific progress, engineering capability, or operational improvement without requiring economic novelty.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects self-policing by interested producers and concludes outside approval is needed, then choose the principle barring sole regulation by financially interested actors.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the conclusion’s regulatory shift to a conflict-of-interest principle rather than to side issues like risk size or expert status.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Does this principle directly bridge distrust of producer assurances to a requirement for independent oversight?”
Use when: Relevant in principle-justify questions involving industry self-regulation, biased stakeholders, and a move to external review or approval.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about how dangerous the activity is, comparative harms, or excluding experts as such.

Transfer rule: If training is non-degree, job-related, and for already employed professionals to update skills, then classify it as continuing education.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking all definitional elements instead of matching only on “education” or “training.”
Diagnostic check: Verify three boxes: current professional/technical workers, purpose is updating or broadening competence, and format is non-academic rather than earning a formal credential.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching items contrasting in-service development with degree study, initial schooling, or retraining for unemployment.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category includes pre-service education, credential programs by definition, or training not tied to existing professional roles.

Transfer rule: If new evidence confirms an effect claimed by one side but does not address another side’s stated criterion, then strengthen only the directly tested claim.
Error pattern: I treated related evidence as supporting both positions, confusing relevance to the dispute’s key condition with relevance to a side issue.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write each view as a testable claim and ask, “Does this fact bear on this exact claim, or only on a neighboring topic?”
Use when: Two arguments discuss the same policy but hinge on different standards, assumptions, or decision criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the evidence explicitly addresses every side’s core criterion or when one view logically entails the other.

Transfer rule: If several full assignments are given with exact hit counts, then score every person’s three claims under each candidate for the asked slot and keep only cases matching the count pattern.
Error pattern: I chose an option from a local-looking fit instead of enforcing the global constraint across all guessers.
Diagnostic check: Build a 4×3 truth table of statements; for each candidate value of the target box, mark true/false, total each row, and verify one row has two truths while the other three have exactly one.
Use when: Apply this to logic puzzles with multiple people making parallel box/item claims and a stated distribution of correct guesses.
Boundary: Ignore when clues are probabilistic, independent, or do not specify exact per-person correctness counts.

Transfer rule: If a legal-rights question asks what is not included, then match each option to the definition’s named powers and reject any option introducing unilateral alteration of the instrument.
Error pattern: Success came from definition-to-option mapping and spotting an action that changes terms rather than enforcing payment or recourse.
Diagnostic check: List the core rights stated in the prompt, then test each option: enforce/collect, preserve payment claim, seek recourse, or impermissibly modify?
Use when: Apply this on commercial paper, contract, or statute questions that distinguish enforcement rights from amendment or creation powers.
Boundary: Ignore this when the governing rule expressly grants modification authority or the question concerns procedure rather than scope of rights.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several contributing conditions and then states an outcome, then choose the option that combines those conditions as the cause of that outcome.
Error pattern: Mistook a supported multicausal summary for an overstated single-cause side effect claim.
Diagnostic check: Underline every stated cause, mark the stated result, and reject any option that drops key causes or adds stronger wording not in the passage.
Use when: The argument is explanatory, with chained facts, conjunctions like “coupled with,” and a final sentence giving a broad consequence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, a definition, or a causal claim directly stated as the author’s sole point.

Transfer rule: If premises mix “most,” “some,” and “all successful have feature F,” then map sets and infer only guaranteed overlaps from existence claims plus subset relations.
Error pattern: Reversing or strengthening quantifiers; treating “most A are B” as “most B are A,” or assuming a sufficient condition from a stated necessary one.
Diagnostic check: Write each claim as set notation, mark direction of inclusion, then test each option with a tiny countermodel before choosing.
Use when: Quantified verbal reasoning questions compare groups with “all,” “some,” “most,” exceptions, and common-feature statements.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on causal, temporal, or numerical calculation rather than quantifier/set relations.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion adds a frequency claim from conditional premises, then require an assumption linking the necessary/sufficient condition to rarity.  
Error pattern: Success pattern: spotting that conditionals about what makes something qualify do not by themselves show how often it occurs.  
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Do the premises state only requirements, and does the conclusion assert uncommonness?” If yes, look for a rarity premise about the qualifying combination.  
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where an argument moves from “only if/whenever” statements to claims that outcomes are common, rare, likely, or unlikely.  
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is purely definitional, or when the premises already directly quantify prevalence or frequency.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a cause from better outcomes in a second setting, then check whether the same people perform both settings.  
Error pattern: I overlooked a hidden group-composition assumption and instead chose a statement about overall performance that was not required.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the conclusion still follow if different workers handled the later cases?” If no, require sameness/no systematic membership difference.  
Use when: Relevant in causal explanations comparing first-pass vs redo, before vs after, or any two stages with different success rates.  
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states identical agents across stages or the conclusion does not compare causes across groups.

Transfer rule: If a conditional set includes “not A → B” and “not B → A,” then test all truth assignments and keep only what every valid assignment forces.
Error pattern: I treated mutually supportive conditionals as proving both participants act, instead of separating what is necessary from what is merely possible.
Diagnostic check: Let A,B each be true/false; eliminate assignments violating any implication; then mark whether each variable is forced true, forced false, or undetermined.
Use when: Apply this to logic items with two actors, negations, and several if-then statements that may interact through contraposition or overlap.
Boundary: Ignore this when extra premises give direct facts, quantifiers, causality, or probabilities rather than pure propositional constraints.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “if not P, then not Q,” then convert it to the equivalent form “P or not Q” before matching choices.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a logically equivalent restatement, not being distracted by stronger, reversed, or differently worded conditionals.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each conditional with symbols, test contraposition only, and ask which option is guaranteed true in every case allowed by the premises.
Use when: Apply this on conditional-logic multiple-choice items with negations, “either/or,” “unless,” or tempting converse/inverse answer choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on factual content, probabilities, causal strength, or definitions rather than strict logical equivalence.

Transfer rule: If premises are conditional dislikes/likes, then chain them by contraposition before testing any option.
Error pattern: Success came from converting “not outings implies Tai Chi” into “not Tai Chi implies outings,” then combining rules.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each statement as implication and contrapositive; start from each option’s premise and see whether the conclusion follows in all cases.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice logic items with categories, negations, and statements like “those who X do not Y” or “those who not X do Y.”
Boundary: Ignore when claims are probabilistic, existential, causal, or require counting rather than strict universal implication.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a model is “most competitive,” then pick evidence showing it directly delivers the named competitive advantages better than alternatives.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the conclusion’s core criterion to a mechanism-level benefit, not choosing background conditions, general needs, or side effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the conclusion’s required advantages and ask which option most directly strengthens the link from the model to those advantages.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/support questions about business models, strategies, or structures described as best under fast-changing conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for assumptions, weakeners, definitions, or when options only compare feasibility rather than competitive payoff.

Transfer rule: If an act imitates a specific competitor’s identifying trade dress or source cues in selling goods, then classify it as commercial confusion.  
Error pattern: I focused on copied imagery or public misunderstanding generally, instead of source-confusing imitation tied to a market rival.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify all three: market transaction, deceptive similarity to a specific competitor, and likely buyers mistake the product’s source.  
Use when: The options involve packaging, branding, store presentation, names, logos, or other identifiers that could make one seller’s goods seem like another’s.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when confusion is only about endorsement, celebrity ownership, copyright copying, or non-competitor imagery without source confusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a cycle could not occur unless X, then test each link and pick the assumption required to make one step necessarily happen.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the causal chain and finding the hidden policy-setting assumption rather than choosing a merely relevant side fact.
Diagnostic check: Write the chain as A→B→C; for each arrow, ask “What must be true for this move to occur?” and negate candidates to see whether the cycle breaks.
Use when: Apply this on necessary-assumption questions built around causal loops, feedback systems, or policymaker responses.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a sufficient cause, best explanation, or strengthener rather than a must-be-true support claim.

Transfer rule: If a payment is made under an agreement as security for performance and is later credited back or returned after performance, then treat it as the target concept.
Error pattern: Confusing a premium, gift, or withheld compensation with a bilateral performance guarantee tied to breach consequences.
Diagnostic check: Verify four elements: prior agreement, payment before full performance, payment secures the obligation, and explicit forfeiture/double-return style consequence for breach.
Use when: A question asks you to distinguish contractual security payments from ordinary payments, bonuses, gifts, penalties, or price surcharges.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the payment is purely consideration, compensation, gratuity, or retention without a linked reciprocal contract-security function.

Transfer rule: If a phenomenon asks about this effect, then choose cases where a light beam becomes visibly traced inside a particle-dispersed medium by scattering.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the defining mechanism, not any situation involving light, brightness, reflection, refraction, or image formation.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is there a medium with suspended tiny particles, and can I see the beam’s path from the side?” If either answer is no, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for examples involving fog, smoke, dusty air, mist, or other colloid-like dispersions illuminated by a beam.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the situation is only mirror reflection, shadow formation, focusing, or bending between transparent uniform media.

Transfer rule: If a rebuttal claims a product isn’t inferior, then check whether its evidence directly addresses the claimed quality criterion rather than history or side facts.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning success: spotting irrelevant support used to defend a conclusion about performance or quality.
Diagnostic check: List conclusion and premises; for each premise, ask “Would this still matter if quality were poor?” If yes, mark it irrelevant.
Use when: Arguments compare suitability, reliability, or quality, especially when a response shifts to background facts, origins, or definitions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the disputed claim is actually about history, sourcing, or process rather than present quality.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats a detectable correlate as a sure indicator, then test whether the same signal can arise without the target condition.
Error pattern: Success pattern: attacked the hidden uniqueness assumption linking a physiological sign to one cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could a truthful or innocent case produce the identical measured reaction, creating false positives?”
Use when: Relevant in causal, diagnostic, or screening arguments that infer certainty from bodily signs, behaviors, or test readouts.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim already rules out alternative causes or the issue is only whether detection is partial, not nonunique.

Transfer rule: If a selection puzzle gives conditional constraints, then translate each into explicit forbidden/required co-occurrences and test every candidate set against them.
Error pattern: Success came from systematic constraint checking instead of guessing from surface plausibility.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark selected people, then ask: does any trigger occur; if yes, are all required additions present and all forbidden members absent?
Use when: Apply this to small-group choice problems with if-then rules, especially where one person’s inclusion forces another’s inclusion or exclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when conditions are probabilistic, comparative, or open-ended rather than strict logical membership constraints.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists severe environmental hardships and then contrasts policy help with continued poverty, then choose the option naming the core obstacle stated by those hardships.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing the passage’s causal focus over broader policy, cultural, or prescriptive distractors.
Diagnostic check: Underline each factual statement, ask “cause, effect, or recommendation?”, and verify the best choice matches the dominant cause rather than a response or extrapolation.
Use when: The stem asks for the main point and the text gives conditions plus outcomes with a contrast like “despite … still …”.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly argues for a solution, compares regions, or emphasizes policy/action more than underlying conditions.

Transfer rule: If a resolution condemns an official while support for the underlying policy remains plausible, then test whether the objection is about authority or procedure rather than substance.
Error pattern: I treated attitude evidence about public sentiment as resolving a procedural contradiction, confusing motive/popularity with institutional power.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could both statements be true if members support the action but reject who announced, authorized, or initiated it?” Prefer the choice that supplies that mechanism.
Use when: Relevant in paradox/resolution questions involving votes, condemnations, endorsements, and government bodies with different roles.
Boundary: Ignore when the discrepancy turns on timing, definitions, causal effects, or factual feasibility instead of decision-making authority.

Transfer rule: If a scheduling question asks what must be true, then test each candidate by forcing the given condition and propagating every rule across all slots before choosing.
Error pattern: I relied on a plausible local pairing instead of doing full constraint propagation to separate necessity from mere possibility.
Diagnostic check: Build a three-slot table, place the fixed relation, apply every conditional both forward and by contrapositive where valid, then try one counterexample for each option.
Use when: Use this for small logic-grid or duty-roster problems with paired assignments, forbidden pairings, and conditional day-to-day rules.
Boundary: Ignore when options ask for simple possibility counts or when rules are independent and no cross-slot propagation is needed.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists multiple risks, consequences, and constraints around one broad change, then choose the option that captures the overall challenge/theme, not a narrower subpoint.
Error pattern: Success comes from distinguishing a main-idea summary from statements that mention only one side detail, cause, or stakeholder.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each option to the passage; reject any option that covers only one sentence or one causal link instead of the full argument.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension questions with contrast markers, cascading effects, and several consequences tied to one central topic.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific fact, inference, attitude, or title explicitly narrower than the whole passage.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires state-purchased temporary relief for a home caregiver of a disabled/impaired elder, then verify every element: payer, temporary nature, home care context, target person, and caregiver respite.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all necessary conditions instead of choosing a merely helpful elder-care service.
Diagnostic check: Make a five-item checklist from the definition and reject any option missing even one item, especially government purchase or temporary substitution for the caregiver.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions with institutional criteria, beneficiary roles, and service purpose.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices ask for best fit by degree, opinion, or causal explanation rather than strict definitional membership.

Transfer rule: If a strengthen-EXCEPT asks about causal support, then prefer choices linking the suspected cause to broader/population-level incidence or ruling out alternatives; reject choices that only raise stakes.
Error pattern: I confused evidence relevance with seriousness, treating a consequence-amplifying statement as support for the causal inference.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “If true, does this make the stated cause-to-effect claim more likely, or merely make the effect more important?” Eliminate mere importance.
Use when: Relevant in argument-strengthening questions involving surveys, causal generalization, representativeness, control groups, or extrapolation from workers to the public.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about policy urgency, harm severity, or what should be done rather than whether the cause-effect claim is true.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires harm from accidental factors alongside an intentional or negligent act, then pick the case where the act is ordinary and the harmful contact is unplanned, not rule-breaking or omission-driven.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every clause of the definition and excluding cases dominated by prior illegality, professional negligence, or failure to guard.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark: intentional/negligent act present, accidental factor present, and harm directly caused by that accidental factor; choose only if all are yes.
Use when: Apply this to legal or conceptual classification questions with multi-part definitions and several superficially plausible examples.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category is broad enough to include omissions, strict liability, or any harmful result without an accidental-factor requirement.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion states “not guaranteed” under a disjunction, then use the observed guarantee to infer the negation of each triggering condition via contrapositive.
Error pattern: I affirmed a tempting antecedent from a conditional chain instead of first blocking the chain with the stated fact.
Diagnostic check: Translate all statements symbolically, contrapose any rule leading to a negated outcome, and test which earlier conditions must be false.
Use when: Relevant in multi-conditional logic problems with disjunctions, contraposition, and a final fact that denies a downstream consequence.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are probabilistic, causal without strict implication, or use nonstandard quantifiers that block clean contraposition.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts schooling/theory with on-site apprenticeship and accumulated experience, then choose the option about practice validating and deepening book knowledge, not mere effort.
Error pattern: I matched a surface theme of “hard work matters” instead of the passage’s core relation between theoretical learning and experiential mastery.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the author’s causal chain in 10 words: school/theory → hands-on stages → real competence; reject choices missing that chain.
Use when: Relevant for summary questions describing apprenticeships, stepwise field exposure, execution under real conditions, or experience as necessary for mastery.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage emphasizes perseverance alone, innate talent, ambition, or moral slogans without a theory-versus-practice contrast.

Transfer rule: If a trend claim relies on comparing two time points, then test whether one point is an abnormal outlier or temporary dip before inferring continuation.
Error pattern: I overfocused on measurement-method criticism instead of challenging the causal/trend baseline behind the prediction.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the conclusion still look strong if last period were unusually low or disturbed?” If not, prefer that weakening factor.
Use when: Relevant for arguments projecting future movement from a recent increase, especially with sparse time-series evidence.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already controls for anomalies, uses long-run data, or the option only attacks reliability without affecting the inference.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts different measurement bases across cases and shows resulting value shifts, then infer the claim is about comparability limits, not any single case judgment.
Error pattern: Success comes from abstracting from examples to the passage’s main implication about metrics; failure comes from fixating on one country or treating examples as the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the metric used in each example and ask: “What broader comparison issue do these differing metrics create?”
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension questions with definitions, cross-case examples, and numerical differences caused by method changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific example’s direct claim rather than the passage’s overarching meaning.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives one necessary route as “A or B required for C,” and C occurs while A is absent, then infer B by disjunctive elimination.
Error pattern: Confusing contraposition of a disjunction/necessary-condition structure with irrelevant sufficiency or conjunction patterns.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the stem symbolically; mark which terms are necessary, then test whether the argument has the form C, not A, therefore B.
Use when: The problem contains “only if,” “essential condition,” or similar wording tying an outcome to at least one of two required alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the condition is sufficient rather than necessary, or when the original link requires both conditions together.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a product’s price depends on fuel costs because manufacturing uses much energy, then infer a fuel-as-energy-source link, not a raw-material or price-correlation claim.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracing the stated causal chain from energy input to production cost and rejecting choices that switch categories or reverse effects.
Diagnostic check: Mark each noun as raw material, energy source, process, or price; keep only options that preserve the same roles and causal direction.
Use when: Relevant for causal-inference multiple-choice items about manufacturing, costs, inputs, and assumptions behind price effects.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem provides direct evidence about composition, market co-movement, or noncausal associations instead of production causation.

Transfer rule: If a figure of speech is defined by cross-sensory substitution, then choose the option that maps one sense quality onto a different sense, not mere resemblance or exaggeration.
Error pattern: I confused a simple simile/comparison with synesthetic transfer and under-checked whether two sensory domains were actually being exchanged.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label the source sense and target sense; accept only if the expression attributes a quality from one sensory channel to another.
Use when: Relevant for rhetoric questions involving sensation words, vivid imagery, “sweet sound,” “warm color,” or personified sensory descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the item tests ordinary simile, metaphor, hyperbole, or personification without cross-sensory mapping.

Transfer rule: If a “motto” question asks what is unsuitable, then prefer the statement least usable for personal self-reminding and behavior guidance.
Error pattern: Success came from separating abstract descriptive theory from concise normative, motivational, self-regulating sayings.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: can a person realistically adopt this as a brief personal reminder that directly steers conduct or attitude in daily situations?
Use when: The definition emphasizes memorability, self-warning, encouragement, restraint, or repeated personal recall rather than mere truth or philosophy.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target category includes general doctrines, explanatory principles, or literary quotations regardless of practical self-guidance.

Transfer rule: If a passage argues that an apparently impressive result is expected because the underlying technology already exceeds humans in that task, then choose the option expressing present maturity, not mere progress.
Error pattern: I focused on the topic area and trend, but missed that the author’s main point was an evaluative claim about current capability level.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the passage mainly describing development, or justifying why current performance should be unsurprising?”
Use when: Apply this to explanatory passages that reframe a striking application by linking it to an already-advanced core technology.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage emphasizes timeline, future expansion, or comparative superiority as the central takeaway.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a prior hidden condition from a stated later intention/change using a one-way “if condition, then likely action” link, then match it to the same direction of inference.
Error pattern: Confused denying a resulting state with inferring an earlier cause; mixed up reverse/contrapositive structure with “cause suggested by later behavior.”
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as variables: “If P, then tends to Q; observed/planned Q; concludes P.” Reject choices that instead use “not Q, so not P” or category exclusion.
Use when: Relevant for causal or behavioral statements involving plans, quitting, avoiding, or future choices used to infer an underlying circumstance.
Boundary: Ignore when the source relies on strict equivalence, valid contraposition, or pure classification rather than action-based causal inference.

Transfer rule: If habitat range depends on tolerance to a limiting condition, then infer the more tolerant subtype can occupy every zone the less tolerant one can, plus additional zones.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning from comparative constraints to relative geographic range, without adding unsupported population or coexistence claims.
Diagnostic check: Mark the limiting variable, list which subtype fails in which conditions, then compare implied possible regions for each subtype.
Use when: A passage links physiology or traits to environmental gradients and asks for the strongest supported conclusion about distribution.
Boundary: Ignore when choices require exact counts, direct competition, trait changes across regions, or any fact not explicitly tied to the stated constraint.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “not indifferent to moral issues” from “depicts crises that raise moral issues,” then require a bridge that depiction engages those issues.
Error pattern: Assumption questions often hinge on a missing link between a subject matter containing X and the work itself addressing X.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected bridge; if the premises can still hold while the conclusion fails, that bridge is necessary.
Use when: Relevant in arguments about books, art, or reports moving from what events/topics involve to what the work treats or ignores.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is directly stated by a premise or when the gap concerns causation, quantity, or comparison instead of topical engagement.

Transfer rule: If a passage centers on where an idea came from and ties it to a school of thought, then choose the title emphasizing origin plus ideological basis.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the paragraph’s organizing thread rather than overweighing isolated definitions, examples, or praise.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each sentence’s role; if most give source, causal setup, and theoretical linkage, prefer an origin-focused summary.
Use when: The question asks for the main content of an expository paragraph with background, institutional setup, and doctrine.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly compares stages over time, defines terms only, or evaluates impact more than source.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites a neighboring source as evidence of prior local knowledge, then prefer facts that block the alleged outside source from supplying that neighbor.
Error pattern: I strengthened a side issue about materials instead of reinforcing the argument’s causal timeline and transmission path.
Diagnostic check: Map the chain “outside source → intermediary/local source → target claim”; ask which choice most severs or confirms a link in that chain.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions about origin, influence, chronology, or whether knowledge could have been independently present before contact.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument turns on capability, quantity, or definitions rather than source-of-knowledge or contact pathways.

Transfer rule: If a claim says the fault “must be” on one side, then prefer evidence that directly rules out the alternative side’s failure.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning focused on eliminating the rival cause, not on background character facts or rare-history anecdotes.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which option most strongly reduces the chance that the nonblamed party caused the event?” Reject facts that are merely suggestive or indirect.
Use when: Relevant in support/strengthen questions involving disputed responsibility, causal attribution, negligence, or exclusive-source explanations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for possibility, motive only, or when no option actually bears on the competing cause.

Transfer rule: If an argument says greater exposure directly causes a harmful deposit, then prefer evidence showing the deposit mainly depends on an internal condition or mechanism instead.
Error pattern: I chose a weak counterexample/alternative occurrence instead of attacking the claimed causal link and necessary mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option explain why the effect happens independently of the cited exposure, or only show the effect can occur elsewhere too?”
Use when: Relevant for causal weakening questions about health risks, buildup, precipitation, or disease formation from consuming or contacting something.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for mere relevance, benefits, or frequency comparisons rather than the main causal driver.

Transfer rule: If a claim projects extinction from a current depletion trend, then prefer evidence showing the trend will be interrupted or reversed.
Error pattern: Successful weakening focused on the prediction’s hidden assumption that present decline conditions will continue unchanged.
Diagnostic check: Underline the forecast assumption, then ask of each option: does this change future causal conditions, merely restate decline, or strengthen it?
Use when: Relevant for argument-weaken questions about time-based predictions, extrapolations, population collapse, depletion, or “at this rate” reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for cause, description, legality, or when choices discuss present facts without affecting the future trend.

Transfer rule: If an evaluation happens during implementation and is used to monitor progress toward preset instructional or project goals, then treat it as formative.
Error pattern: Success came from matching process-oriented, ongoing feedback rather than endpoint judgment, selection, or approval decisions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this assessment occur before completion and use current performance to guide teaching or implementation?
Use when: Apply this on questions contrasting classroom/project monitoring with final acceptance, expert review, admission, hiring, or other one-time gatekeeping evaluations.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks about summative, selection, certification, or post-completion appraisal rather than in-process improvement.

Transfer rule: If an argument goes from “If P, then Q” plus “not P” to “not Q” or an opposite of Q, then match it with the same denied-antecedent form.
Error pattern: I focused on surface plausibility and missed the exact conditional structure, especially switching between contrapositive and denied antecedent.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite both source and choices as P→Q; given not P; conclude not Q/opposite Q, and verify term positions stay aligned.
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions with categorical or causal statements, especially with negatives, antonyms, or property judgments.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument includes biconditionals, quantified reversals, or a valid contrapositive from “not Q” to “not P.”

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both a green/sustainability theme and enterprise public-relations activity aimed at image, trust, or competitive benefit, then choose the option explicitly containing all of those parts.
Error pattern: I matched on environmental language alone and ignored the full actor-purpose-activity structure in the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list three boxes—enterprise actor, green-themed communication/publicity, reputational or support/advantage outcome—and reject any option missing one.
Use when: Apply this to “which fits the definition” questions with multi-part necessary conditions and several superficially related examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is broad, disjunctive, or describes products/policies rather than a targeted public-relations process.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires planned, organized measures to prevent, reduce, or handle a crisis, then exclude outcomes caused by spontaneous personal luck or traits without prior planning.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking every option for the definition’s process element, not just whether a crisis occurs.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is there an intentional prearranged action or response plan aimed at prevention, mitigation, or control?” If no, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions contrasting formal management actions with incidental events or individual reactions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes accidental survival, instinctive behavior, or unplanned post-event facts.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends an action for every day or all cases, then look for evidence that a common subset of situations lacks the stated risk or need.
Error pattern: Successful weakening by attacking an overgeneralized recommendation with a realistic exception domain rather than disputing background facts.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does any option show a frequent context where exposure is much lower or protection is already provided, making the universal advice unnecessary?
Use when: Conclusions use broad prescriptions like always, every day, everyone, or regardless of season/location.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is explicitly conditional, already limited to high-risk contexts, or asks about strengthening rather than weakening.

Transfer rule: If asked which question is least important to predicting acceptance, then test each option for direct impact on the decision-maker’s costs, feasibility, or bargaining leverage.
Error pattern: I overvalued an indirectly relevant bargaining factor and undervalued whether a financial-detail question actually changes acceptability of the proposal.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: if I knew this answer, would it materially change a rational accept/reject decision; rank by decision impact and pick the weakest.
Use when: Relevant in “least helpful/important” strengthen-weaken-style questions about negotiations, hiring, contracts, budgets, or strategic choices.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for truth, ethics, legality, or a specific causal mechanism rather than comparative decision relevance.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts image-only with meaning-only and ends by combining both, then choose the option expressing their integration as the main idea.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s central synthesis rather than over-weighting one supporting requirement or a process detail.
Diagnostic check: List each paragraph function—problem, limitation, solution—and verify the answer covers the final solution that subsumes earlier points.
Use when: Apply on main-idea questions where the text discusses design, symbols, communication, or criteria and includes balancing language like “at the same time” or “requires.”
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a specific detail, example, necessary condition, or step instead of the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If a claim gives broad correlations, then weaken it by finding a case where one cited factor moves the “wrong” way while the outcome still rises or stays high.
Error pattern: Success came from targeting the stated causal/correlational link directly, not choosing an option that merely matches the trend or adds background.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark each mentioned variable as supporting, neutral, or contradicting the claimed direction; prefer the option with the clearest contradiction tied to the outcome.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions built on multi-factor correlations, especially with positive/negative relation language and observational findings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is to strengthen, explain mechanisms, or when an option changes definitions, timing, or population.

Transfer rule: If a logistics case involves many independent firms in the same industry jointly sharing a distribution channel via a coordinating platform, then classify it as horizontal integration.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking all defining elements, not matching on any single cue like shared delivery or internal coordination.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify three boxes: same-industry participants, multiple independent enterprises, and a shared logistics-demand/supply coordination mechanism handling substantial volume.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about logistics structures, alliances, distribution organization, or integration types across firms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the case is vertical supply-chain control, a single company’s internal logistics, or merely one firm consolidating its own shipments.

Transfer rule: If an argument says members of a group generally have property P and a named individual is in that group, then match it to an argument with the same group-to-member inheritance.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking quantifier structure and membership direction, not topic words.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “Group G have P; x is G; therefore x has P,” then compare whether the candidate preserves that exact form.
Use when: Apply this on analogy questions involving classes, individuals, and attributed traits, behaviors, or training.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when choices reverse direction, use negation/contraposition, or shift from “all” to “most/some.”

Transfer rule: If a pronoun appears after “A is B, and it is C,” then first test the nearest singular abstract noun phrase as its antecedent, not a broader theme word.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized to the topic and ignored local grammatical attachment within a definition/apposition structure.
Diagnostic check: Replace the pronoun with each candidate noun phrase from the previous sentence; choose the one that yields a parallel, coherent statement without shifting abstraction level.
Use when: Apply this to reading questions with pronouns referring to abstract concepts in tightly linked explanatory sentences.
Boundary: Ignore this when later discourse clearly resets the subject, or when number/gender agreement rules eliminate the nearest noun phrase.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims rising publicity mainly caused rising sales, then prefer evidence showing the exposed audience rarely buys or exposure does not track purchase behavior.
Error pattern: This is a causal-weaken task; success comes from attacking the proposed cause-effect link directly rather than offering merely alternative motives or background facts.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option show publicity fails among people who actually received it?” If yes, it strongly weakens; if it only adds another possible cause, it weakens less.
Use when: Relevant for causal claims based on two trends occurring together, especially media attention, advertising, or awareness versus behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for strengthening, explanation, or when an option directly rules out all other causes with stronger evidence.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a true claim is being inserted irrelevantly to blur distinctions, then choose the option about rhetorical confusion, not the true claim itself.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the author’s main point about misuse in argument from background concessions everyone already accepts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each statement as premise, concession, or thesis; pick the choice matching the thesis sentence, especially evaluative words like “misleading” or “deliberately confuse.”
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items contrasting methods, viewpoints, or debates where the author comments on how a claim is used.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a factual takeaway, summary of all claims, or the passage lacks criticism of argumentative misuse.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle says exactly one statement is false, then formalize each claim and test each answer choice against the full truth pattern before choosing.
Error pattern: Misread ordinary-language connectives and jumped from a perceived contradiction to eliminating an option without checking consistency globally.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite every statement with symbols for negation, disjunction, conjunction, and implication; for each candidate, mark T/F for all speakers and verify that exactly one mark is false.
Use when: Applies to multi-speaker deduction problems with “only one wrong,” especially where claims contain “or,” “both,” “if…then,” or negated implication wording.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not truth-evaluation across fixed options or when wording is probabilistic, ambiguous, or nonclassical.

Transfer rule: If one person belongs to a group where all members have trait T and also to a subgroup where members lack T, then infer they cannot belong to that subgroup.
Error pattern: I failed to combine universal statements through a shared individual and instead chose an unsupported claim about a different person.
Diagnostic check: For each named person, list every stated category membership and every category rule; test for trait conflicts that force exclusion from some category.
Use when: Relevant in logic questions with “all,” “not,” subgroup restrictions, and individuals belonging to multiple sets.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are probabilistic, defeasible, or when no person is explicitly linked to both rules.

Transfer rule: If a sanction is imposed by other sectors unrelated to the original misconduct domain, then classify it as social punishment.  
Error pattern: Success came from separating direct legal/administrative penalties and public opinion from cross-department collateral restrictions.  
Diagnostic check: List each consequence and ask: same authority or same field as the violation, mere public condemnation, or unrelated agencies limiting other services?  
Use when: Relevant in definition-matching items about punishment types, especially when choices mix on-site penalties, reputation effects, and service-access limits.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept includes direct penalties, moral criticism alone, or consequences within the original regulator’s ordinary authority.

Transfer rule: If committee/group assignments have fixed slot totals and overlap restrictions, then convert them into member-occurrence counts and pairwise co-membership requirements before testing options.
Error pattern: Chose by loose narrative elimination instead of enforcing all constraints on a concrete assignment structure.
Diagnostic check: Compute total seats, infer the repeated-member pattern, list every forbidden pair, then see which candidate pair appears in every feasible completion.
Use when: Relevant in set-partition, scheduling, or committee-overlap problems with small numbers, exact group sizes, and “must be true” choices.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is probabilistic, asks for sufficiency without fixed totals, or lacks enough structure for exhaustive constraint propagation.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires danger to arise after tension drops near success, then reject choices that only contrast high-vigilance safety with routine-time mistakes without any “approaching success → relax → disaster” sequence.
Error pattern: I matched broad “relaxed state causes problems” cues and ignored the definition’s required temporal structure and near-goal context.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark Tense phase, Near-success phase, Relaxation, and Result; accept only if all four appear in order.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions built on causal chains, sequencing, or necessary conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this check when the target concept is a loose similarity, simple association, or lacks a staged process.

Transfer rule: If comparing which subgroup produced an observed event, then compare base rate × event rate for each subgroup.
Error pattern: Confused conditional risk within a group with posterior likelihood after the event; ignored prevalence.
Diagnostic check: Compute unnormalized contributions for all groups, then see which is larger before choosing any comparison claim.
Use when: An event has already occurred and choices ask which category is more likely responsible, while both category frequencies and event rates are given.
Boundary: Ignore this when only within-group risk is asked, or when priors are equal/irrelevant, or dependence changes the simple product rule.

Transfer rule: If a claim says future discoveries will fit existing theory and cause little surprise, then choose evidence showing new findings violate that theory’s predictions.
Error pattern: Success pattern: target the claim’s strongest assumption—completeness and explanatory adequacy of the current framework—not weaker side issues.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the conclusion’s two hinges: “few/new discoveries left” and “current theory can explain them”; prefer the option that directly breaks both or the more central one.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/refute questions about scientific theories, prediction, completeness, or whether future observations will be surprising.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for support, comparison of theories without a future-claim, or when an option only shows uncertainty without conflicting evidence.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one option is more environmentally friendly, then compare full lifecycle harms of both alternatives and seek offsetting impacts in the favored one.
Error pattern: Success came from countering a one-sided comparison by introducing neglected environmental costs on the supposedly greener side.
Diagnostic check: List each option’s impacts across production, use, and disposal; prefer the choice that adds a substantial omitted harm to the currently preferred alternative.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/challenge questions about comparative claims, especially when the stimulus discusses only one side’s drawbacks.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only discuss price, appearance, or future possibilities without affecting the present comparison.

Transfer rule: If an argument defends a proposal by citing famous past successes, then test whether it establishes that the current case is relevantly comparable.
Error pattern: I focused on wording ambiguity instead of the core analogical leap from celebrated examples to the proposal at issue.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What premise must connect the historical examples to this present recommendation, and is that premise actually supported?”
Use when: Relevant for arguments using precedent, analogy, or eminent cases to justify funding, policy, or research value.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument independently provides direct evidence for the present case rather than relying on comparison.

Transfer rule: If categories are stated as different and one category is tied to not having property P while another group is tied to having P, then map each set relation before inferring.
Error pattern: Confusing a one-way conditional with its converse and missing how “different categories” plus negation partitions the groups.
Diagnostic check: Write symbols for each group/property, derive subset or disjointness links, then test each option against the diagram without reversing arrows.
Use when: Statements mix class labels, negations, and outcome requirements such as employment, eligibility, or permission.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question depends on quantities, probabilities, or causal claims rather than set/conditional logic.

Transfer rule: If a sequencing question asks “could be true,” then construct one full valid order for each candidate instead of relying on local plausibility.
Error pattern: I accepted an option after checking only a few constraints, not global compatibility among precedence and adjacency rules.
Diagnostic check: For any candidate position claim, place that item there, then complete all remaining slots while enforcing every rule at each step; reject if no full schedule exists.
Use when: Apply this to ordering/logic problems with multiple items, category alternation limits, and before/after dependencies.
Boundary: Ignore this exhaustive build when the question asks for a necessary fact provable directly by one rule alone.

Transfer rule: If a statement says some members completed every activity in each listed category, then infer each activity in those categories has at least one such member attending.
Error pattern: Mistook an existential “some did all of type X” for a claim about nonparticipants or missing attendance elsewhere.
Diagnostic check: List all categories covering the activity set; for each category, ask whether “some person did all in this category” guarantees every activity there has an attendee from that group.
Use when: The prompt partitions items into exhaustive types and gives “some ... all ...” participation facts about a subgroup.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are not exhaustive, “some” refers to different populations irrelevantly, or “all” modifies people rather than activities.

Transfer rule: If an argument uses “if J, then X or Y” plus “not Y” to conclude X, then verify it also assumes or establishes J.
Error pattern: Dropping a necessary antecedent and replacing it with an overly strong converse or sufficiency claim.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the logic as J → (X ∨ Y), ¬Y, therefore X; ask, “Do I have J anywhere?” If not, the missing assumption is J.
Use when: Relevant in conditional-assumption questions with disjunction elimination from a triggered consequence.
Boundary: Ignore when the antecedent is explicitly given, or when the task asks for a stronger statement than the minimal required assumption.

Transfer rule: If a condition chain from choosing one person forces choices that violate any “at most one” rule, then eliminate that choice as impossible.
Error pattern: I failed to propagate all conditional constraints jointly and tested an option in isolation instead of checking consistency against every rule.
Diagnostic check: Assume each candidate answer is true; derive all forced selections/exclusions step by step, then stop if any pair exceeds an “at most one” limit.
Use when: Apply this on selection-logic problems with minimums, maximums, and “if selected, then also select” dependencies among people/items.
Boundary: Ignore this when options ask only for local effects of a single rule, not a globally necessary conclusion from all rules together.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a direct practical takeaway, then prefer the option restating that takeaway over broader descriptive summaries.
Error pattern: Chose a thematic paraphrase of background information instead of the author’s final inferential claim.
Diagnostic check: Mark conclusion cues like “therefore/so”; ask which option is the closest restatement of the sentence after that cue.
Use when: The passage includes setup facts followed by a recommendation, consequence, or user-oriented implication.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the main idea, definition, or a globally supported summary rather than an inference.

Transfer rule: If deciding whether something is a final product, then ask whether the buyer uses it directly rather than reselling it or using it to make something else.
Error pattern: Confusing production inputs or indirect outcomes with the good or service that reaches the end user.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate, run this test: identify the immediate purchaser and ask, “Will they consume/use it as-is, or use it in further production/distribution?”
Use when: Relevant in economics questions contrasting final goods/services with intermediate goods, donated goods, production inputs, or intangible outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task concerns value added, welfare effects, project goals, or environmental benefits rather than market classification.

Transfer rule: If an argument says some condition would limit the press’s power by restricting a specific activity, then infer that the power depends on that activity.
Error pattern: Mistook a causal support point about attracting audiences for the passage’s stated basis of institutional power.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What does the author explicitly say would be curtailed, and what consequence is tied to that curtailment?”
Use when: Relevant in inference questions where one clause explains survival or incentives and another names what would reduce power, freedom, or effectiveness.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage independently defines power in market, storytelling, or truth-seeking terms rather than via restricted criticism.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists causes of a social craze and includes criticism of participants’ motives, then predict a next section that evaluates the issue or gives a balanced understanding, not logistics or background.
Error pattern: I overweighted topic continuity and chose a descriptive follow-up instead of matching the author’s evaluative, corrective direction.
Diagnostic check: Ask: is the paragraph mainly describing facts, or building toward a judgment/advice? If it ends with blame, anxiety, or misconception, prefer a “how to view/respond” continuation.
Use when: The stem asks what comes next after an analysis of reasons, motives, and problems behind a trend.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly signals a shift to methods, definitions, market status, or practical selection criteria.

Transfer rule: If a statement is presented as a broad lesson from an example and then applied to justify a policy claim, then treat it as a general premise supporting the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Confusing background motivation or illustration with an evidentiary principle in the argument’s support structure.
Diagnostic check: Mark the final recommendation, then ask whether removing the broad lesson would weaken the link from example to recommendation; if yes, it is supporting evidence.
Use when: Arguments move from a concrete case to a general lesson and then to a prescriptive conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement is explicitly rejected, merely rhetorical, or only explains why the issue matters.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which choice would not support a theory, then test each option for whether it strengthens a required link; pick the one that is neutral, contradictory, or irrelevant.
Error pattern: Success came from using support/undermine logic instead of being distracted by details that merely sound scientific.
Diagnostic check: List the theory’s needed conditions, then mark each option as helps, hurts, or unrelated to one condition; choose the non-helper.
Use when: Apply this on strengthen/weaken/except items about causal stories, historical explanations, or feasibility chains.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for the most likely explanation, a direct factual recall, or when every option is evidence rather than support status.

Transfer rule: If asked for the literal meaning of a passage, then choose the option that restates the passage’s central claim most directly, without adding purpose, theory, or broader doctrine.
Error pattern: Success came from matching explicit repeated ideas rather than chasing abstract themes or inferred intentions.
Diagnostic check: Underline the passage’s repeated subject and predicate; pick the choice that preserves both with the fewest added concepts.
Use when: The stem asks for literal meaning, main idea, direct statement, or straightforward paraphrase of an expository or persuasive passage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for implication, author’s intent, hidden meaning, best title, or rhetorical function.

Transfer rule: If a study claims a habit lowers a specific health risk, then prefer evidence giving a plausible mechanism directly affecting that risk.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the support option to the claimed outcome rather than to broader health benefits or group differences.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it causally connect the habit to the exact measured disease outcome, not just to health in general?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about observational findings, especially when choices include mechanisms, irrelevant benefits, or demographic contrasts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for a weakener, a methodological flaw, or when mechanism evidence is unnecessary compared with direct comparative data.

Transfer rule: If a plan depends on combining a drug with a second agent to fine-tune dosage, then test whether that agent’s effect is reliably standardized.  
Error pattern: I focused on background/history evidence instead of attacking the plan’s practical controllability and safety.  
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could two supposedly equal administrations produce meaningfully different effective doses because one input varies unpredictably?”  
Use when: The argument recommends substituting or adjusting dosage through an interacting food, supplement, environment, or co-treatment.  
Boundary: Ignore when the interaction’s magnitude is measured, fixed, and controllable for each administration, or the claim is purely causal rather than prescriptive.

Transfer rule: If an argument says “if P, then Q,” then do not infer “not Q” from “not P”; look for that same denial-of-the-antecedent pattern.
Error pattern: Treating a stated sufficient condition as if it were necessary for the outcome.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the core claim as P → Q, mark the evidence as either P, not P, Q, or not Q, and verify the conclusion is not deriving not Q from not P.
Use when: Conditional arguments where one event is presented as enough to produce another, especially in parallel-reasoning questions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the statement uses “only if,” “unless,” or explicitly gives a necessary condition instead.

Transfer rule: If a one-to-one assignment puzzle gives a fixed difference, then list all feasible ordered pairs for that relation before placing anyone else.
Error pattern: I anchored one person to a specific position without enumerating alternatives, then built contradictions from that unsupported assumption.
Diagnostic check: Write every allowed pair for the offset clue, mark occupied positions, apply parity/order/adjacency constraints to each case, and keep only cases that satisfy all clues simultaneously.
Use when: Relevant in linear arrangement or house-number puzzles with distinct positions, numeric offsets, inequality, parity, and neighbor restrictions.
Boundary: Ignore when positions are not unique, clues are probabilistic/soft, or the task is not a constrained assignment/elimination problem.

Transfer rule: If a passage diagnoses one specific obstacle in rights protection, then predict the next part will propose a remedy targeting that obstacle directly.
Error pattern: I shifted from the stated bottleneck to a broader educational theme instead of following the passage’s immediate problem-solution structure.
Diagnostic check: Name the final paragraph’s core problem in five words; eliminate any option that does not explicitly fix that exact problem.
Use when: Apply this on “what comes next” questions where the text emphasizes a single cause, supporting examples, and practical consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage already broadens to multiple themes, compares solutions, or signals a shift to background, contrast, or case detail.

Transfer rule: If a paragraph states a rule first and then lists several functions/effects, then choose the option that combines the requirement with its overall significance.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions often fail when one supporting function is mistaken for the thesis instead of the broader synthesis.
Diagnostic check: Mark the opening claim and each later reason; ask whether an option covers both the policy statement and the summed value of the reasons.
Use when: The passage has an authoritative statement followed by multiple benefits, roles, or consequences of a system or policy.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific supporting point, detail, purpose of one sentence, or a single causal reason.

Transfer rule: If a statement is conditional, then translate it into logic and compare choices only by equivalence forms: contrapositive, disjunction, or necessity.
Error pattern: Success came from separating logical reformulations from choices that add new causal or probabilistic content.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “not B -> not A,” derive the contrapositive and “A or not B,” then reject any option mentioning frequency, luck, causes, or extra qualifiers.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items asking which statement is different, equivalent, or follows from an if-then warning or advice.
Boundary: Ignore this when the source includes quantified terms, temporal order, modal words, or nonconditional semantics that change equivalence rules.

Transfer rule: If reported frequency rises while underlying causes are said to be stable, then look for changes in detection, reporting, classification, or surveillance rather than in the phenomenon itself.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning reconciles an apparent contradiction by separating true incidence from recorded incidence.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the count increase even if the real rate stayed constant?”; list observer coverage, technology, incentives, and record-keeping changes.
Use when: A stimulus contrasts stable causal conditions with rising or falling measured cases, records, or discoveries.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a direct cause of the phenomenon or when evidence rules out measurement/reporting changes.

Transfer rule: If a bias claim rests on uneven interview counts, then test whether the imbalance simply mirrors the underlying population split.
Error pattern: Mistaking a representative sample for slanted coverage; ignoring a neutral base-rate explanation for skewed evidence.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the same interview ratio be expected if selection were proportional to supporters and opponents?” If yes, the bias inference weakens.
Use when: An argument infers media, survey, or reporting bias solely from unequal airtime, quotes, or examples from opposing sides.
Boundary: Ignore when selection rules were equalized, base rates are irrelevant or unknown, or independent evidence shows intentional favoritism.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts declining one format with rising another, then separate total interest in the activity from shifts in medium before judging statements.
Error pattern: Confusing a change in channel or behavior with a change in overall preference; success comes from tracking exactly what trend each claim matches.
Diagnostic check: List each explicit trend, label its subject and direction, and reject any option that broadens a format-specific decline into a universal decline.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension questions with trend data, contrasts, and options that paraphrase beyond the passage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage directly states overall attitudes or provides comprehensive evidence about total participation.

Transfer rule: If a definition targets one management function, then reject options outsourcing unrelated business functions even if they use external partners or technology.
Error pattern: I overmatched any external service/training to the definition and ignored whether the activity was actually part of that management domain.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is the task about acquiring, developing, planning, administering, or self-managing personnel/capability rather than marketing, production, or other operations?
Use when: The stem gives a formal definition with purpose, scope, and mechanisms, and the options mix same-structure examples from adjacent business areas.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition is broad enough to cover general business outsourcing, not a specific functional domain.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which fact supports “ability is cultural, not innate,” then prefer evidence showing ability varies sharply with cultural exposure or tools.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matching evidence to the dispute’s causal source rather than to examples that merely show the ability exists.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as supporting innate origin, cultural dependence, or irrelevant; select only one that most directly links ability level to culture.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions contrasting inborn talent versus learned or culturally produced capacities.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is about performance differences caused by training, age, or species without bearing on origin.

Transfer rule: If an argument says education or classification split two fields and thus weakens a market, then choose evidence showing the split directly deters the target audience from engaging with that field.
Error pattern: I picked a fact about experts’ preferences instead of evidence linking the stated cause to reduced mass readership.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map claim chain as cause → audience effect → outcome, and reject choices that support only the outcome or discuss the wrong population.
Use when: The question is a strengthen item where the stimulus proposes a causal explanation involving background knowledge, field separation, or audience formation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the best support is about supply, pricing, distribution, or another competing cause rather than audience disengagement.

Transfer rule: If an argument links taxes to spending to growth, then identify the unstated bridge connecting each causal step and test whether the conclusion needs it.
Error pattern: Success comes from spotting a missing causal assumption rather than choosing a broad value judgment or an extreme exclusivity claim.
Diagnostic check: Remove the suspected bridge; if the reasoning no longer connects policy to outcome, that statement is necessary.
Use when: Apply this on assumption questions with chained economic or behavioral causation and a policy recommendation at the end.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for evidence, principle, or a sufficient condition rather than a required assumption.

Transfer rule: If a blank is followed by an explanation and example, then choose the option that states the paragraph’s immediate claim, not a broader policy benefit.
Error pattern: I selected a plausible, more general inference instead of the sentence directly supported by the surrounding sentences.
Diagnostic check: Replace the blank with each candidate and test whether the next sentence begins as explanation/example of it without adding a topic shift.
Use when: This applies to passage-completion questions with nearby cues like “for example,” definitional wording, or a sentence unpacking the blank.
Boundary: Ignore this when the blank is meant to summarize the whole passage or introduce a new contrast/turn.

Transfer rule: If a claim says one factor is more effective because outcomes improved after a policy change, then check for concurrent changes that could also cause the improvement.
Error pattern: Mistaking a weak or indirect challenge to the outcome for a direct attack on the causal comparison; overlooking confounding alternatives.
Diagnostic check: List the conclusion’s compared causes and ask, “Did anything else increase at the same time that supports the rival cause?”
Use when: The argument infers superiority of one intervention over another from before/after data following a new law, campaign, or policy.
Boundary: Ignore this when the evidence explicitly isolates causes with controls, randomization, or clear proof that no relevant co-interventions changed.

Transfer rule: If an argument links an exposure to altered microbes and higher infection risk, then prefer evidence showing the exposure is followed by more of that infection in practice.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched the claim’s full causal chain rather than getting distracted by advice, caveats, or statements that weaken it.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice strengthen exposure → flora change/pathogen presence → increased infection outcome, instead of merely discussing prevention, uncertainty, or unrelated frequency?
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions involving studies, microbiome shifts, pathogen prevalence, and a causal conclusion about disease risk.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks to weaken, evaluate methodology only, or choose a recommendation rather than support a causal claim.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends more research as a cost-effective way to address a problem, then prefer support showing the underlying intervention is cheaper than the alternative costs it aims to avoid.
Error pattern: Success came from matching new evidence to the argument’s stated criterion rather than choosing facts merely related to the topic.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conclusion’s standard, ask “What exact comparison must be supported?”, and eliminate choices that do not strengthen that comparison directly.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions with policy or funding conclusions justified by efficiency, feasibility, or savings.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not depend on comparative cost or when another missing link is clearly more central than efficiency.

Transfer rule: If a claim compares group ability from admitted proportions, then first compare each group’s share in the applicant/test-taker pool before judging ability.
