Use when: This applies to main-point questions using salary, hiring, and scarcity examples to argue about labor-market valuation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for a phenomenon summary, social disparity, or a directly quantified comparison rather than the author’s central claim.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists reasons supporting an asset’s appeal, then choose the option capturing overall popularity/attractiveness, not a narrower mechanism mentioned inside.
Error pattern: Mistook supporting evidence about price drivers or context for the author’s main communicative purpose.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Do most sentences answer ‘why people favor it’ or ‘what determines its price’?”; if the former, reject factor-only summaries.
Use when: The passage gives several advantages, contrasts with alternatives, and adds examples as support for a broader evaluative claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text systematically categorizes determinants, forecasts movement, or centers on market analysis rather than appeal.

Transfer rule: If a scenario involves a deliberate fight, attack, or other purposeful harmful contact, then treat it as intentional conduct, not negligence.
Error pattern: I misclassified based on foreseeability of harm while overlooking the actor’s mental state toward the harmful act itself.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label the conduct as intentional, reckless, negligent, or accidental by asking: was the harmful contact itself chosen on purpose?
Use when: Apply this in criminal-law questions contrasting negligence with cases involving quarrels, retaliation, self-protective acts, dangerous handling, or risky driving.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the issue is only causation, justification, or degree of care after it is already clear the act was unintentional.

Transfer rule: If a definition limits randomness to creation or performance, then exclude choices where randomness only sets pre-performance logistics.
Error pattern: I matched anything “random” to the term and ignored the activity stage required by the definition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark where the accidental factor operates: composing, performing, sound production, or merely planning; reject planning-only cases.
Use when: Definitions specify both a key property and the process or phase in which it must occur.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept includes organizational setup, staffing, duration, or instrumentation decisions as part of the defined process.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts missing mechanism with later direct observation, then choose the principle that empirical detection can justify acceptance without a full causal account.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matching the author’s acceptance criterion to an abstract statement instead of chasing broader claims about science.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the theory’s two statuses—mechanism explained? phenomenon observed?—and select the option reproducing that exact combination.
Use when: Relevant in science-method questions where a theory was first doubted, then accepted after improved measurement or observation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage emphasizes prediction, statistical method, unification, or discovery of the underlying cause itself.

Transfer rule: If a logic-grid setup gives ranked score patterns plus seat/opponent constraints, then map every table’s allowed scoreline and identity before selecting a top scorer.
Error pattern: I jumped from one locally plausible leader cue to a global winner without exhausting all table-person assignments.
Diagnostic check: Build a 4-table matrix; for each table mark allowed first-three-round totals, tie/no-tie status, and player-placement constraints, then verify only one person can occupy the maximum total.
Use when: Relevant in arrangement puzzles combining matchup identities, left-right positions, and partial score-comparison facts.
Boundary: Ignore when the question can be answered directly from a single explicit statement without cross-table consistency work.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “this diet guarantees the result” from traits shared by top performers, then check for people with those same traits who did not get the result.
Error pattern: Mistaking a pattern among the most successful cases for a sufficient condition for everyone.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is there any counterexample in the cited group that matches the recommended features but lacks the promised outcome?”
Use when: A study-based ad moves from correlations in a subgroup to a universal prediction about anyone following certain behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already establishes necessity/sufficiency through controlled comparison, not just selective success-group description.

Transfer rule: If a scheduling question asks who can occur on any day, then map each person’s allowed days from every rule and test each option against the full day-domain.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting relational clues into day restrictions instead of chasing one concrete schedule too early.
Diagnostic check: For each person, list forbidden days from each clue, intersect them, and verify whether at least one valid completion exists for every candidate day.
Use when: Use this for multi-day assignment problems with adjacency, fixed-day placements, repetition limits, and pairing constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about counting total schedules or optimizing, not about possible placement domains.

Transfer rule: If asked for a “point at issue,” then test each option by asking whether one speaker is committed to yes and the other to no.
Error pattern: I matched a stated premise both speakers accept instead of isolating the disputed assumption underlying their opposing conclusions.
Diagnostic check: For every option, mark Mayor yes/no/unknown and Councillor yes/no/unknown; keep only options with opposite commitments, not shared facts or mere background.
Use when: Two arguments interpret the same evidence differently, especially in LSAT-style dialogue questions about disagreement, assumption, or issue.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a supported inference, a shared assumption, or a flaw rather than a disputed issue.

Transfer rule: If premises form a one-way conditional chain, then test answer choices by valid contrapositive links only; never infer causes from effects.
Error pattern: Mistaking a sufficient-condition chain for a reversible explanation, especially affirming the consequent.
Diagnostic check: Write symbols for each link, derive contrapositives, and ask whether the choice is a direct link/contrapositive or an illegal converse/inverse.
Use when: Arguments connect multiple comparisons or rates through “if,” “when,” or “shows that,” especially in market, cost, or causation chains.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage gives biconditionals, explicit “only if/iff,” or independent evidence supporting reverse causation.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a condition is necessary for survival or cultivation, then infer that this condition existed where/when the activity occurred.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: linking a stated necessity to a minimally required background fact, rather than choosing stronger historical or comparative claims.
Diagnostic check: Underline each necessity word (“need,” “cannot,” “essential”), then ask: which option states a prerequisite that must have been true?
Use when: Apply on inference questions with causal chains, environmental requirements, and a dated or located event.
Boundary: Ignore when options require trend claims, exclusivity, or exact timing not guaranteed by the stated prerequisite.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a policy will harm a group because it raises that group’s costs, then check whether it assumes the group’s gains won’t fully offset those costs.
Error pattern: Causal-impact arguments often hinge on an unstated net-effect assumption linking a predicted downside to the final “worse off” claim.
Diagnostic check: State the claimed harm and all direct benefits; ask, “Could the benefits still equal or exceed the harm?” If yes, that negation would weaken the argument.
Use when: The conclusion compares help versus harm after a policy change affecting prices, income, or purchasing power.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only that some prices rise, not that the target group is overall worse off.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about a legal-protective status, then choose the case where an authorized person assumes ongoing responsibility for a minor or legally limited person.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the formal legal relationship, not just spotting general care, safety, affection, or financial help.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify three elements: protected person lacks full legal capacity, a specific guardian-like actor is identified, and the act involves sustained supervision/protection rights.
Use when: Relevant for civics or law items contrasting guardianship/custody with charity, medical care, security work, or ordinary family support.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept asked is broad caregiving, emergency protection, employment duty, or temporary assistance without legal authority.

Transfer rule: If premises say most remaining cases are fragmented and such cases need regular intervention to keep their full species set, then infer a broad “without intervention, some loss occurs” claim, not a survival claim about a special subset.
Error pattern: I overreached from species-maintenance premises to extinction of endangered members by chaining in unsupported severity.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, map each premise to the conclusion and ask whether it supports only loss/reduction or the stronger outcome of non-survival.
Use when: Argument asks what is most strongly supported and mentions “maintain full complement,” “fragmented ecosystems,” and intervention requirements.
Boundary: Ignore when premises explicitly state extinction, survival failure, or quantify the endangered subset directly.

Transfer rule: If a passage starts with background/praise but ends with a normative takeaway, then treat the final call to action as the main point.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions often tempt by vivid examples or opening statements; success comes from separating support and illustration from the author’s intended emphasis.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as background, example, problem, or recommendation; choose the option that best integrates the recommendation with the stated problem.
Use when: Relevant for short expository passages that include examples, contrast words, and an ending about what people should do.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, example purpose, tone, or when no recommendation/conclusion is stated.

Transfer rule: If a choice attacks who designed a survey rather than wording, sample, or results, then treat it as irrelevant unless design expertise affects data quality.  
Error pattern: I overvalued “different survey” as irrelevant and missed that conflicting replication directly weakens a survey-based generalization.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this change representativeness, question framing, respondent reliability, or outcome consistency; if none, it likely cannot weaken.  
Use when: The argument generalizes from poll or survey responses to real-world preferences or behavior.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument explicitly depends on expert methodology, technical measurement, or designer qualifications.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives examples first and ends with consequences or warnings, then choose the option matching the author’s ultimate caution, not just an example/theme.
Error pattern: I fixated on a prominent supporting detail and missed the broader evaluative takeaway signaled by result-focused language.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark problem, reason, and warned outcome; pick the choice that covers the warned outcome and can subsume the earlier details.
Use when: The passage criticizes a trend, adds permanence/impact, and closes with social judgment or future consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific cause, detail, or directly stated topic sentence rather than overall intent.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives conditional warnings about what prevents a better society, then abstract the needed joint conditions into a broad main-point summary.
Error pattern: Success came from integrating linked conditions instead of fixating on a single cause, effect, or prerequisite.
Diagnostic check: List the stated necessities and blockers, then ask which option preserves all major elements without adding one-way causation.
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions with “if,” “but,” and “impossible/unless” structures about social outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific inference, detail, tone, or the author’s stance on only one factor.

Transfer rule: If a definition explicitly includes work given to an overseas subsidiary, then count that as outsourcing/offshoring rather than excluding it as merely internal.
Error pattern: I over-relied on a common-world assumption (“subsidiary means not external”) and ignored an inclusion clause in the stated definition.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, list each required element from the definition and test every option against them, especially any “includes” or special-case clauses.
Use when: The question is definition-based, asks for the exception, and options hinge on whether an example matches a broadened or counterintuitive category.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task depends on real-world business practice beyond the provided definition or when no explicit inclusion/exclusion clause is given.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers atmospheric conditions from fossil survival, then identify the hidden necessity linking that condition to the organism’s ability to exist or persist.
Error pattern: Chose a tempting mechanism/detail about organism behavior instead of the assumption required for the evidence-to-conclusion link.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If this statement were false, could the fossils still exist while the atmospheric conclusion fails?” Keep the option whose negation breaks the argument.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where a discovery is used as evidence for an earlier environmental threshold or timeline shift.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a direct implication, specific mechanism, or historical estimate rather than a necessary assumption.

Transfer rule: If a statement says one factor slows development, then infer only limited progress or immaturity, not that fixing that factor guarantees rapid success.
Error pattern: Treated a causal contributor as a sufficient condition and overread a remedy into a guaranteed outcome.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the passage assert necessity/sufficiency, or only describe an obstacle and current status?” Reject answers adding certainty about what will happen after a fix.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions with causal language, percentages, market-development claims, or contrasts between current performance and a benchmark.
Boundary: Ignore when the text explicitly states a guaranteed result, a policy requirement, or a direct equivalence between solving one issue and the outcome.

Transfer rule: If an option is an independently registered enterprise organization that can bear civil liability itself, then treat it as an enterprise legal person.  
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by legal status and liability bearer, not by business activity, size, or financial condition.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it an enterprise organization, separately approved/registered, with its own name/charter/structure/domicile, and able to assume liability independently?  
Use when: The prompt asks which entity has enterprise legal-person status among individuals, family businesses, branches, offices, or formal enterprises.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question concerns natural persons, non-enterprise legal persons, partnerships without legal-person status, or purely factual business operations.

Transfer rule: If one group’s every member exceeds another group’s maximum, yet the overall top earner is outside the first group, then infer existence of at least one person outside both named groups.  
Error pattern: Chose an attractive comparative claim instead of the only necessary existence claim forced by the quantifiers and extremum statements.  
Diagnostic check: Mark sets and extremes; ask, “Who must exist for the global maximum to be outside the first group while the second group is entirely below the first?”  
Use when: Statements compare all members of one group to another group’s maximum and mention the organization-wide highest or lowest person.  
Boundary: Ignore when extra groups or outsiders are already stated, or when the conclusion depends on averages, causes, or rankings not logically forced.

Transfer rule: If a travel-assignment puzzle has pair/group constraints plus country-type restrictions, then convert each person into a fixed two-country set and eliminate options by consistency, not by leftover choice.
Error pattern: Risk of shallow elimination from misread categories; success comes from integrating all constraints globally, especially linked travelers and “only-this-type” limits.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, make a 5×4 grid, mark forced pairings and forbidden countries, tally each country’s required headcount, and verify every candidate statement fits all rows and column counts.
Use when: Relevant in multi-person, multi-destination logic problems with exact visit counts, together/apart rules, and regional membership restrictions.
Boundary: Ignore when choices can be tested directly without global consistency, or when quantities/links are uncertain or not fixed.

Transfer rule: If a sample comes from current members of a role or group, then test for attrition or survivor bias before treating its rate as representative.
Error pattern: I favored an irrelevant fact about group size instead of checking whether the sample was systematically filtered by outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Would people who develop the measured condition be less likely to remain in this sample?” If yes, observed prevalence may be understated.
Use when: Relevant for surveys of employees, participants, patients, or members where the condition could cause quitting, exclusion, or nonresponse.
Boundary: Ignore when membership is unaffected by the condition or when the sample includes former members and dropouts.

Transfer rule: If a definition targets troubles in using or trying to use a product, then exclude outcomes that are only emotional reactions or social judgments after purchase.
Error pattern: Distinguishing functional/usage friction from subjective disappointment or embarrassment.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does the problem arise from operation, preparation, maintenance, access, or time/effort in consumption? If not, reject it.
Use when: Relevant in definition-matching questions contrasting practical inconvenience with feelings, opinions, or identity-related reactions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes satisfaction, reputation, aesthetics, or psychological experience as part of the consumption issue.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses analogy to compare media, then identify the shared mechanism and map it to the author’s main claim.
Error pattern: Success came from following the analogy’s function rather than getting distracted by side comparisons or descriptive details.
Diagnostic check: State in one sentence what the compared example demonstrates, then verify that your choice expresses that same abstract point.
Use when: Apply this on inference or main-point questions built around analogies, metaphors, or illustrative comparisons between forms or media.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific fact, definition, or detail explicitly stated rather than an illustrated takeaway.

Transfer rule: If a cost question asks about administrative spending, then first verify the actor is a government/public agency and the activity is public management or public service.  
Error pattern: Success comes from classifying by institutional role and function, not by whether the action sounds efficient, helpful, or service-oriented.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Who pays? Is it a state body? Is the spending tied to governance/public service rather than ordinary market operations?  
Use when: Relevant in public-finance, administration, or public-service questions mixing government bodies with businesses or quasi-public entities.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the term is explicitly broadened to include private-sector operating costs or when ownership/control is redefined.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires independently generating a new mental image for a preset purpose, then choose the case that invents rather than reconstructs from memory or description.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating original creation from recall, passive evocation, or image-building strictly guided by another person’s account.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the image mainly copied from memory/external description, or newly composed beyond given input? Reject if it depends on a source template.
Use when: Apply to items contrasting imagination types, especially where options mix remembering, following descriptions, immersive listening, and novel production.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is about accuracy of representation, emotion, or spontaneity without a prior purpose.

Transfer rule: If harm is caused by state personnel using official resources while performing or extending an official task, then test for administrative compensation first.  
Error pattern: Success came from separating job-related state action from personal retaliation, lawful enforcement, and disputes over protected illegal interests.  
Diagnostic check: Ask three yes/no questions: actor tied to an agency? conduct connected to duty/tools of office? alleged loss from unlawful state action rather than lawful control?  
Use when: Claims involve government staff, police, regulators, seizures, license actions, vehicles, or other mixed official/private conduct.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the issue is criminal liability, civil employer liability only, or compensation is barred because the underlying interest lacks legal protection.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “this practice produces a beneficial effect” to “that effect explains why the practice exists,” then flag a consequence-to-motivation flaw.
Error pattern: Confusing functional benefit or outcome with the actual cause, reason, or motive behind adoption.
Diagnostic check: Underline the claimed effect and ask, “Does the evidence show people adopted it because of this, or only that it happens to help?”
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions about customs, policies, norms, or behaviors where survival, efficiency, or other benefits are cited as explanations.
Boundary: Ignore when independent evidence links the agents’ intentions, selection process, or adoption history to that benefit.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines something by necessary conditions and enabling medium, then choose the option matching that dependency, not one that restates loosely or overgeneralizes identity.
Error pattern: I collapsed a “uses X to do Y” relation into “is X,” confusing mechanism with essence.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is this stated as necessary, sufficient, identical, or merely partial in the passage? Reject identity claims unsupported by explicit equivalence.
Use when: Definitions explain a system by components, infrastructure, access conditions, and functions, especially in reading-comprehension paraphrase questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text explicitly gives a synonym, formal redefinition, or says one thing literally is another.

Transfer rule: If a causal claim depends on movement from a stated direction, then test whether any source exists in that direction before accepting the explanation.
Error pattern: I weakened with a merely alternative location instead of attacking a necessary geographic precondition of the proposed cause.
Diagnostic check: List the conclusion’s required conditions; ask, “Must there be an origin site along the claimed route or direction?” If not, the claim collapses.
Use when: An argument explains an object’s presence by transport, migration, flow, or drift from elsewhere using directional or route-based premises.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not rely on a specific source region, path, or directional mechanism.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites correlations tied to one social condition and asks what follows if that condition declines, then pick the outcome that most directly mirrors a cited trend, softened with probabilistic language.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the conclusion’s scope and certainty to the evidence, avoiding extreme or unsupported extrapolations.
Diagnostic check: List each stated effect, ask which answer restates one effect as a likely consequence, and eliminate choices using absolutes or new outcomes.
Use when: A stimulus argues from observed study patterns or associated benefits to a prediction about a decrease or increase.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument provides causal mechanisms supporting broader effects beyond the listed associations.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from better juvenile survival to population increase, then check for downstream factors that can cut reproduction or adult numbers before accepting it.
Error pattern: I focused on reducing the stated predator threat instead of testing whether the final population conclusion is blocked later in the life cycle.
Diagnostic check: Trace the causal chain stage by stage; for each step, ask whether any effect of the same change increases harvest, lowers reproduction, or reduces surviving adults.
Use when: Relevant in ecology, growth, or policy questions that infer total population trends from one improved early-stage survival factor.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about that early-stage survival rate, not about overall population size or future abundance.

Transfer rule: If evidence compares rates of increase across periods, then check whether the conclusion illegitimately claims an absolute decrease or improvement in level.
Error pattern: I accepted a peripheral criticism instead of spotting a mismatch between comparative evidence and a stronger conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the premises and conclusion using symbols like “up less,” “up more,” and “down/fewer now”; if the conclusion is stronger than the premises, reject it.
Use when: Relevant in arguments about trends, percentages, before/after comparisons, or claims that one side caused a better outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises directly measure the same quantity and direction asserted in the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why a specific ability survives after general language loss, then prefer an explanation that posits a separate neural system for that ability.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing a causal mechanism that directly explains the dissociation, not a fact about frequency, effects, or related phenomena.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option explain both the impairment and the preserved behavior by locating them in different processes or brain regions?”
Use when: Relevant in explanation questions about patients, brain damage, selective deficits, or surprising preservation of one behavior despite loss of a broader function.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is about prevalence, benefits, definitions, or when no dissociation between capacities is described.

Transfer rule: If premises chain “result → reason → knowable” and add “knowable not irregular,” then infer results cannot be irregular and reject any option claiming possible irregular results.
Error pattern: Failed to compose all linked conditionals and missed that a possibility claim can be ruled out by a universal implication.
Diagnostic check: Translate each sentence into arrows/sets, take the transitive closure, then test each option for direct contradiction versus mere non-entailment.
Use when: Relevant for quantified verbal-logic items with categories like all/any/some, modal words like may/must, and multi-step property inheritance.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are causal, probabilistic, or defeasible rather than strict universal relations.

Transfer rule: If a choice strengthens or absolutizes a passage’s comparative claim, then reject it as the inaccurate understanding.
Error pattern: Misreading qualified statements about performance or observed advantages as universal, causal, or biological claims.
Diagnostic check: For each option, map every key term to the text and flag any added absolutes like “all,” hidden causes, or stronger scope.
Use when: The passage contrasts groups, mentions advantages in specific skills, and asks which interpretation is inaccurate or unsupported.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for an implied conclusion requiring synthesis beyond direct wording.

Transfer rule: If an argument defends a limit on one principle by comparing it to an accepted limit on a similar principle, then classify it as reasoning by analogy about principle-boundaries.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the argument’s function and structure, not getting distracted by the topic or vivid example.
Diagnostic check: Mark the conclusion, then ask: “Is the support mainly an analogy showing two rights/principles are similarly restricted under harm-risk conditions?”
Use when: The stimulus cites one familiar case to justify restricting another liberty, rule, or doctrine in parallel.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the support is data, a direct application of a rule, or a counterexample to an explanation.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives an average plus a general increasing trend, then infer an existential “at least some cases exceed the average,” not a universal stronger claim.
Error pattern: Success pattern: combining baseline statistics with directional trends to justify a modest supported claim while resisting causal or absolute overreach.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each choice as existential vs universal and weak vs strong; reject any option adding new causes, extremes, or “all/none” language.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen-supported questions using averages, trends over time, and exceptions or mitigating behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus supplies hard totals for every case or when answer choices are direct restatements without quantifier shifts.

Transfer rule: If a flaw question asks “overlooks each possibility EXCEPT,” then eliminate choices that would weaken the argument by adding an overlooked scenario and select the one that instead attacks a premise/evidence link or is irrelevant to the oversight.
Error pattern: Confusing a true overlooked alternative with the non-overlooked option in an EXCEPT-format flaw question.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “If added, does this create a missing possibility the argument should have considered?” If yes, eliminate it; keep the one that does not.
Use when: Arguments draw a conclusion from competing interpretations of a trait, especially in LSAT flaw questions with EXCEPT wording.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is strengthen/weaken without EXCEPT, or when choices are direct factual contradictions rather than possible overlooked scenarios.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires top members leaving and the group’s average quality dropping, then choose the case showing departure-caused decline, not mere expansion or outside competition.
Error pattern: Confused a decrease from adding lower-quality members with a decrease from losing higher-value members.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list three boxes—same-purpose group, high-value members exit, remaining group’s overall level worsens—and reject any option missing one box.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about group averages, member turnover, and causal effects on collective quality.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns growth dilution, external market effects, or individual loss without evidence of group-average decline.

Transfer rule: If color constraints apply to every three consecutive finishers, then map positions first and test each answer by assigning the listed athletes that color and checking every adjacent triple.
Error pattern: I jumped from pair plausibility to a conclusion without exhaustively propagating the sliding-window constraint with the fixed order facts.
Diagnostic check: Build positions 1–7, place the fixed athlete and before/after relations, mark how many are before the referenced runner, then scan triples 1–3, 2–4, 3–5, 4–6, 5–7 for any all-same forbidden pattern.
Use when: Ordering puzzles combine partial rankings with repeated local constraints on consecutive positions and ask which group cannot share a property.
Boundary: Ignore when constraints are global counts only or do not depend on adjacency/order.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists two parallel pressures on one group, then choose the option that captures the combined predicament at the same abstraction level.
Error pattern: Success came from synthesizing multiple constraints into one overarching issue instead of chasing a single cause or policy response.
Diagnostic check: Underline each distinct obstacle, ask “who is affected?” and “is the author describing a problem, urging action, or predicting adaptation?”.
Use when: The stem asks what the text is intended to illustrate, and the passage emphasizes worsening conditions plus weakened motivation or feasibility.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage clearly argues for a remedy, evaluates one factor only, or gives evidence for a broader social policy claim.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a claim plus several mechanisms, then choose the option naming the main recommended action/outcome, not the supporting causal explanation.
Error pattern: I centered the biological mechanism and overgeneralized it as the thesis, instead of identifying the passage’s practical focus.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state in one sentence “The author mainly wants to say that ___”; verify it includes the subject repeatedly emphasized and the measurable effect.
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions where examples, statistics, and mechanisms are used to support a broader behavioral or policy point.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the underlying reason, mechanism, or strongest support rather than the passage’s central message.

Transfer rule: If a claim about the case is compared with a modern or familiar pattern to support a later claim, then treat that case-claim as the basis of an analogy, not the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Success came from separating intermediate evidence from the final inference and spotting analogy structure.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as observation, inferred case-claim, comparison premise, or final conclusion; ask which statement the comparison uses as its shared feature.
Use when: Relevant in argument-role questions with evidence from tracks, behavior, or science that invokes an animal or real-world comparison.
Boundary: Ignore when no cross-case comparison is doing support work or when the target statement is itself the stated endpoint.

Transfer rule: If asked which option is not logical reasoning by a definition of “deriving a new proposition from known propositions,” then choose the one whose conclusion is not inferable from the stated premises at all, not merely false or unsound.
Error pattern: I treated an invalid or paradoxical argument as “not reasoning,” instead of separating bad reasoning from absence of derivation.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could the conclusion be generated using only the given statements, with no extra world knowledge or hidden causal assumption?”
Use when: The task is definitional classification of reasoning, especially when some choices are valid, some invalid, and one imports unstated assumptions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks which conclusion is true, valid, strongest, or factually correct rather than whether it qualifies as reasoning.

Transfer rule: If a passage attacks something as only apparently rational yet practically powerful, then choose the option matching both the anti-rational claim and the effectiveness claim.
Error pattern: Success came from integrating the author’s two-part stance instead of grabbing only the positive or only the negative wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s evaluative claims, mark each as positive or negative, and eliminate choices that preserve only one side.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/support questions where the stimulus contrasts surface credibility with underlying irrationality or manipulation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for a weaken, resolve, or purely descriptive inference without evaluative contrast.

Transfer rule: If a story shows learned helplessness from past barriers, then choose the theme urging updated thinking after conditions change.
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting the behavioral mechanism before matching it to a broader moral.
Diagnostic check: Identify the obstacle, note whether it later disappears or becomes irrelevant, then ask which option addresses adapting behavior rather than praising endurance or unrelated social claims.
Use when: Apply to animal fables, parables, or analogy questions that map repeated failure into a life lesson.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives direct factual conclusions, stable obstacles, or evidence for a specific non-metaphorical claim.

Transfer rule: If one category stays innovative despite a conservative sponsor, then look for a plausible route to create outside that sponsor.
Error pattern: Success came from finding an alternative-resource explanation that breaks the sponsor’s control differently across the two groups.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What extra funding, lower cost, or easier access lets one group work independently more often than the other?”
Use when: Relevant in contrast questions about two fields under the same institution but showing different outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the gap is directly explained by different rules, skills, demand, or evidence not involving independence from sponsorship.

Transfer rule: If asked which statement does not weaken, then separate attacks on necessity/causation from claims adding other necessary conditions.
Error pattern: I treated an alternative route to the same intermediate outcome as harmless, but it can undercut the claimed necessity of the stated condition.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If this statement were true, could the conclusion still say this factor is essential?” If it supplies another way or denies the goal/link, it weakens.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken items where the argument says a factor is required because it enables some needed governmental outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only that the factor helps, contributes, or is insufficient by itself.

Transfer rule: If a verbal-logic item feels inconsistent, then re-read the stem and match each choice to the required direction before choosing.  
Error pattern: I misread the task’s polarity and jumped to the strongest contradiction instead of checking whether the prompt wanted support or attack.  
Diagnostic check: Mark each option S, W, or N relative to the claim; only keep choices whose label matches the stem’s instruction.  
Use when: Arguments use cue words like because, natural, safe, most, some, or not all, and options differ by quantifier strength.  
Boundary: Ignore when the question is pure fact recall or when every option clearly points in the same argumentative direction.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists ways a supposedly protected thing can still fail, then choose the broad vulnerability claim those examples support.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: moving from specific mechanisms and examples to the paragraph’s main generalized conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the topic in one phrase, list each cited danger, and verify one option covers all of them without adding a narrower side point.
Use when: Relevant for main-point questions where the text contrasts expected safety or strength with exceptions, failure modes, or damaging consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, cause comparison, definition, or when an option summarizes only one example.

Transfer rule: If a passage compares dates across sites and says one local find is roughly contemporaneous with the earliest known elsewhere, then infer “among the earliest,” not “the earliest” or broader civilizational claims.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the weakest justified comparative claim and rejecting overgeneralization from pottery origins to all culture or civilization.
Diagnostic check: Underline every time marker and comparison; ask whether the text supports equality, precedence, or only approximate contemporaneity, then match the option’s strength to that support.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions with chronology, archaeological discovery, cross-regional comparison, and tempting absolute wording.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives direct causal proof, explicit uniqueness, or the question asks for main idea rather than safest inference.

Transfer rule: If a passage mainly lists risks, safeguards, and calls for discussion, then choose the option emphasizing attention to negative effects, not a balanced "pros and cons" summary.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a brief mention of benefits into a two-sided thesis instead of tracking where the text’s emphasis actually stayed.
Diagnostic check: Count concrete sentences about harms, security, regulation, or warnings versus concrete support for benefits; if one side dominates, match that focus.
Use when: The prompt asks for the main idea and the passage contains rhetorical questions, cautionary language, and policy or safety recommendations about new technology.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text explicitly develops both advantages and disadvantages in comparable detail.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires inhibited helping due to others’ presence, then choose the case where witnesses reduce personal responsibility for acting.
Error pattern: I matched any failure to help, ignoring the mechanism that inaction must be caused specifically by diffusion of responsibility.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Are other people present, and is the person withholding help because they assume someone else will handle it?”
Use when: Apply this to social-psychology items distinguishing crowd-caused inaction from fear, inability, role limits, or active helping.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when no bystanders are present or when nonintervention is driven by danger, rules, selfish motives, or uncertainty alone.

Transfer rule: If an argument gives reasons and then a “so/as a result” claim, then choose the claim those reasons support, not a side remark.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the main conclusion from premises and from an additional opinion offered after the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as premise, intermediate claim, main conclusion, or aside; then ask which claim all other claims are trying to justify.
Use when: Apply this on conclusion-identification questions with causal support, policy claims, and extra commentary before or after the core argument.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for an assumption, inference, or principle rather than the author’s main conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “some A are B” to “A are C,” then test choices for exact term/quantifier alignment before treating a seeming contradiction as decisive.
Error pattern: I overvalued a strong-sounding negation and failed to verify whether the option actually targets the claim using the same category scope and wording.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite premise and conclusion as quantifiers; underline every class term, and reject any option that changes a term, shifts from whole-class to instance claims, or leaves the inference gap untouched.
Use when: Relevant in categorical-logic items with “some/all/no,” subset language, and answers that look refutational because they sound opposite.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is factual-domain knowledge, causal explanation, or the credited answer depends on definitions supplied outside the quantifier structure.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers one treatment is better from a single side-by-side result, then check that the compared items started equivalently and differed only in that treatment.
Error pattern: Causal comparison succeeds only when baseline conditions are controlled; otherwise it confuses preexisting differences with treatment effects.
Diagnostic check: List all relevant starting factors, ask “Were they matched or randomized?”, and negate any needed match; if the conclusion could fail, that match is an assumption.
Use when: Relevant for ads, experiments, product tests, or before/after comparisons based on one or few examples.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus already states proper randomization, equal baselines, or asks about a different flaw type.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers improvement from a lower rank, then ask whether the underlying measure itself changed rather than only the item's position relative to others.
Error pattern: Treating comparative or ordinal movement as proof of absolute change in the target condition.
Diagnostic check: Replace the claim with a scenario where all peers changed more; if the conclusion still follows, the reasoning is invalid.
Use when: Rankings, standings, percentile positions, or “most/least” labels are used to support claims about better or worse real-world status.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument also provides direct before-and-after measurements on the same scale for the item.

Transfer rule: If asked for the statement NOT supporting an action, then test each option for support and choose the one that weakens, limits, or redirects the action’s rationale.
Error pattern: Mistaking a generally positive or moral-sounding statement for the exception instead of checking whether it actually supports the specific practice.
Diagnostic check: For each option, complete “This supports the action because ___”; if the blank cannot be filled without changing the claim, mark it as the exception.
Use when: Relevant in “except/not supported” multiple-choice questions where several choices sound favorable but only one is misaligned with the stated goal.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for the best support, a direct inference, or factual recall rather than identifying a non-supporting statement.

Transfer rule: If an argument says “if X, then chain to unacceptable Y” and “Y must not happen,” then infer rejection/prevention of X, not a downstream certainty.
Error pattern: Mistaking a speculative causal chain with “may” for a definite effect, instead of using the stated prohibition to infer policy intent.
Diagnostic check: Mark each link as certain or possible; if any later link is only possible, do not conclude it must occur; instead ask what must be blocked to avoid the forbidden endpoint.
Use when: Multi-step policy, economics, or logic passages connect an initial condition to a prohibited outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the text denies control over the initial condition or gives alternative ways to avoid the endpoint.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a proposal is bad because it will create downstream capacity strain, then look for a fact showing the proposal may prevent the triggering events instead of increasing them.
Error pattern: Success comes from attacking the causal link between the action and the predicted burden, not from discussing side costs or partial process leakage.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this choice reduce, block, or reverse the assumed increase in cases, rather than merely describing what happens after cases occur?”
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions built on forecasts about increased workload, chain effects, or resource shortages caused by a proposed change.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion depends on morality, legality, definitions, or a direct budget shortfall unrelated to the predicted causal chain.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined as a coordinated agreement among peer firms on market, output, price, or technology, then exclude choices centered on ownership takeover or merger control.
Error pattern: Success came from separating alliance-by-contract from consolidation-by-acquisition instead of matching on superficial same-industry wording.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: "Are independent firms still separate and merely agreeing on competitive terms?" If no, reject it as outside the concept.
Use when: Apply this to definition questions about market structures, collusion, alliances, or other organization forms with explicit required features.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept itself includes mergers, equity control, or hierarchical integration as defining features.

Transfer rule: If a passage links a trait to a firm's long-term survival or elimination, then choose the option about enterprise sustainability, not the broader system.
Error pattern: I matched vivid background framing to the main point and overgeneralized from market-level context instead of the conclusion's target.
Diagnostic check: Identify the final claim's subject and predicate; ask, “Who is being evaluated, and what outcome is said to depend on what?”
Use when: The stimulus gives contextual premises about society, law, or systems, then ends with a claim about what enterprises need to persist.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion explicitly evaluates the economic system itself or asks for a legal-purpose interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a change leaves unit price and unit margin unchanged, then look for an option that increases sales volume or lowers other business-wide costs.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracing the missing profit driver; failure comes from choosing facts that merely justify the change or show it is harmless.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “With per-unit profit fixed, does this fact create more buyers, more units sold, or lower non-unit costs?”
Use when: Apply on strengthen/explain questions featuring an apparent profit increase despite no change in sticker price, direct cost, or per-sale profit.
Boundary: Ignore when options already alter margin, demand is irrelevant, or the question asks about feasibility, necessity, or consumer preference alone.

Transfer rule: If asked which fact should not challenge a causal conjecture, then prefer information that is a side effect consistent with the proposed mechanism, not evidence adding costs or alternative causes.
Error pattern: I treated a new downside as irrelevant instead of recognizing it weakens a “net benefit/compensation” claim.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it introduce an alternative explanation, undermine a link, or reduce the claimed payoff? If yes, it challenges; if it merely co-occurs without touching those, it does not.
Use when: Applying this is useful on strengthen/weaken/except questions about behavioral changes explained as adaptive compensation.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is only descriptive, not causal or net-benefit based.

Transfer rule: If a premise says one factor is necessary but not sufficient, then infer only limits on sufficiency, not comparative importance or guarantees.
Error pattern: Mistook “many other causes belong to X” for “X is more important,” adding a ranking not supported by the statements.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each factor as necessary, sufficient, both, or neither, and reject any option asserting priority, certainty, or hidden correlations.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic items about outcomes caused by multiple traits, especially with words like “cannot,” “may not,” and “most other factors.”
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly gives a comparison, causal weight, or statistical dominance between factors.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers an individual health recommendation from population-level correlation, then prefer evidence about individuals that breaks the intake-outcome link within the same population.
Error pattern: Mistaking a possible national-level confounder for the strongest attack when the core flaw is an ecological leap from group averages to individual causation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If low-exposure individuals inside high-exposure groups still show the group’s outcome rate, would the recommendation fail?” If yes, favor that evidence.
Use when: The stimulus moves from cross-group averages or national statistics to advice about what a person should do.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about groups, or when individual-level causal evidence is already provided.

Transfer rule: If a recommendation shifts a gatekeeping task to a different group, then check whether the argument assumes that group can reliably perform the task.  
Error pattern: Success comes from spotting a hidden capability assumption required for the proposed solution to work.  
Diagnostic check: Remove the assumption “the substitute group can make the needed judgments”; if the recommendation no longer supports its goal, that assumption is necessary.  
Use when: A stimulus argues that one role should take over screening, triage, evaluation, or selection because experts are overloaded.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument already provides evidence of competence or when the conclusion is only descriptive, not prescriptive.

Transfer rule: If a proposed explanation merely restates the observed effect as its own cause, then reject it as circular and seek an independent mechanism.
Error pattern: Mistaking the phenomenon to be explained for an explanatory reason instead of providing a separate causal account.
Diagnostic check: Remove the “because” clause; if what remains is essentially the same claim in different words, the explanation is circular.
Use when: An argument explains a behavior, trait, or outcome by citing preference, tendency, or benefit that just paraphrases the original observation.
Boundary: Ignore when the cited factor is independently supported and predicts new evidence beyond the original phenomenon.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites a disputed observation, then ask whether it is the author’s conclusion or the phenomenon a rival view is offered to explain.
Error pattern: Success pattern: separating the target claim, the rival explanation, and the author’s rebuttal instead of treating every early statement as the main conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as observation, rival view, or author inference; if a clause says “some say/because,” link it to what that view explains.
Use when: Role-in-argument questions feature an initial fact, an attributed explanation, and a later “however/therefore” rebuttal.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement is directly supported by later premises as the author’s own conclusion rather than a phenomenon under debate.

Transfer rule: If a schedule argument concludes exact days from weekly totals, then test what unstated non-overlap or overlap rule is required to force those placements.
Error pattern: I ignored a hidden exclusivity assumption and chose an irrelevant coexistence fact instead of the condition needed to make the count-based inference work.
Diagnostic check: Write each activity on a 7-day grid, mark all fixed-day events, then ask, “If a fixed-day event could coincide with the counted activity, would the conclusion still be forced?”
Use when: Apply this to logic questions about weekly schedules, frequencies, and conclusions naming specific days from totals plus one or two fixed-day constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument does not infer exact placements from counts, or when overlap rules are explicitly stated rather than assumed.

Transfer rule: If an argument-structure question starts with a broad claim, then test whether that opening is the main conclusion before classifying later statements.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating conclusion-first structure from premise-first structure and spotting a two-option contrast used to justify a stronger overall claim.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as conclusion, premise, example, or contrast; then ask whether the final comparison excludes other alternatives and props up the main claim.
Use when: Relevant for stimulus questions about how an argument proceeds, especially with an opening thesis, supporting reasons, and a final either-or comparison.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is about flaw identification alone or when the opening statement is clearly background, not an asserted conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a new mechanism and then gives its scope, then match the option that restates that stated scope exactly, not an unstated comparison.
Error pattern: Chose an answer by importing an unsupported inference about older methods instead of using the explicitly described target range.
Diagnostic check: For each option, underline the exact sentence support; reject any choice needing assumptions about other drugs, causes, or effects not directly mentioned.
Use when: Relevant in passage-based multiple-choice items contrasting a new treatment with existing ones and describing mechanism, coverage, safety, or resistance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question requires outside domain knowledge, numerical calculation, or evaluating claims beyond the passage.

Transfer rule: If asked for the subject matter of litigation, then select the disputed civil legal relationship or right, not the item, amount, event detail, or criminal-law relation.
Error pattern: I confused the object/facts of the dispute with the underlying legal relation/right the court is asked to adjudicate.
Diagnostic check: Rephrase each option as “What legal relation or right exists between the parties?”; reject any option that is only property quantity, conduct description, or prosecution/offense status.
Use when: This applies to civil-procedure or legal-definition questions distinguishing claims, rights, relationships, facts, and remedies.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for the disputed object, amount in controversy, cause of action label, evidence, or criminal legal relations.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts fallback methods with one enduring approach and says others never escape subordinate status, then choose the option naming the primary approach.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a vivid side remark about rivalry instead of the author’s hierarchy and main emphasis.
Diagnostic check: Ask: which claim could stand as the paragraph’s thesis if examples and colorful metaphors were removed?
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where the text mentions alternatives, exceptions, or temporary revivals but signals one method as dominant.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a local detail, causal relation, or the metaphor itself rather than the overall emphasis.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a decision is “economic, not safety-based,” then test whether the cited costs are created by safety requirements themselves.
Error pattern: I treated a dispute about causes versus public meaning as the flaw, instead of checking whether the supposed alternative cause already embeds the first cause.
Diagnostic check: List each stated cost driver; mark any that arise from precautions, inspections, compliance, or maintenance, and ask whether calling them “purely economic” is double-counting away safety.
Use when: Relevant in arguments contrasting economic motives with safety motives, especially when expenses come from protective measures.
Boundary: Ignore when the costs discussed are independent of safety or regulation.

Transfer rule: If a choice shifts a statement’s key term between two senses within one exchange, then flag it as disguised displacement.  
Error pattern: I favored surface renaming or wordplay instead of checking whether one concept was silently replaced by another in the same reasoning.  
Diagnostic check: Underline the pivotal term, restate each speaker’s meaning in plain words, and test whether the reply answers the original meaning or a substituted one.  
Use when: Apply this on verbal-reasoning items involving dialogue, puns, ambiguous predicates, or rebuttals that seem clever but off-target.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is only decorative wording, metaphor, or relabeling without an actual argumentative shift in meaning.

Transfer rule: If two parties owe due obligations to each other from linked dealings with no agreed performance order, then treat refusal until the other performs as simultaneous-defense.
Error pattern: Confusing a broad cooperative relationship or contract setting with the stricter requirement of mutual, due, reciprocal debts between the same parties.
Diagnostic check: Verify four boxes: both sides owe something, both duties are already due, no priority of performance is set, and the refusal targets the counterpart’s corresponding demand.
Use when: The facts describe each side demanding performance while withholding its own in an exchange-like or paired obligation context.
Boundary: Ignore this when duties are one-sided, not yet due, performance order is specified, or the obligations are unrelated.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a specific migration route from timing plus limited present-day distribution, then look for evidence of a nearer ancestral source or alternative path.
Error pattern: Success pattern: weakened a necessity claim by attacking the “must have come from there” step, not by noting irrelevant differences or unrelated species.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What fact would show these organisms could have existed closer by earlier, making the proposed origin unnecessary?” Prefer that over facts merely showing change.
Use when: Relevant in origin, dispersal, ancestry, or biogeography arguments that move from geography and chronology to a single required explanation.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only possibility/probability, or when new evidence does not provide a genuine alternative source or route.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for empathy, then choose the response that explicitly reflects and checks the other person’s felt experience without judging, fixing, or reassuring.
Error pattern: Confusing empathy with problem-solving or encouragement; selecting action-oriented help instead of accurate emotional attunement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this statement name or verify the person’s likely emotion or perspective, rather than offer advice, approval, or comfort?”
Use when: Relevant for items contrasting reflective listening with helping, minimizing, moral evaluation, or persuasion in interpersonal communication.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target skill is intervention, instruction, validation of behavior, or practical assistance rather than empathic understanding.

Transfer rule: If items are compared on two ordered dimensions and no item may weakly exceed another in both, then model each item as a rank pair and require every pair to trade off.
Error pattern: I overcounted by treating dimensions too independently and missed that an antichain in a small product order has a tight maximum.
Diagnostic check: List all possible ordered pairs, group them by equal total rank, and verify only one same-sum layer can be pairwise incomparable; count that layer.
Use when: Use for dominance, Pareto, “none is better than another,” or maximum mutually non-comparable arrangements on small discrete grids.
Boundary: Ignore when comparison is not coordinatewise ordered, ties/duplicates are allowed differently, or dimensions are not finite ordinal categories.

Transfer rule: If a passage explains why a method defeats concealment and highlights precision or anti-shielding, then choose the option matching that direct claim, not one extending it to coverage or range.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from stronger technical performance to an unsupported broader capability.
Diagnostic check: For each option, underline the exact sentence support; reject any choice requiring an extra step such as “therefore wider area,” “faster,” or “more complete.”
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items that compare technologies and list several attractive paraphrases of stated advantages.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly states the broader consequence or when the question asks for an inference rather than a directly supported statement.

Transfer rule: If a passage attacks evidence as non-discriminating and says a conclusion is risky because it relies on that evidence, then classify it as questioning an assumption the other argument needs.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the argument’s target as an underlying link between evidence and conclusion, not the conclusion’s truth directly.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What must be true for the original evidence to support the claim?” Then see whether the passage argues that this support-link is unreliable.
Use when: Relevant in method-of-reasoning questions featuring criticism of another view, especially where common features could arise from background conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage mainly contrasts premises, gives supporting examples, or traces consequences of a general principle.

Transfer rule: If a plan relies on making service intentionally worse to protect a premium tier, then test whether the plan assumes no backlash that undermines demand.  
Error pattern: I focused on a profit comparison outside the plan instead of a necessary condition about customer reaction to the proposed action.  
Diagnostic check: Negate each candidate assumption; if the plan would likely fail because customers avoid or resent the firm, treat that assumption as required.  
Use when: The argument proposes a strategy change, especially deliberate degradation, delay, restriction, or inconvenience to influence customer choices.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument is only forecasting outcomes from external conditions, not defending a company-controlled action.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts two valuation rules and tracks who captures the gap, then infer claims about that gap’s recipient, not broad institutional restraints.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a specific incentive/accounting comparison to a stronger policy conclusion about limiting abuse.
Diagnostic check: List each rule, compute the difference conceptually, and mark who receives that difference in each scenario; only choose options matching that mapping.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions about compensation, expropriation, pricing standards, or distribution of surplus between owners, state, public, and developers.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage gives explicit causal evidence about deterrence, legality, or abuse prevention beyond allocation facts.

Transfer rule: If low observed harm follows widespread preventive action, then test whether the prevention itself could explain the low harm before inferring exaggeration or bad motive.
Error pattern: Ignoring a plausible preventive cause and treating weak outcomes as proof the threat was unreal or the warning insincere.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What interventions occurred after the warning, and would expected damage be much higher without them?”
Use when: An argument compares alarming predictions with mild results after many people adopted protections, safeguards, or treatments.
Boundary: Ignore when no meaningful preventive action happened or when evidence already isolates outcomes from any intervention effects.

Transfer rule: If a benefit is asked to be inside a formal security system, then require it to be law-based, institutional, and funded/organized through public redistribution rather than ad hoc charity.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating statutory social insurance/assistance from temporary humanitarian relief by private or voluntary organizations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option for three traits: legal entitlement, stable government/social-insurance administration, and ongoing income-redistribution funding.
Use when: Apply this to questions contrasting public welfare programs with donations, emergency relief, or nonprofit aid.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question explicitly includes nongovernmental charity or only asks about broad social support in general.

Transfer rule: If a passage repeats inward, mindset-based imperatives across activities, then infer a theme about internal attitude rather than social defiance or broad life advice.
Error pattern: Mistaking a reflective, mental-state summary for a rebellious independence slogan because both mention ignoring others.
Diagnostic check: List each instruction’s target; if most target motives, attention, forgiveness, or perception, choose the option that abstracts a mental stance across them.
Use when: The text is aphoristic, uses parallel commands, and contrasts doing or living with thoughts about reward, audience, resentment, or outlook.
Boundary: Ignore this when the options hinge on concrete actions, external constraints, or explicit claims not reducible to a shared inner attitude.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires occupation choice or retraining in response to social needs, then pick the case linking skill acquisition to labor-market demand and actual occupational entry/change.
Error pattern: I overweighted personal interest and training alone, while ignoring the required social-demand trigger and formal move into an occupation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the case shows all three: external social need, systematic learning/certification or retraining, and engagement in the occupation afterward.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching items about vocational socialization, career selection, professional training, or reskilling.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept does not require social demand or actual occupational transition/practice.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a hidden behavior from ticketed-or-observed cases, then require an assumption linking being observed to actually doing that behavior more often.
Error pattern: Strength is spotting when evidence is about enforcement outcomes but conclusion is about underlying frequency; the needed bridge is often unstated.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the observed subgroup be overrepresented for reasons unrelated to true rate?” If yes, look for an assumption tying observation to regular behavior.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions comparing a small subgroup’s share in the population versus its share among caught, measured, or reported cases.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about getting caught, detection rates, or reporting rates, not about underlying conduct.

Transfer rule: If a measure creates a new body to fix redundancy, then test whether it worsens the original issue before inferring commitment or effectiveness.
Error pattern: Mistaking stated intention and visible action for real problem-solving, while ignoring structural side effects and self-contradiction.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this step remove, merge, or reduce overlapping entities, or does it add another layer? Choose based on net structure change.
Use when: Relevant for policy, management, or organizational-design questions where a reform is proposed to solve duplication, bloat, or inefficiency.
Boundary: Ignore when the new unit is explicitly temporary, replaces old units, or comes with actual elimination/merger evidence.

Transfer rule: If a definition stresses structured control for accomplishing performance goals, then choose the option showing leaders pushing completion through demands, supervision, or pressure on task execution.
Error pattern: I overmatched “hands-off delegation” to task focus and ignored whether the leader actively monitors and enforces performance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the behavior includes clear task emphasis plus active control tools (oversight, deadlines, rewards, punishment, pressure); reject options missing active control.
Use when: Apply this on leadership-style items contrasting production/task orientation with relationship concern, favoritism, or laissez-faire delegation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is empowerment, autonomy, trust-based delegation, or people-centered support rather than performance enforcement.

Transfer rule: If a claim links a property to a judgment, then assume the link holds universally and test it on an accepted comparison case.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a true reductio: accept the opponent’s premise temporarily and derive an implausible consequence without changing the premise.
Diagnostic check: Restate the argument as “If X has feature F, then X has status G”; substitute a familiar Y with F; ask whether Y absurdly gets G.
Use when: The prompt asks for reduction to absurdity, indirect refutation, or challenging a general principle by extension.
Boundary: Ignore when the response merely gives a counterexample, denies a premise directly, or changes definitions mid-argument.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by stating what one group “must pay attention to,” then choose the option capturing that broader takeaway, not an earlier supporting example.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward tracking the author’s final evaluative claim and how examples build to it.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 7–12 word paraphrase of the last sentence; reject any option that only restates setup details or overfocuses on a side caveat.
Use when: The passage contrasts groups, gives evidence first, and closes with a consequence, implication, or required response.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, attitude, purpose, or when the conclusion is stated at the beginning instead of the end.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion claims “no health hazard” from data on only one outcome, then test whether harmful effects could appear in unmeasured outcomes.
Error pattern: Mistaking an unchanged proxy measure for proof that the broader target phenomenon is absent.
Diagnostic check: List the study’s measured variable and the conclusion’s full scope; ask, “Could the scope include harms not captured by this variable?”
Use when: An argument infers overall safety, effectiveness, or harmlessness from comparisons involving a single indicator such as deaths, crashes, or complaints.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is explicitly limited to that same indicator or when evidence covers all relevant harm categories.

Transfer rule: If a statement uses “only by/only if P, Q,” then translate it as Q → P and use its contrapositive ¬P → ¬Q.
Error pattern: I treated a necessary condition as a sufficient one by reading the sentence in the forward direction.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim with arrows, then test each choice against the original conditional and its contrapositive only.
Use when: Relevant for exclusives like “only if,” “only by,” “only when,” especially in inference questions about conditionals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sentence is causal, biconditional, or explicitly adds a separate sufficient-condition marker like “as long as” or “if.”

Transfer rule: If a rule bans something only within a named jurisdiction, then verify the subject is actually within that jurisdiction before applying the ban.
Error pattern: I focused on category labels and ignored a needed scope/link assumption connecting the person or case to the rule’s domain.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “What fact must place this person, object, or event under the authority of the stated rule?”
Use when: Arguments move from a general law, policy, code, or definition to a conclusion about a specific case.
Boundary: Ignore when the case is already explicitly stated to fall under that authority or the issue is purely definitional, not jurisdictional.

Transfer rule: If a change applies labor that physically transforms or customizes an existing good, then treat it as increasing added value.  
Error pattern: Success comes from separating production-created value from value due only to pricing, branding, scarcity, or resale conditions.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “After the action, is the item itself altered by work so a buyer gets a newly created feature independent of market circumstances?”  
Use when: Relevant for questions contrasting manufacturing, processing, customization, packaging, marketing, signatures, or opportunistic selling.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when value is defined by exchange price, legal rights, rarity, or pure service experience rather than product production.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts audience behavior from the quality of current live performers, then check whether audience appreciation mainly comes from a different source.  
Error pattern: I weakened a subsidiary link but ignored a stronger attack on the argument’s dependence on one causal pathway.  
Diagnostic check: Map the chain, mark each necessary link, and ask for each: “Could the conclusion still hold if this link were bypassed?”  
Use when: The stimulus argues that declining participant quality will reduce popularity because audiences learn value through direct exposure or performance.  
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not rely on audience formation through that channel or when alternatives are already ruled out.

Transfer rule: If premises establish that only some members of a category have a helpful property, then do not conclude that every member of that category has it.  
Error pattern: Illicit generalization from a subset to the entire class.  
Diagnostic check: Mark the quantifiers; compare “some/at least one” in the evidence with “all/any/every” in the conclusion, and reject if scope expands without support.  
Use when: A stimulus links a beneficial trait to certain items, then shifts to a broad claim about all items of that type or all choices involving them.  
Boundary: Ignore when an added premise guarantees uniformity across the whole category or the conclusion stays limited to the supported subset.

Transfer rule: If a choice seems worse on one stated metric, then look for a baseline replacement effect that makes total real-world impact lower.
Error pattern: Success comes from comparing net system outcomes, not isolated direct emissions of the new option.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What existing process or facility would this option displace, and does the combined before-vs-after pollution decrease?”
Use when: A support/justify question presents an apparently environmentally worse option backed by environmental advocates or other outcome-focused groups.
Boundary: Ignore when no displacement, substitution, or total-impact comparison is relevant, and the decision is purely between standalone alternatives.
