Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the evidence directly demonstrates reversal, eradication, or long-term absence of the condition itself.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts current protection with future integration, then choose the option capturing the full transition and overarching task, not a single outcome.
Error pattern: I fixated on the concluding effect statement and mistook a downstream role/result for the passage’s central thesis.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each paragraph in 8–12 words, then pick the option matching all major parts: present problem, future context, and proposed direction.
Use when: The text has both urgency and future planning, with causal links and a final sentence that sounds emphatic.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, or author attitude rather than the main idea.

Transfer rule: If an argument contrasts mechanical rule-following with human inner experience, then choose the option restating the core limit, not a broader value judgment.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from examples about superiority/comparability and missed the author’s central claim about what cannot be captured.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the thesis in 8–12 words; verify the option matches that wording and not merely a consequence or contrast.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items where examples support a main claim about limits, essence, or definition.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an implication, attitude strength, or the best-supported consequence rather than the main view.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires post-service data leakage plus long-term harassment by other organizations, then choose the case containing all those elements, not merely normal follow-up.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definitional condition and rejecting tempting cases that fit only service contact or one-time annoyance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark three boxes: used an intermediary service, information reached unrelated outside parties, repeated unwanted contact continued afterward.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about privacy leakage, third-party solicitation, or downstream harassment after using a service platform.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the follow-up is expected service support, the contact stays within the original provider, or there is no evidence of leaked information.

Transfer rule: If a question asks to reconcile declining use of one medium with rising desire for the underlying goal, then prefer an option showing substitution to another medium that serves the same goal.
Error pattern: I focused on a cause of decline alone, not a bridge that explains both decline and continued enthusiasm.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it account for the drop and preserve or redirect the underlying motivation?
Use when: The stem presents an apparent contradiction between behavior decreasing and interest, demand, or motivation increasing.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is only to explain a decline, not to reconcile two opposing trends.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires evolved high visual resemblance to another organism or the environment that yields protective advantage, then choose the case matching both resemblance and protection.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking every clause of the definition rather than matching any single cue like adaptation, sound imitation, or exploitation.
Diagnostic check: Test three boxes—appearance/form similarity, evolutionary development, and protection for the mimicking organism or both species; reject any option missing one.
Use when: Apply this to biology or concept-definition MCQs about camouflage, resemblance, imitation, adaptation, or protective similarity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept is about behavior, vocal signals, parasitism, or general adaptation without close visual resemblance.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists quotations, then infer the main idea from the shared theme and speaker’s purpose, not from the fact that many quotes appear.
Error pattern: Mistook surface evidence of cultural knowledge for the deeper unifying concern expressed across the selected lines.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each quote in 3–5 words, find the repeated concern, and choose the option matching that concern rather than the rhetorical vehicle.
Use when: The stem asks for the “main embodiment” or central meaning of a quote-filled passage, especially with public figures or value statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets style, memory, source knowledge, or explicit praise of literature/culture itself.

Transfer rule: If a claim uses “only X are Y,” then translate it as “Y implies X,” not “X implies Y.”
Error pattern: Confusing a necessary-condition statement with a sufficient-condition statement by reversing the implication.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the sentence as an arrow or “all Y are X,” then test whether the rebuttal attacks Y→X or the reversed X→Y.
Use when: Relevant for quantified statements with “only,” “all,” “if,” category membership, and counterexamples involving one person or case.
Boundary: Ignore when the wording already states the reverse direction explicitly or the task is about truth from added premises, not interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a social effect and explains step-by-step how it changes responsibility, motivation, guilt, and later behavior, then choose the option about its mechanism, not remedies or background.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the text’s explanatory chain rather than latching onto emotionally charged outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s main verbs; if they mostly explain how one factor leads to another, classify the question as mechanism/causal explanation.
Use when: Apply this on theory-definition passages in psychology or sociology that center on why a behavior occurs.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly proposes interventions, gives historical context, or compares categories without causal links.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a problem with another place and then highlights missing laws/remedies, then choose the option targeting the legal/institutional fix, not a broader comparison.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions are solved by identifying the author’s primary complaint and proposed remedy, not by selecting a merely related social observation.
Diagnostic check: Underline the complaint, cause, and consequence; if two clauses stress lack of regulation/protection and no relief, verify your choice matches that governance focus.
Use when: The text mentions privacy, rights, enforcement, legal gaps, institutions, or inability to seek remedies.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly measures public awareness, behavior, or cross-country differences without linking them to absent legal protection.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a necessary condition with “only by/only if,” then keep it necessary only; do not flip it into a sufficient guarantee.
Error pattern: Treated a prerequisite as enough, and overlooked how chained necessities constrain later outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each claim as arrows; test every choice by contrapositive and by asking whether it adds any new “guarantee” not stated.
Use when: Relevant for verbal-logic items with “only,” “impossible without,” linked conditions, and choices that paraphrase or strengthen them.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on causal evidence, probabilities, or ordinary-language intent rather than strict conditional logic.

Transfer rule: If a statement mixes quantifiers and time words, then translate it into logic first and compare negations before judging what must be false.
Error pattern: I treated a universal claim about one individual as conflicting, instead of checking the stronger contradiction created by negating the existential-over-time content.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “there exists at least one subject and at least one time with property not-P”; then test each choice by asking whether it can still be true in that model.
Use when: Apply for verbal logic items using some, all, not all, any, always, sometimes, and time qualifiers.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on real-world facts, definitions, or causal relations rather than formal quantifier structure.

Transfer rule: If a cited cause is absent in some cases yet the same outcome risk remains, then infer that other factor(s) also affect the outcome.
Error pattern: Good pattern: comparing groups to test whether a proposed factor is necessary or sufficient instead of overreading unsupported comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “If this factor does not occur, does the stated risk change?” If no, mark the factor as not the only determinant.
Use when: Arguments describe one mechanism, then state equal outcomes or equal risks for people lacking that mechanism.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives no cross-group risk comparison or when equal risk is only assumed, not stated.

Transfer rule: If a loss-making mandatory product is still heavily contested, then test whether it serves as a gateway to profitable bundled or follow-on business.
Error pattern: I focused on causes of the losses instead of explaining why firms still rationally compete despite those losses.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it create a profit path, customer-acquisition advantage, or cross-selling benefit that outweighs direct losses?
Use when: A question asks to explain an apparent business paradox where observed competition conflicts with poor standalone financial performance.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is to identify the source of losses, legal compliance motives, or operational inefficiencies rather than competitive incentives.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which principle justifies a reply, then choose the principle that directly bridges that speaker’s stated values to the recommended action.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching each premise in the reply to a normative rule instead of picking a merely attractive or generally plausible value claim.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, paraphrase the reply’s core reason and test whether the principle would make that conclusion follow over the competing concern.
Use when: Apply this on principle-strengthen items featuring a dispute, tradeoff, and a speaker appealing to duty, value ranking, or family obligation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for assumption, flaw, evidence, or when the answer choice only restates facts without supplying a norm.

Transfer rule: If a metaphor in an art theory maps creation to something airborne but tethered, then choose the option preserving innovation while requiring grounding in lived reality.
Error pattern: Success came from extracting the central constraint from the metaphor instead of chasing broader slogans or extreme claims about art’s purpose.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the metaphor into a plain sentence with subject, requirement, and reason; then reject choices adding stronger aims not stated.
Use when: A passage explains a concept through analogy and asks which statement aligns with the author’s view on art and reality.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for criticism, historical facts, or the analogy is only decorative rather than argumentative.

Transfer rule: If the category depends on who decides treatment, then identify the decision-maker first and match willingness separately.
Error pattern: I conflated “others take the patient” with the category, ignoring the distinction between family-decided cooperation and unwilling compelled treatment.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark two tags: decision made by self/others and patient cooperative/unwilling; choose the one with others+cooperative.
Use when: Relevant in definition-matching questions that split cases by authority, consent, and motivation rather than symptom severity.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when options differ by medical urgency, diagnosis, or outcome instead of who made the treatment decision.

Transfer rule: If a statement compares how outliers affect average, median, and mode, then recall that the mean is usually most sensitive, the median less so, and the mode often unchanged.
Error pattern: I accepted a familiar-sounding real-life interpretation instead of checking each claim against the formal properties of the statistics.
Diagnostic check: For any effect-of-extremes claim, test a tiny dataset, then replace one value with an extreme and see which measure changes most.
Use when: This applies to multiple-choice items defining mean, median, and mode or asking about robustness, calculation method, or everyday interpretation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on weighted averages, grouped data conventions, multimodal sets, or domain-specific wording beyond basic definitions.

Transfer rule: If an argument balances individual freedom against fairness and rejects subsidies, then choose the solution that limits excess without banning participation.
Error pattern: Success pattern: integrating all stated constraints and selecting the compromise that resolves both competing principles.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each required condition and verify the choice satisfies all of them while adding no stronger restriction than necessary.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/completion questions presenting a policy dilemma, competing values, and one explicitly ruled-out remedy.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt seeks empirical effects, moral ranking, or a principle that does not require reconciling every stated constraint.

Transfer rule: If an argument credits a policy change for improvement, then test whether the targeted activity was substantial before the policy; if not, the policy likely is not the cause.
Error pattern: Mistaking a surface difference between comparison cases for evidence, instead of checking whether the claimed cause had enough baseline presence to matter.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Before the intervention, was the restricted behavior common enough at the improved case to plausibly drive the original problem?”
Use when: Causal arguments compare two places or times and infer that a ban, rule, or treatment produced the better outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the policy’s mechanism does not depend on prior prevalence of the restricted activity.

Transfer rule: If a definition targets norms that regulate profession-specific relations/behavior, then exclude acts that are mainly ordinary personal ethics or isolated perks unless they govern that professional communication role.
Error pattern: Success came from separating domain-defining ethical standards from conduct merely adjacent to the job.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it state a standard for evaluating and regulating journalism/communication behavior itself, or just mention a personal act/benefit occurring around the work?
Use when: The stem gives a formal definition with functions like evaluation, regulation, and standardization within a profession.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when choices hinge on legality, factual causation, or broad morality rather than scope of a profession-specific ethical concept.

Transfer rule: If a case assigns a trait or behavior to someone mainly from group membership, then classify it as social stereotyping.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definition element and rejecting options that describe personal feelings, adaptation, or broad social change.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is there a group label, a generalized expectation tied to that label, and weak evidence about this individual?”
Use when: Apply this on definition-match questions involving judgments about people, groups, traits, or expected behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement is about an individual’s direct experience, a causal trend, or a fact-based description without group-based generalization.

Transfer rule: If a passage states unity is required for efficient operation, then infer solidarity as a necessary condition for a well-functioning organization.
Error pattern: Valid inference by converting explicit conditional claims into a necessity claim without adding stronger exclusivity or extra consequences.
Diagnostic check: Map statements as conditionals, mark which direction is supported, and reject any choice using “only,” “all,” or new effects not stated.
Use when: Applicable to organizational or causal arguments linking one trait to efficiency, effectiveness, or outcomes through if-then language.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives merely examples, correlations, or reversible definitions rather than directional requirements.

Transfer rule: If a logic question gives statements plus a fixed truth-count, then test each possible case and count true statements before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from exhaustive case analysis instead of assuming uniqueness from wording or from a statement that sounds globally informative.
Diagnostic check: Build a truth table over all candidate culprits, mark each speaker’s statement true/false, and keep only rows matching the stated number of truths.
Use when: Apply this to suspect/culprit, liar-truth teller, and constraint-satisfaction multiple-choice problems with several interdependent claims.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous, or require outside facts rather than pure consistency checking.

Transfer rule: If an argument concludes a thing is not a category because of its origin, then require an assumption making that origin a necessary condition for category membership.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the conclusion’s exclusion to a missing classification rule, rather than to background facts or timeline details.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What bridge principle turns the stated history into ‘not a true member’?”; negate that principle and see whether the conclusion could still fail.
Use when: Relevant in necessary-assumption questions where premises describe how something was formed, acquired, or originated, and the conclusion denies status.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is causal, predictive, comparative, or already supported without any category-definition gap.

Transfer rule: If a passage opens with value but then centers on a cause-plus-consequence chain, then choose the option emphasizing the main causal agent, not just the visible trend.
Error pattern: I focused on repeated decline statistics and missed that they were evidence supporting a broader human-impact claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as background, claim, cause, or evidence; pick the option matching the claim/cause sentence, not the densest data.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where alarming figures, extinction data, or examples are introduced after a statement about human behavior or influence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, title, or when no causal framing is present.

Transfer rule: If an argument explains fewer published reports by reduced opportunity to produce them, then test whether publication-stage factors could independently reduce the count.
Error pattern: Strong performance came from separating production causes from selection/filtering causes in a causal explanation.
Diagnostic check: Map the chain source → study done → article submitted → article accepted → article counted; ask whether any later link changed.
Use when: Relevant for arguments inferring cause from a drop in observed outputs such as publications, approvals, sales, reports, or diagnoses.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim already controls for downstream filters or the evidence measures underlying activity directly rather than published/recorded outcomes.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires breaking from fixed methods and expanding outward from a core problem, then choose the case showing a novel, cross-angle strategy rather than simple classification, combination, or pattern-following.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the deepest functional features of the definition, not surface creativity or usefulness.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Does the actor start from one problem cue, abandon standard categories, and generate an unconventional intervention from a different angle?
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching items about creative thinking, innovation styles, or reasoning modes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept is about sorting, routine optimization, biological adaptation, or passive regularity without deliberate problem-solving.

Transfer rule: If a claim generalizes from a survey at a self-selected event, then test whether nonattenders are systematically different from attendees.
Error pattern: I focused on arithmetic/internal wording instead of representativeness and selection bias in the sample frame.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could people with the opposite preference be missing because they had no reason to attend this event?” If yes, weaken the inference.
Use when: The argument moves from questionnaire or event attendees to a broad population trend or social norm.
Boundary: Ignore when sampling is random or evidence directly covers both attendees and nonattendees.

Transfer rule: If a passage surveys historical and modern examples to support one broad theme, then choose the heading that states that overarching theme, not a single example or region-specific claim.
Error pattern: Success comes from prioritizing the passage’s main thesis over vivid supporting details and narrower paraphrases.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each paragraph in 5–8 words, then ask which option covers all summaries without adding extra emphasis.
Use when: The question asks for the best heading/title and the passage lists multiple examples, time periods, or effects under one idea.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a detail, inference, author attitude, or a title for a passage focused on one specific program only.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers local causation from a higher local rate, then test whether selective migration or sorting could create that rate without causing new cases.
Error pattern: I attacked the stated cause directly instead of checking whether the observed population was preselected by who moved there.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Could the people counted already have the condition before arriving, making the rate high without local causation?”
Use when: Apply this to geographic, school, workplace, or demographic comparisons that explain prevalence by something about the location or group.
Boundary: Ignore this when migration/selection is impossible, negligible, or already controlled for by incidence-based evidence.

Transfer rule: If a virtue is described as serious yet also harmonious and comfortable, then reject choices that turn it into rigid rule-following.
Error pattern: Success came from testing options against all stated qualifiers instead of matching only the “serious” part.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it preserve both discipline and ease, or does it add absolute, mechanical compliance not stated?
Use when: Apply this on passage-based concept questions defining a trait with a balance or explicit “not X but Y” contrast.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text directly endorses strict formal obedience or when the task asks for the strongest procedural interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires “state the rumor, then explicitly mark it false,” then choose the option with claim-first rebuttal, not double negation.
Error pattern: I matched surface negativity instead of checking whether the sentence order and function fit the defined method.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the option as two parts—rumor content and rebuttal—and verify it reads “X. That is false/rumor,” without nested negatives.
Use when: Relevant for concept-classification questions about procedures, definitions, or examples where wording structure determines membership.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on factual truth, causal reasoning, or the method allows indirect paraphrase rather than fixed presentation order.

Transfer rule: If an explanation question shows more effort but worse results, then prefer a choice naming a mechanism that both weakens the effort and independently increases the bad outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the answer to both sides of the paradox rather than to only one statistic or a side issue.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: does this option causally explain why the main intervention became less effective and why harm still rose despite more use?
Use when: Relevant for paradox, discrepancy, or explain-result questions involving rising inputs, stable background conditions, and worsening outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for strengthening, necessary assumptions, or simple correlation, not reconciliation of conflicting trends.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires inferring hostility under ambiguity, then choose the case where intent is unclear yet interpreted as malicious.
Error pattern: Success came from separating hostile-intent attribution from evidence-based suspicion, trait judgments, or policy disagreement.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the other person’s motive genuinely unknown, and does the subject add a hostile meaning not warranted by the facts?
Use when: Relevant for psychology/definition questions about bias, attribution, intention reading, or reactions to ambiguous social behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when hostility is directly evidenced, the judgment concerns ability or outcomes, or the dispute is about known interests rather than inferred intent.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a trait matters despite missing evidence, then choose the option that directly explains how that trait bridges informational gaps.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the conclusion’s causal need, not picking a tempting fact about correlation, outcomes, or general causes.
Diagnostic check: Identify the conclusion and blank; ask, “What premise makes this trait sufficient under the stated handicap?” Reject choices that do not answer that exact why-question.
Use when: Relevant for sentence-completion or strengthen items where incomplete information is emphasized and a personal ability is claimed to enable good decisions.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for evidence, examples, rankings, or external effects rather than a mechanism linking trait to result.

Transfer rule: If a disaster is defined by harm from handling or exposure to disease-causing microbes or infected material/people, then choose the option centered on infection and pathogen spread.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the core definitional elements instead of being distracted by broader ecological or agricultural harms.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the required agents and mechanism: microbe/pathogen, infection/exposure, and harm to people handling or contacting it.
Use when: Apply this on definition-based multiple choice where several options describe disasters, infestations, invasions, or ecosystem imbalance.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target category includes noninfectious biological events broadly, such as pests, invasive species, or food-web disruption.

Transfer rule: If several observers are each “half right” about paired assignments, then encode every claimed person-role pair and enforce exactly one true claim per observer plus one-to-one matching.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting verbal clues into binary constraints instead of choosing the option that merely looks most compatible.
Diagnostic check: Make a small grid; mark each stated pair as true/false, require one true in each speaker’s pair, and verify every person and role is used exactly once.
Use when: Apply this to permutation-style logic problems with exclusive categories and statements containing two linked claims per source.
Boundary: Ignore this when categories are not mutually exclusive or “half right” does not mean exactly one subclaim is true.

Transfer rule: If evidence cites repeated trials with an unusually tight range, then test whether an added trial from the same setup shows wider variation that weakens the claimed generalization.
Error pattern: I attacked source credibility generically instead of probing the sample’s representativeness and whether the observed pattern is stable across trials.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does any choice introduce a same-method result that remains on the same side of the threshold yet greatly expands the spread?
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions built on experimental repetitions, ranges, averages, or conclusions from a small controlled sample.
Boundary: Ignore when a choice directly attacks methodology, measurement validity, or causal relevance rather than the stability of the reported pattern.

Transfer rule: If a claim says inhaling a material may cause cancer, then prefer evidence that directly links that material’s inhalation-relevant behavior to carcinogenesis.
Error pattern: Strengthening questions are best answered by the most specific causal support, not by weaker analogy, unrelated exposure route, or non-cancer harm.
Diagnostic check: For each option, test: same material? same exposure path? same disease outcome? explicit causal mechanism or observed cancer link? Choose the strongest match.
Use when: Relevant in causal-support multiple-choice items about health risks, especially when choices vary by mechanism, similarity, route of exposure, or endpoint.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for assumption, weakening, policy choice, or broad plausibility rather than strongest direct support.

Transfer rule: If an argument gives evidence that a sample is biased, then treat any broad claim about the population as the main conclusion under attack.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguished the author’s overall claim from a supporting explanation of why the sample may be skewed.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase each statement as conclusion or support; ask which claim the bias evidence is meant to justify.
Use when: The stimulus discusses polls, surveys, representativeness, sampling locations, or subgroup overrepresentation.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a subsidiary conclusion, an assumption, or a method-of-reasoning description instead of the main conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts an earlier phase with a “new stage” defined by a different basis or framework, then choose the option claiming a qualitative shift, not a single cause, guarantee, or timeline.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking contrast-and-stage language and avoiding stronger unsupported claims.
Diagnostic check: List the passage’s explicit claims; reject any option adding “key,” “ensure,” duration, or other modal strength absent from the text.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items asking what is directly supported, especially with reform phases, transitions, or institutional changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly argues causation, necessity, sufficiency, or time span.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists exclusive legal conditions, then match each option only to those conditions and eliminate any case with a disqualifier or wrong sentence type.
Error pattern: Success came from strict element-by-element rule matching instead of sympathy-based or loosely analogous reasoning.
Diagnostic check: Make a checklist for eligibility, sentence category, required circumstance, and exclusions; mark each option pass/fail on every element before choosing.
Use when: Apply this on statute-style multiple-choice questions with necessary-and-sufficient criteria, exceptions, and eligibility limits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for moral judgment, policy preference, or open-ended interpretation rather than formal definitional fit.

Transfer rule: If a statement contrasts belief in the facts with doubt about the statement’s truthfulness, then choose an option about falsification, not omission.
Error pattern: I conflated withholding information with actively misrepresenting it; I ignored the difference between silence and false content.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase each option as either “left things out” or “said false things,” then match the wording to whether the speaker questions completeness or accuracy.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic items testing fine distinctions among truth, disclosure, concealment, and distortion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about memory limits, uncertainty, hearsay, or inability to know rather than dishonest reporting.

Transfer rule: If an argument says no single private actor can do X, then test whether multiple private actors could jointly do X.
Error pattern: Mistaking a missing implementation plan for a flaw, while missing an unstated assumption that rules out coordination or cooperation.
Diagnostic check: List every excluded alternative; for each, ask “single actor only, or could a coalition achieve it?” before choosing a weakness.
Use when: Claims compare government action with private actors and justify one side by citing limited resources or coordination problems.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already explicitly rules out joint ventures, partnerships, or collective financing among non-government actors.

Transfer rule: If an argument says an effect in one group does not show treatment value for another group, then favor evidence directly comparing the target group’s response with the non-target group’s response.
Error pattern: Success pattern: strengthening came from closing the population-gap and showing the observed effect fails in the intended treatment population.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this choice test subjects from the target condition and report weaker or absent effects there than in those without it?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions involving external validity, subgroup differences, and a mismatch between study participants and the population the conclusion concerns.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only attack sampling generally, discuss placebo noise, or impose unrealistically universal treatment effects.

Transfer rule: If a passage links continued living to even minimal hope, then infer a broad dependence of survival on hope, not claims about priorities or purposes.
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting the author’s causal relationship rather than chasing tempting but unsupported value judgments.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map the chain “condition exists → psychological support appears → survival continues,” and reject choices adding new aims, rankings, or mechanisms.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions built from illustrative anecdotes that generalize from endurance, hope, belief, or inner support.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text explicitly compares priorities, defines purposes, or provides evidence for material rather than psychological causes.

Transfer rule: If category percentages in a survey exceed 100% or seem incompatible, then test whether respondents could select multiple causes or hold overlapping views.
Error pattern: Success came from checking exclusivity assumptions instead of treating percentages as automatically contradictory.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Must each person belong to exactly one category?” If not, sketch an overlap set model and see whether coexistence removes the conflict.
Use when: Relevant for poll, diagnosis, blame, or cause-attribution questions reporting several percentages about beliefs, reasons, or classifications.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly states one-choice-only categories, mutually exclusive groups, or a fixed partition of all respondents.

Transfer rule: If premises chain necessary conditions from an activity to background resources, then infer those resources existed wherever that activity occurred.
Error pattern: Success pattern: correctly followed a conditional-necessity chain instead of treating causes, examples, or speculations as the main conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List each “only if/unless/must” link, rewrite as activity → prerequisite, then connect the chain and see which option states that required backdrop.
Use when: Relevant in arguments with conditional language, historical examples, and distractors about sufficiency, causation, or accidental discovery.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is probabilistic, comparative, or about a different activity than the one anchoring the conditional chain.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers income changed in step with price from an unchanged spending share, then require consumption amount and quality to be held constant.
Error pattern: Success pattern: spotting a hidden ceteris paribus assumption linking price changes to expenditure changes rather than jumping to unrelated market facts.
Diagnostic check: Write share = spending/income; ask whether spending would necessarily track price, or could quantity/quality substitution keep the share unchanged.
Use when: Relevant in percentage, ratio, budget-share, inflation, or spending arguments that move from stable proportions to conclusions about another variable.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already fixes consumption behavior or directly measures spending instead of inferring it from prices.

Transfer rule: If a choice shows the central bank changing economy-wide interest rates or money/credit conditions, then treat it as a monetary policy tool.
Error pattern: Success came from separating active policy levers from routine obligations, fiscal administration, or emergency operational support.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this action directly alter borrowing costs, reserve conditions, or aggregate credit for the whole economy, rather than just handle accounts or individual institutions?
Use when: Apply this on questions about central-bank functions, especially when options mix policy instruments with supervisory, fiscal-agent, or liquidity-management duties.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about legal mandates, bank operations, or crisis lending details rather than standard policy instruments.

Transfer rule: If a claim explains avoidance by detecting a current cue, then prefer evidence showing avoidance persists when that cue is absent but the context remains.
Error pattern: Strong causal testing succeeds by separating the proposed mechanism from alternative drivers like place memory, learning, or conditioning.
Diagnostic check: Ask: would the behavior still occur if the suspected signal were removed while location/history stayed the same? If yes, the mechanism is weakened.
Use when: Relevant for weaken/evaluate questions about animal or human behavior explained by a sensory ability or present stimulus.
Boundary: Ignore when choices do not isolate variables, or when multiple mechanisms could produce the same persistence pattern without contradiction.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts a price rise from a cost increase, then check for hidden alternatives the firm could use instead of raising prices.
Error pattern: I accepted a sales/advertising side effect instead of identifying the necessary assumption linking higher taxes to higher prices.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the company absorb or offset the added cost another way?” If yes, the price-rise step is unsupported.
Use when: Relevant in causal or policy arguments about taxes, costs, pricing, and reduced demand through a business response chain.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states no offsetting adjustments are possible or is about direct effects not mediated by firm choices.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives conditional rules about permission, payment, and infringement, then infer the broader legal principle those rules establish.
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting multiple case-specific conditions into the single supported general statement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each stated condition and ask: what overarching principle is true in every listed case without adding new claims?
Use when: Relevant for legal or policy passages that describe exceptions, permissions, duties, and penalties, then ask for the best overall interpretation.
Boundary: Ignore this when options require outside law, compare unstated difficulties, or claim unlimited freedom not explicitly granted.

Transfer rule: If an option names a measuring device, then verify it depends on frequency shift from relative motion, not merely light beams, imaging, or speed calculation.
Error pattern: I matched on familiar wording and surface associations instead of testing each option against the precise definition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: what wave is sent, what relative motion occurs, and is the output derived from a received-frequency change?
Use when: Apply this on concept-definition multiple choice items where several technologies sound related to waves, sensing, or motion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is defined by non-wave mechanisms or the question asks about branding, fiction, or naming only.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus links a subgroup to a sufficient condition for an outcome, then infer the outcome for that subgroup only, not for everyone or for comparisons beyond the given group.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning isolates the overlap between a described majority/minority subgroup and a causal rule, avoiding universal or cross-group leaps.
Diagnostic check: Mark each quantifier and set relation; test whether the conclusion stays within those sets and whether every causal step is explicitly licensed.
Use when: Apply to argument questions with quantifiers like most/all/rest and chained claims about behavior leading to a condition.
Boundary: Ignore when key terms shift meaning, causation is negated or uncertain, or the conclusion requires outside population data.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a topic and then emphasizes multiple dangers/effects, then choose the option combining definition plus overall harm/theme.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the text’s structure instead of locking onto one repeated detail.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as definition, cause, or consequence; if most content is consequence after a brief definition, prefer the summary covering both.
Use when: The question asks for main content/central idea and the passage mixes introduction with several impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a specific detail, cause only, or a single supporting point rather than the whole passage.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “if none of several protective actions are taken, then bad outcome,” then only infer the contrapositive: avoiding the bad outcome requires at least one protective action, not any single one.
Error pattern: Treating one missing condition as sufficient for failure; confusing a conjunction inside an antecedent with separate standalone implications.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the statement as “NOT(any action) → bad”; then test each choice by asking whether it follows by contraposition or wrongly isolates one action.
Use when: Conditional reasoning problems with multiple actions, negations, “unless/otherwise,” or claims about crisis, elimination, or prevention.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when premises explicitly give separate if-then rules for each action or state biconditional/equivalence.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives overlapping category counts, then model people as set intersections and optimize by maximizing overlap for the minimum and minimizing overlap under exclusivity limits for the maximum.
Error pattern: I treated categories as too independent and missed a hidden cap created by “only” groups and total coverage.
Diagnostic check: Draw each attribute set, mark which can overlap, which are exclusive, then compute min by nesting counts and max by separating them without violating “only” conditions.
Use when: Apply to headcount/range questions where every person is covered by several descriptors like origin, region, and occupation.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are not exhaustive, counts refer to events not people, or wording does not constrain overlap/exclusivity.

Transfer rule: If asked for roles of boldface claims, then first identify the main conclusion and test whether each boldface statement supports it or is itself being supported.
Error pattern: Success came from separating premises from conclusions instead of assuming earlier statements are intermediate conclusions.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the argument as “Because [claim 1] and because [claim 2], therefore [conclusion]”; if both fit naturally, mark both as premises.
Use when: Relevant in boldface role questions with a recommendation or judgment backed by factual observations and behavioral evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this when a boldface statement is explicitly inferred from another or when the task is not about argumentative roles.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires legal recognition plus a limited statutory source, then choose only relationships explicitly created by those legal procedures.
Error pattern: Success comes from applying all necessary conditions and rejecting choices that match everyday kinship language but lack formal legal basis.
Diagnostic check: For each option, verify two boxes: no blood tie, and the relationship is established under the named laws rather than by care, cohabitation, or marriage alone.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about legal or institutional categories with restrictive source conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category is based on social custom, broad ordinary language, or when legal source limitations are not stated.

Transfer rule: If an argument alleges a paradox between a field’s goal and method, then test whether the method depends on the current omission the goal aims to correct, and look for hidden escape clauses.
Error pattern: I chose an overstated restatement instead of evaluating the conclusion’s support under the argument’s actual dependency structure.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Could the conclusion fail only if the target decisions have no real effect on the items being valued?” If yes, prefer the conditional that captures that exception.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/support questions about paradox, circularity, or methodology-versus-objective conflicts in economics or policy.
Boundary: Ignore when choices hinge on factual prevalence, definitions, or causal claims not tied to the argument’s core dependency.

Transfer rule: If premises compare one case’s traditions or path with others, then choose only the conclusion that restates a supported difference, not extra policy or inevitability claims.
Error pattern: Success came from separating a modest comparative conclusion from stronger unsupported recommendations, predictions, or harmony claims.
Diagnostic check: Underline each claim in the premises; for each option, mark whether every key term is explicitly supported and reject any option adding necessity, sufficiency, or value judgment.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions where statements describe distinct characteristics, traditions, or developmental paths across countries or groups.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks for causation, evaluation, best policy, or external knowledge beyond the stated premises.

Transfer rule: If an argument says harsher/faster consequences deter behavior, then ask whether the behavior is typically deliberative enough for anticipated punishment to affect it.
Error pattern: I attacked a procedural side issue instead of the core causal assumption linking knowledge of punishment to reduced offending.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, state the needed chain “anticipate consequence → pause/hesitate → avoid act”; reject choices that do not break one of these links.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about deterrence, incentives, punishment speed, or claims that expected consequences change criminal behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about legality, fairness, rights, or investigation accuracy rather than deterrent psychology.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a subgroup has a trait, then infer that some members of the broader group have that trait.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by moving upward from category membership, while avoiding unsupported comparisons or superlatives.
Diagnostic check: Mark any sentence as “All/most/some subgroup are broader-group members” plus “those subgroup members have feature”; then test whether “some broader-group members have feature” follows.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension inference questions with taxonomy words like type, kind, species, member, or belongs to.
Boundary: Ignore when the choice adds rankings, totals, leadership, causation, or cross-group claims not explicitly linked by membership.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a specific actor “should provide funding,” then test whether it assumes that actor is a necessary funding source, not merely that the goal is valuable.
Error pattern: I shifted from a required bridge about means/responsibility to a broad value claim that can support many policies without being necessary.
Diagnostic check: Remove the chosen assumption and ask: could the conclusion still stand if some other party could fully fund the research?
Use when: The conclusion prescribes who should pay, regulate, or act, especially in policy arguments with beneficial outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument is only about desirability of research, not about assigning the funding source.

Transfer rule: If a passage rebuts a popular causal claim with evidence and a qualified explanation, then choose the option capturing the negation/qualification of that causation, not an absolute extreme.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions often tempt overstatement or side-issue choices; success comes from tracking the author’s central rebuttal and preserving qualifiers.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state in one sentence the claim being challenged, the evidence offered, and the final qualified takeaway; reject any option stronger, narrower, or more tangential.
Use when: The text contrasts rumor vs. study, discusses cause-and-effect, and ends with a limited conclusion rather than a total denial.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, attitude, inference, or when the passage truly makes an unqualified absolute claim.

Transfer rule: If statements form a chain of conditionals and one person is stated to be elsewhere, then convert that fact into a negation and propagate it through the chain before choosing.
Error pattern: Failed to use contraposition/negation from a factual statement, and guessed a specific mode instead of deriving the necessary companion outcome.
Diagnostic check: Write each rule as implication; mark the factual sentence as “not doing X”; infer what that blocks, then see which option is forced in all remaining cases.
Use when: Relevant for verbal-logic items with “if,” “as long as,” companions, travel modes, and a concrete fact about someone’s current location or action.
Boundary: Ignore when options depend on unstated exclusivity, probabilities, time shifts, or facts that do not negate any conditional trigger.

Transfer rule: If a stem says a conjecture is true and asks which view is most questioned, then target the option that directly contradicts the conjecture’s core causal or origin claim.
Error pattern: Success comes from isolating the conclusion and eliminating choices that merely restate background facts, dates, or descriptive features.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conjecture’s key claims; for each option, ask “If the conjecture holds, does this become less credible, or is it still compatible?”
Use when: Apply this on strengthen/weaken, challenged-view, or inference items built around origin, dependence, independence, or source relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for support, paraphrase, or details not logically tied to the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both profit-seeking enterprise use and actual participation in producing/circulating goods or services, then exclude assets held by non-enterprise public institutions first.
Error pattern: I focused on immediate use or payment purpose and missed the owner/user qualification and profit-oriented nature in the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option against a two-part filter: legal-person enterprise seeking economic benefit, and asset used within production/circulation for profit.
Use when: Relevant for definition-based classification questions where several choices partly fit by function, timing, or accounting treatment.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes nonprofits, personal users, or assets judged only by physical use status.

Transfer rule: If a theory explains international behavior mainly by physical location, access, terrain, or spatial position, then treat it as geopolitical; if it centers on culture or ideology, reject it.
Error pattern: Success came from separating geographic determinism from nonspatial civilizational or ideological explanations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, underline the causal driver; ask “Could this claim stand unchanged without any map-based feature?” If yes, it is likely not geopolitical.
Use when: Apply on definitions or examples contrasting geography-based strategy with cultural, religious, economic, or ideological theories.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt broadens “geopolitics” to include nongeographic grand-strategy frameworks or mixed-cause theories.

Transfer rule: If an argument says firms can gain share only via mergers, then look for evidence that ordinary competitive tactics can force rivals out and shift share.
Error pattern: I focused on a choice about consumer preferences instead of testing the conclusion’s exclusivity claim about how market share can change.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option create a non-merger path to higher share for existing firms, even if total market demand stays flat?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about mature, fixed-size, or population-tied markets where the conclusion rules out marketing, pricing, or operations as growth routes.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about total market growth rather than relative share, or when options affect taste without changing firms’ share mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If a claim includes a causal/support chain, then attack the earliest factual premise rather than restating or endorsing later advice.
Error pattern: I chose a statement that agreed with the speaker’s recommendation instead of one that undermined the foundation of the argument.
Diagnostic check: Split the argument into premise(s) and conclusion; for each option, mark whether it weakens a premise, weakens the link, or merely repeats/supports the conclusion.
Use when: Relevant for weaken/refute questions where the argument mixes descriptive claims about what usually happens with a normative or evaluative takeaway.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for support/strengthen, or when all choices target only the conclusion directly.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers prevention from a high share of outcomes having a prior trait, then check the reverse base rate: how many with the trait ever reach the outcome.
Error pattern: Confusing a common antecedent among cases with a strong causal or predictive pathway from antecedent to outcome.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is the outcome rare among those with the proposed cause?” If yes, the policy link is weak.
Use when: Claims move from “most outcome cases had X first” to “reducing X will greatly reduce the outcome.”
Boundary: Ignore when evidence gives intervention effects, temporal necessity plus high transition rates, or controlled causal data.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “the test sometimes merges different sources” to “a nonmatch cannot clear someone,” then check whether it is confusing false positives with false negatives.
Error pattern: Reversing the direction of test error and treating one kind of unreliability as evidence for the opposite kind.
Diagnostic check: Name the two possible mistakes the test can make, then ask which one the stated evidence supports and which one the conclusion needs.
Use when: The stimulus discusses imperfect identification, matching, screening, or classification tests and draws a conclusion from test unreliability.
Boundary: Ignore when the flaw is about bad sampling, scope shifts, or unsupported assumptions unrelated to error direction.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats a difference between groups as caused by one event, then test whether a third group lacking that event shows the same difference.
Error pattern: Mistook irrelevant background variation for a stronger alternative explanation about selection or baseline group differences.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Would the conclusion weaken if a comparable group that never experienced the alleged cause still had the same worse outcome?”
Use when: Relevant for causal claims from observational comparisons, especially marriage/divorce, health, education, or income outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already controls for preexisting differences or comes from randomized/longitudinal designs isolating the event’s effect.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “immigrants died out” from “no current subgroup is very different,” then test whether all current members could descend from the immigrants instead.
Error pattern: I attacked a background assumption instead of the conclusion’s key exclusivity claim about present descendants.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the evidence rule out assimilation/common ancestry, or only rule out coexistence of two independently originating lineages today?
Use when: Relevant in causal-history arguments comparing current variation to infer whether an external source persisted, vanished, or merged.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already excludes universal descent from the external source or when present-day diversity is not the basis of the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage says someone founded or anticipated a later field by studying certain topics, then infer that those topics belong to that later field.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by linking “laid the foundation for” with inherited subject matter, while avoiding stronger claims about fame, total rejection, or permanence.
Diagnostic check: Underline causal/temporal bridge phrases; test each option for exact support versus overstatement, especially words like “determines,” “never,” or claims of motive/status.
Use when: The stimulus is historical/expository and asks what follows from stated influence, foundations, neglect, or contrast with dominant methods.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question requires outside knowledge, definitions not given, or options hinge on unstated chronology or exclusivity.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers less pollution from fewer commuters, then check whether it assumes fewer active cars overall rather than just fewer commute trips.
Error pattern: Chose a broad source-of-pollution claim instead of the bridge linking a reduced subgroup behavior to a reduced total causal activity.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the same or more vehicles still be operating despite fewer people commuting?” If yes, the missing assumption is about total operation, not pollution share.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where a change in one behavior is used to predict a change in an aggregate outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion already concerns only that subgroup, or when total activity is independently established.

Transfer rule: If a definition gives a core mechanism plus extra traits, then choose the option centered on the mechanism, not a merely true side detail.
Error pattern: I latched onto a salient descriptive feature and ignored the sentence defining what primarily produces the effect.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, paraphrase the claim as “X is mainly education through ___” and verify the option fills that blank better than any option about scope, users, or flexibility.
Use when: Relevant for definition, main-idea, or “supported argument” questions with one central causal/process statement and several partial summaries.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an example, an implication, or specifically the most complete rather than the most central summary.

Transfer rule: If a claim says one factor caused an outcome, then prefer evidence showing the factor remained while the outcome did not.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning used a counterexample to break an asserted causal link rather than merely offering another possible cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is there a time or case where the alleged cause is present but the alleged effect is absent or reversed?”
Use when: Relevant for arguments blaming one driver for price rises, pollution, or other broad trends in causal multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore when choices concern definitions, moral judgments, or when the claim is explicitly multi-causal rather than a single-cause accusation.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both fabrication/imitation and passing as genuine, then choose only an option containing both acts, even for foreign legal tender.
Error pattern: I matched on “using fake money” and ignored the required production element and the broader scope of currency.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark two boxes—made/imitation? and circulated as real?—and reject any choice lacking either box.
Use when: A legal or definitional multiple-choice item asks which case fits an offense described by necessary elements.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the offense is defined to include mere possession, purchase, or use without requiring manufacture.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which added premise does not make an ordering argument valid, then test each option by chaining the comparisons needed for the conclusion and reject any option that cannot complete that chain.
Error pattern: I treated a tempting equivalence as insufficient without explicitly checking whether it links premises transitively to the target comparison.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite all statements as X>Y or X=Y, build a path from conclusion-left to conclusion-right, and verify whether the option guarantees that path under transitivity/substitution.
Use when: Relevant for logic items about comparative relations, added premises, and validity of arguments with “more than” or “equal to.”
Boundary: Ignore when relations are nontransitive, causal, probabilistic, or depend on domain facts beyond formal comparison rules.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a rise in a real phenomenon from more recorded cases, then test whether definitions, classifications, or reporting practices changed.
Error pattern: Treating administrative counts as direct evidence of underlying reality without checking measurement consistency.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could the later period include more things under the same label, or record them more often, even if the real rate stayed flat?”
Use when: The evidence compares totals across time, places, or institutions using official records, arrests, reports, or categories.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes stable definitions and constant detection, recording, and enforcement methods.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a flawed trend with a new successful remedy, then choose the option naming that remedy against the trend, not a broad value statement.
Error pattern: I abstracted to a generic principle and missed the author’s specific corrective proposal signaled by contrast.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the “problem state,” the “counterexample/remedy,” and the “claimed effect”; pick the choice containing all three.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea or intended-point questions built around “however,” “under this background,” and positive examples after criticism.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a local detail, tone, or a directly stated general principle without a remedy structure.

Transfer rule: If a passage praises past works for turning imagined technology into reality and expresses hope for more such questioning, then choose the option about continuing to inspire innovation.
Error pattern: I overweighted broad thematic discussion and ignored the author’s evaluative purpose signaled by praise plus a forward-looking wish.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark verbs of approval and hope; ask which option directly matches what the author wants works to keep doing.
Use when: Apply this on author-intent questions where the text contrasts future themes with a valued historical function of a genre.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the passage’s main topic, a factual detail, or the best paraphrase of a contrasted idea.

Transfer rule: If a transaction appears unfair, then check for compelled transfer through threats, pressure, or exploitation of urgent dependence before calling it predatory.
Error pattern: Success came from separating mere price imbalance or hard bargaining from coercion that overrides voluntary consent.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Could the weaker party realistically refuse and keep their interests without facing imposed harm or nonmarket pressure?
Use when: Apply this to scenarios about contracts, exchanges, emergency pricing, authority influence, or one side seeming disadvantaged.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the issue is legality under a different doctrine, fraud about facts, or capacity/ownership disputes rather than coercion.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires care for those beyond cure or alongside disease-directed therapy, then reject choices describing routine perioperative symptom control within active curative treatment.
Error pattern: I matched any symptom relief to the term and ignored the treatment context and eligibility criteria.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is the person in end-of-life/non-curative care, or explicitly receiving supportive care alongside ongoing disease treatment? If neither, exclude it.
Use when: A concept is defined by both goals and setting/population, especially in medical or policy classifications.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the term is defined purely by the intervention itself, regardless of disease stage or care context.

Transfer rule: If a passage piles up destructive imagery but then sharply contrasts one person as unaffected, then infer the trait highlighted by that contrast.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s emphasis and contrast, not choosing broad background themes suggested by the setting.
Diagnostic check: Mark the strongest contrast word and ask, “What single quality of the focal person is being proved by everything before and after it?”
Use when: Relevant in literary inference questions with vivid scene description, personification, and a final turn toward one character’s reaction or immunity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for overall theme, social conditions, or the passage gives no character-centered contrast.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts one country’s much smaller relic and museum counts with others’ larger protected collections, then infer criticism of protection/attention rather than a call for specific actions.
Error pattern: Mistaking comparative evidence about insufficiency for a policy prescription that adds new content not directly stated.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Do the facts only show a gap in current attention/protection, or do they explicitly argue for one remedy?” Choose the weaker, directly supported claim.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions built on cross-country statistics, especially when options include both evaluative summaries and action-oriented recommendations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly endorses a concrete measure, assigns causes, or argues for a named policy response.

Transfer rule: If a bold claim is introduced as study/data and later a recommendation or preference follows, then treat the study/data as support and the later recommendation as the conclusion.
Error pattern: Mistaking the author’s own evidence for an opponent’s evidence because of contrast words and mention of a rival view.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the author’s main point in one sentence, then ask which bold part could stand after “therefore”; if only the later bold part fits, the earlier one is support.
Use when: Role-of-boldface questions with competing viewpoints, contrast markers, and factual findings followed by a judgment or plan.
Boundary: Ignore this when both bold parts are facts, both are conclusions, or one is presented only as someone else’s stated opinion.

Transfer rule: If seating clues include a fixed relative position and a diagonal relation, then map all seats explicitly and test each eligible driver against every identity constraint.
Error pattern: I jumped from a plausible family-role assumption to a conclusion without exhausting the constraint combinations.
Diagnostic check: Draw a 2x2 seat grid, place the fixed rider first, encode diagonal/opposite relations, then eliminate any driver option that forces a role, hobby, or major conflict.
Use when: This applies to logic-grid problems with family identities, seat positions, and cross-linked attributes like hobby-major-person relations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on arithmetic, wording nuance only, or when the driver is directly stated.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires migration to protect/restore ecology or because the environment is too harsh for local poverty relief, then choose only options matching that stated purpose and scope.
Error pattern: Success came from applying all necessary criteria instead of matching on any relocation alone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the trigger, the purpose, and whether movement is collective; reject any choice missing one required element.
Use when: Apply this on definition questions about social policies, relocation types, or category membership with multiple conjunctive conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is defined by a single broad feature or when examples are explicitly nonexclusive.

Transfer rule: If evidence found at a site is used to date the site’s occupation, then require a link showing the evidence was created or deposited during occupation.
Error pattern: Success pattern: identifying the hidden temporal-link assumption connecting an artifact’s subject or age to the timing of site use.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could this object or marking have been made earlier, elsewhere, or added later while the conclusion still fails?” If yes, that timing link is required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions involving archaeological finds, depictions, fossils, or artifacts used to infer when people were present.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns only the object itself, or when independent dating already fixes the artifact’s creation to the occupation period.

Transfer rule: If overall inflation seems low but people report high price pain, then check whether heavily weighted categories moved opposite to salient household purchases.
Error pattern: Chose a broad, noncausal summary instead of a mechanism that reconciles aggregate data with lived experience through weighting and offsetting movements.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map “overall index” versus “noticed items”; ask what basket weights or declines elsewhere could keep the average low despite spikes in frequent essentials.
Use when: A question contrasts official averages with public perception, especially mentioning a few sharply rising everyday goods alongside a modest aggregate measure.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks only for definition, source reliability, or no evidence suggests category weights or offsetting price changes.

Transfer rule: If a bold claim is backed by later premises and then used to justify an earlier thesis, then classify it as an intermediate conclusion.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping support direction rather than matching keywords like “confirms” or “for one thing.”
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as premise, sub-conclusion, or main conclusion by asking what supports it and what it supports.
Use when: Apply this on argument-structure questions with boldface text, especially when one sentence appears between the thesis and supporting reasons.
Boundary: Ignore this when the highlighted text is merely background, a definition, or a premise that receives no support within the passage.

Transfer rule: If rising revenue from one product is paired with no matching gain in prosperity, then check whether other major income streams or necessary costs moved adversely enough to offset it.
Error pattern: I focused on a vague market-pressure statement instead of an offset that directly explains how overall well-being could stagnate despite higher revenue in the named area.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this option create a concrete net-offset to total prosperity, rather than merely restating tougher conditions?”
Use when: Apply to paradox questions contrasting increased earnings, output, or sales with unchanged overall welfare, profit, or prosperity.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for a cause of the increase itself, or when prosperity is defined only by that single revenue source.

Transfer rule: If an argument generalizes from an observed majority to a universal claim, then prefer choices that undermine sample representativeness or inference scope, not mere exceptions.
Error pattern: I overvalued a counterexample-style detail and missed that the conclusion depended on an inductive leap from limited observations.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this option attack the evidence base, the causal link, or only note a few anomalies; choose the one that weakens the broadest necessary support.
Use when: Apply this to questions moving from “most observed cases” or “the farther, the more” patterns to sweeping claims about all cases or the whole system.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is existential, probabilistic, or already allows exceptions, where a single contrary case can be decisive.

Transfer rule: If two speakers agree an act is wrongful but argue over degree based on consequences, then choose the option about comparative seriousness, not category or possibility.
Error pattern: Mistook a dispute about severity/extent for one about type, definition, or whether harm can ever occur.
Diagnostic check: List shared premises and the single contested claim; if both accept criminality and discuss worse vs less serious, eliminate options about classification or mere existence.
Use when: Dialogue compares two wrongs, cites added harms, and one side rebuts by showing the first can produce similar harms.
Boundary: Ignore when the speakers dispute legality itself, causal possibility alone, or whether the acts belong to the same class.

Transfer rule: If two speakers offer different explanations for one action, then test each answer by asking whether one explanation would negate the action while the other leaves it possible.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing disagreement about a conditional link from mere discussion of costs or prediction accuracy.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, mark Justine’s implied commitment and Simon’s stated commitment; keep only a statement one supports and the other rejects or questions.
Use when: Apply on dialogue questions asking what speakers disagree about, especially with causal or conditional claims behind a decision.
Boundary: Ignore when both speakers could accept the statement, or when the choice adds assumptions not grounded in either speaker’s remarks.

Transfer rule: If several statements about two binary outcomes must leave exactly one true, then encode each claim symbolically and test every allowed scenario by truth count.
Error pattern: Success came from systematic case enumeration instead of relying on the most direct-sounding speaker or option.
Diagnostic check: Make a 2×2 table for the two outcomes, mark each statement true/false in each row, and keep only rows with exactly one true.
Use when: Apply this to logic puzzles with conditional, negation, and conjunction claims about a small number of yes/no possibilities.
Boundary: Ignore this full table method when variables have many states or quantifiers, where direct formal deduction is more efficient.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists many concrete activities by one person, then infer only a broad, evidence-backed scope claim matching those activities.
Error pattern: Success comes from choosing the least exaggerated paraphrase and rejecting metaphor-literal confusion and universal claims beyond the text.
Diagnostic check: Underline each explicit action, then compare options by asking: does this restate the list without adding motives, judgments, totals, or hidden meanings?
Use when: The question asks what can be inferred from descriptive prose, especially with figurative language plus an enumeration of achievements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task requires outside knowledge, causal explanation, or evaluation rather than a text-supported inference.

Transfer rule: If a legal rule lists required elements, then verify each candidate against every element and reject any with one missing or excluded condition.
Error pattern: Success came from element-by-element statutory matching instead of choosing by severity, sympathy, or job title.
Diagnostic check: Make a checklist: time, place, work causation/duty, travel-status exception, and fault limits; mark yes/no for each option before answering.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice questions about legal recognition, eligibility, exceptions, or definitions with several fact patterns.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for policy evaluation, open-ended interpretation, or facts outside the stated rule text.

Transfer rule: If a definition includes both resource loss and land-productivity damage, then require all core components, not just a matching external force.
Error pattern: I matched a salient cue from the definition and ignored a missing required element, causing an overinclusive choice.
Diagnostic check: For each option, make a two-column checklist: listed causes/mechanisms present, and every required outcome present; reject any option failing either column.
Use when: Apply this on definition-based multiple choice with necessary-and-sufficient conditions, especially environmental process categories with several conjunctive criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for a broad example, typical cause, or best illustration rather than strict membership under a formal definition.

Transfer rule: If a set mixes fixed exclusions with conditionals/disjunctions, then translate each into logic and derive forced picks/forbidden picks before checking options.
Error pattern: Treated a disjunction as excluding one side and ignored that “likely/assumed selected” can still be tested against hard constraints.
Diagnostic check: Write T/F status for each person after propagating implications from any unconditional statement; verify every eliminated choice has a direct contradiction, not just absence of support.
