Use when: Relevant in selection puzzles with “or,” “if…then,” and one explicit must-not or must statement across several candidates.
Boundary: Ignore when options ask for probability, preference strength, or independent facts rather than strict logical entailment.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a method is essential because it eliminates bad cases, then require that the method can reliably identify those bad cases.
Error pattern: I confused a necessary effectiveness assumption with an overly strong exclusivity claim about the method’s purpose.
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption; if the method could not accurately detect the target trait, would the conclusion that it is essential collapse?
Use when: Relevant for assumption questions where a tool, test, or procedure is justified by its supposed screening or filtering power.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about motives, historical importance, or exclusive purpose rather than operational effectiveness.

Transfer rule: If a term is defined by issuer + audience + purpose, then verify every candidate matches all three before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from using strict definition matching instead of picking by surface importance or official tone alone.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes: authorized public organ, directed to the general public, and concerns important/statutory matters; accept only all-checked items.
Use when: Apply this on definition-based multiple choice involving public notices, legal instruments, administrative documents, or institutional communications.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for best fit by context, metaphorical usage, or when the definition does not require all listed conditions.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a condition caused an outcome despite common alternatives being restricted, then choose the option giving a direct mechanism from that condition to the outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from matching causal support to a plausible pathway rather than picking facts that are merely consistent or tangential.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice explain how the stated cause could produce the observed effect, without adding a new issue?”
Use when: Apply on strengthen/complete-the-argument questions about causation, especially with controls excluding exercise, access, or other obvious causes.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for weaken, resolve, or pure description, or when no causal claim needs mechanistic support.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers reliable future reidentification from a stored unique pattern, then require that the pattern remain stable and readable over time.
Error pattern: Success pattern: spotting the hidden continuity assumption between uniqueness at scan time and successful recognition later.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the identifier change or become unreadable after storage while still being the same object/person?” If yes, that stability premise is required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions about biometrics, signatures, records, or any recognition system moving from prior scan to later identification.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns only one-time differentiation, or the prompt already guarantees permanence and recognizability.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by centering on a current reform and resistance, then summarize the main point as that reform’s predicament, not the broader background cause.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from supporting history and causes, choosing a thematic explanation instead of the passage’s immediate focal issue.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the final two sentences’ subject and ask: is the paragraph mainly explaining a system, or highlighting one present conflict/problem?
Use when: The passage gives background, then shifts to a specific policy change, controversy, or implementation difficulty.
Boundary: Ignore this when the whole passage stays expository and never narrows to a concrete present policy dilemma.

Transfer rule: If a management theory emphasizes social needs and enthusiasm through relationships, then choose the option that increases participation, belonging, and interaction at work.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the theory’s core human motive, not getting distracted by money, training, or demographic tailoring.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it directly strengthen workplace relationships or shared involvement rather than individual incentives or skill improvement?
Use when: The prompt defines a theory by what workers value most and asks which practice reflects that management view.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the theory centers on pay, efficiency, authority structure, or individual capability rather than interpersonal connection.

Transfer rule: If one existential group is wholly inside a broader set and all of that broader set has a property, then infer that some members of the existential group have that property.
Error pattern: Successful use of chaining an existence claim with a universal claim; avoid adding unsupported negations or exceptions.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as set statements: “some X are Y” and “all Y are Z”; then test whether “some X are Z” follows directly.
Use when: Relevant for categorical syllogisms mixing “some” and “all” about overlapping classes or subsets.
Boundary: Ignore when premises are conditional, comparative, probabilistic, or when the conclusion introduces “not,” exclusivity, or quantities not licensed by the premises.

Transfer rule: If a definition question asks for what is not required, then mark only conditions explicitly stated or logically necessary from the definition and reject added specifics.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering out plausible but unsupported domain assumptions rather than choosing the most ideal-sounding practice.
Diagnostic check: For each option, point to matching words in the definition; if no direct phrase or necessary implication supports it, flag it as the likely nonrequirement.
Use when: Relevant for definitional multiple-choice items listing production, process, certification, or standards-based criteria.
Boundary: Ignore when the question depends on outside subject knowledge, hidden regulations, or broad causal inference beyond the given definition.

Transfer rule: If attitudes seem inconsistent with improved relative standing, then test whether the comparison baseline changed over time.
Error pattern: Success came from reconciling subjective reports with objective measures by spotting a shifted reference frame.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could both surveys be true if the broader average worsened or improved?” and verify whether that removes the tension.
Use when: Relevant for paradox/resolution questions comparing two time points, local conditions, and satisfaction versus average benchmarks.
Boundary: Ignore when the discrepancy is explained by sampling flaws, wording changes, or no cross-time comparison standard is involved.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses an analogy, then map each role precisely and test every choice against the exact direction of dependence and purpose.
Error pattern: I accepted the tempting analogy-based option and missed a statement that subtly reversed who persists through whom.
Diagnostic check: For each option, rewrite it as “X exists/acts for Y” or “X controls Y”; reject any choice that swaps agent and vehicle from the passage.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items with metaphors, biological agency, or “for the benefit of” claims about control, survival, or replication.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for external facts, tone, or implications not grounded in role-mapping within the text.

Transfer rule: If a passage says many people know health basics yet fail to act because they lack self-discipline, then infer existence of people with knowledge but without self-discipline.
Error pattern: I wrongly treated a one-way conditional about disciplined people as supporting its converse or contrapositive without a valid negative premise.
Diagnostic check: List each claim as existential, universal, or conditional; only derive statements preserving quantifier strength and direction, and verify whether “some/many” supplies existence.
Use when: Relevant for verbal-logic items mixing examples, “many/some,” and conditionals about traits, habits, and outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument explicitly gives biconditionals, negations, or formal contrapositives.

Transfer rule: If asked which fact best supports a claimed cause of a species’ survival threat, then prefer the option giving a direct causal chain from that cause to concrete harm.
Error pattern: I favored a superficially related effect that reduced the trait’s usefulness instead of evidence that the proposed cause actively damages survival.
Diagnostic check: For each option, test: does it explicitly link the proposed cause to reduced survival via intermediate mechanisms, rather than merely changing relevance, background, or diversity?
Use when: Apply in strengthen/causal MCQs about biological traits, environmental change, and claims that one factor threatens survival.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for explanation of adaptation, definition, comparison, or broad ecological context rather than strongest causal support.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a cell type detects and attacks bad or infected cells, then infer it helps prevent disease from those cells, not that it causes or cures everything.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: making the weakest necessary inference from described function and avoiding stronger causal or comparative claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each choice as function-consistent, causal overreach, speed/comparison overreach, or unsupported attribute, and keep only the minimally entailed one.
Use when: Relevant in biology or process passages that contrast roles of systems and describe what one component directly does.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for external knowledge, mechanisms beyond the text, or explicit strongest-explanation rather than strict inference.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several implementation issues and ends with broad needed actions, then choose the option summarizing the overall reform direction, not one specific measure.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing the author’s main emphasis over supporting details.
Diagnostic check: Mark problem statements, proposed fixes, and the final takeaway; if multiple details support one umbrella change, select the umbrella.
Use when: The text contrasts current practice with difficulties, then names several attention points or reforms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, example, cause, or directly quoted focus.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts lawful procedure with broader consequences and ends by stressing trust damage from misconduct, then choose the option centered on protecting credibility from abusive enforcement.  
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing the author’s final, highest-level takeaway over supporting points about legality or social effects.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s supporting points, then state the single warned-against outcome; pick the option matching that outcome, not a premise.  
Use when: Relevant for summary/main-idea questions where several choices restate details but one captures the concluding caution or core consequence.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, policy principle, or direct factual restatement rather than the overall message.

Transfer rule: If a promotion bundles a “free” add-on, then check whether the target customers already possess or prepaid that add-on, eliminating incentive value.
Error pattern: Success came from testing the offer’s marginal appeal to likely buyers rather than judging the add-on’s general popularity or scale.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “For the intended audience, does this free bonus create new value now?” Verify timing, prior commitments, and overlap in existing subscriptions.
Use when: Relevant in causal-explanation questions about disappointing marketing results, especially with subscriptions, renewals, bundled freebies, or seasonal purchase habits.
Boundary: Ignore when failure is driven by awareness, price, delivery, eligibility, or when the bonus is newly valuable and not commonly already owned.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is correct according to a passage, then choose the statement explicitly asserted, not a stronger policy inference.
Error pattern: I replaced the author’s stated conclusion with a plausible generalization about prevention strategy.
Diagnostic check: Underline the passage’s direct claim; reject any option adding superlatives, priority rankings, or new abstractions not literally supported.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items where one option paraphrases the text and others sound reasonable but extend it.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for implication, best inference, main purpose, or evaluation beyond explicit statements.

Transfer rule: If a passage frames a tension but ends with a concrete resolving method, then choose the resolution as the core point, not the tension itself.
Error pattern: Mistaking background conflict and qualification language for the main claim, while underweighting the author’s endorsed solution.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark problem, constraint, and proposed remedy; if one element is presented as “while developing, do X to reduce harm,” treat X as central.
Use when: Expository passages first note realism, limits, or tradeoffs, then introduce a practical measure or strategy.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the text only compares positions or describes a conflict without endorsing any remedy.

Transfer rule: If a claim chains “ahead/behind” comparisons across references, then assign signed offsets to each link and combine them before judging the conclusion.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking relative differences instead of trusting everyday wording or irrelevant details.
Diagnostic check: Define standard time as 0; write each device’s offset with +/− signs, compute the target offset, and compare it to the stated inference.
Use when: One object is compared to a second, and the second is compared to a third benchmark in timing, distance, score, or other directional quantities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relations are not directional, not additive, or the comparison baseline changes mid-argument.

Transfer rule: If a figurative description maps a quality from one sense onto another sense or object, then mark it as synaesthesia.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking for cross-sensory transfer, not just any vivid image, comparison, or personification.
Diagnostic check: Underline the sensory words; if at least two different senses are linked in one description, and one is used to characterize the other, accept it.
Use when: The choices are literary descriptions involving perception words such as visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, or gustatory imagery.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the language is literal, uses only one sense, or relies on metaphor without any sensory crossover.

Transfer rule: If premises chain a trait to distrust and distrust to refusal to cooperate, then infer the end-of-chain result for that trait only.
Error pattern: Success came from following a strict conditional chain and avoiding converse, inverse, or opposite-trait generalizations.
Diagnostic check: Write the links as Trait → not trusted; not trusted → no cooperation; then verify the choice matches the composed direction exactly.
Use when: Apply this on verbal-logic items with universal statements, causal/conditional links, and tempting answers about the opposite trait.
Boundary: Ignore this when premises are probabilistic, hedged, exception-filled, or require outside knowledge rather than pure linkage.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts an emotionally appealing action with cautions about its consequences, then infer the author’s main point as a call for rational, measured handling, not the side remark.
Error pattern: I selected a stated supporting principle and missed the higher-level stance formed by the warning plus the follow-up justification.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, summarize the passage in one sentence that includes both the author’s caution and purpose; choose the option matching that full sentence.
Use when: The passage discusses policy or action, warns against one approach, and then explains broader values or goals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, definition, or directly quoted claim rather than the overall intended message.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts superficial cultural borrowing with core values, then choose the summary about limited impact on basic culture, not side examples.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the author’s thesis from illustrative cases and from a narrower supporting contrast.
Diagnostic check: State the claim in one sentence without examples; verify each paragraph supports it, and reject choices focused on causes, examples, or one subgroup.
Use when: Apply to main-point questions with cross-cultural examples, concessions, and a final contrast between surface adoption and deeper institutions or values.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an inference, attitude, specific detail, or when examples themselves are the author’s actual conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the statement inconsistent with a passage, then test each option against only what the passage explicitly states or directly implies.
Error pattern: Replacing a precise claim in the text with a broader paraphrase and treating that as supported.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark quoted support, direct implication, or unsupported leap; choose the one with no clear textual basis.
Use when: The passage gives specific causes, limits, and conditional factors, and options vary in scope from narrow restatements to broad summaries.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for best explanation, main idea, or a reasonable inference beyond strict textual support.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one work type could be by a person but another could only be by someone with traits that person lacks, then infer only the split attribution, not a universal impossibility.
Error pattern: Overgeneralized from claims about one candidate’s limits to a claim about what no single author could have done.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as possibility, necessity, or exclusion; then verify your choice restates only those tags without adding stronger scope.
Use when: Relevant in authorship, capability, or qualification arguments contrasting what someone may have done versus could not have done.
Boundary: Ignore when premises explicitly rule out all candidates jointly or state that no one person could satisfy both conditions.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a moral motive from a costly business choice, then prefer evidence showing they acted against expected profit.
Error pattern: I overvalued audience-shift facts and ignored the need to rule out ordinary financial explanations for behavior.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: which option makes the action economically disadvantageous yet still taken, thereby isolating a nonfinancial motive?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about motives, especially when conduct could stem from either ethics or self-interest.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about market effects, readership changes, or causation rather than inferred motivation.

Transfer rule: If asked whether a document is “law,” then verify both issuing authority with legislative power and formal enactment as a statute, not just its title or topic.
Error pattern: I overfocused on the word “regulations” and ignored the deeper screen of whether the document is a state-issued legal norm at all.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark 1) legislative organ? 2) enacted through legislative procedure? 3) generally binding legal norm? Eliminate any failing any item.
Use when: This applies to classification questions distinguishing laws from codes of conduct, school rules, policies, or lower-level normative documents.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about morality, internal discipline only, or legal effect within a non-state organization.

Transfer rule: If an argument gives a negated fact plus two conditionals, then match the exact variable chain and polarity, including any contrapositive needed.
Error pattern: I matched surface plausibility instead of preserving the argument’s formal structure across all three statements.
Diagnostic check: Rename statements as P, Q, R; mark negations; test whether the candidate reproduces “not P; if P then not Q; if Q then R” or its exact equivalent.
Use when: Relevant for analogy questions built from short conditional statements, negations, and linked implications.
Boundary: Ignore when choices depend on causal meaning, quantifiers, modality, or extra premises rather than structural equivalence alone.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a treatment is unnecessary because a condition resolves on its own and the treatment only eases symptoms, then look for evidence the treatment also improves the underlying outcome or speeds recovery.
Error pattern: Success pattern: attacked the hidden premise that symptom relief has no curative benefit.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the conclusion’s required assumptions; test whether any option makes “only symptomatic, not curative” false.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about self-limiting conditions, conservative care, or claims that an intervention lacks necessity because it does not cure.
Boundary: Ignore when choices merely restate symptom relief, support rest/watchful waiting, or do not change recovery itself.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from a trait’s evolved function to how instances of that trait should be judged, then look for a principle linking origin/function to evaluation standard.
Error pattern: Correctly identified a bridge-principle question and matched the conclusion’s evaluative criterion to the premise about purpose.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the premise, conclusion, and missing link as “because it developed for X, it should be assessed by X”; choose the option that exactly supplies that conditional.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/justify questions involving adaptation, purpose, function, or design used to support a normative or evaluative claim.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument needs causal evidence, a definition shift, or a comparison rather than a function-to-standard bridge.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus links a group’s perceptual preference to better sales under equal price/constant conditions, then infer sales reflect that preference in at least one respect.
Error pattern: Success comes from making the weakest supported inference and avoiding added claims about causes, rankings, or strongest factors.
Diagnostic check: List the stated facts, note what is held constant, then ask which choice merely restates the observed correlation without introducing new variables.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen-supported questions involving preference, perception, and comparative purchasing outcomes with a controlled comparison.
Boundary: Ignore when choices require causal mechanisms, broad generalizations, or extra distinctions not explicitly established by the stimulus.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus says some belief or “fiction” is necessary for stability, then infer that losing that belief would tend to reduce stability.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: converting a stated necessary condition into the supported consequence, without strengthening it beyond the passage.
Diagnostic check: Mark necessity words like “vital,” “necessary,” or “without”; then test each option by negating the named belief and checking whether the predicted result follows directly.
Use when: Necessary-assumption or most-supported questions about institutions, legitimacy, public belief, or stability.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage gives only correlations, alternative causes, or no claim that the belief is required.

Transfer rule: If a passage focuses on how people assign identity labels or stereotypes from an event, then choose the option about labeling/interpretation, not the event’s moral theme.
Error pattern: I over-weighted the vivid example and inferred the author’s value judgment instead of identifying the passage’s meta-level discussion target.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the author mainly evaluating the act itself, or criticizing how observers categorize the actors?” Pick the option matching that level.
Use when: The text describes public reactions, speculation about people’s traits, hidden assumptions, or “subtext” behind comments.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage directly argues for a moral principle or discusses behavior without discussing others’ framing.

Transfer rule: If a passage says flourishing needs not only material conditions but also spiritual support, then infer both are necessary, not a hierarchy or identity claim.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating “not only ... but also ...” into joint necessity and resisting stronger comparisons or redefinitions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each claim as necessary condition, comparative claim, definition, or relation; choose only an option matching the same claim type.
Use when: Apply this to inference questions built from contrastive or additive wording about material and spiritual factors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text explicitly ranks factors, defines terms, or discusses causal sufficiency rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If a claim is introduced as “it is a mistake to think that…,” then treat the negation of that thought as the main conclusion, not a supporting reason.
Error pattern: I collapsed the author’s target claim into a broader premise and missed the conclusion about what a process will not produce.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What exact proposition is being denied as mistaken?” Then verify which choice preserves the same subject and modality.
Use when: Relevant in arguments with a belief-report setup plus “after all/since/because” support and choices that paraphrase both premise and conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for a subsidiary conclusion, inference, or the argument lacks an explicit attacked belief.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires introducing expertise without changing the person’s original employment relationship, then choose arrangements like part-time, temporary, or dual-affiliation roles.
Error pattern: I overfocused on cross-region movement and prestige, while ignoring the key constraint that the original unit relationship must remain unchanged.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the person keep their original employer/personnel ties while serving another organization by contract or limited-term work?
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about talent introduction, personnel systems, labor affiliation, secondment,兼职, external experts, or contract-based appointments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept instead requires full transfer, permanent relocation, household registration change, or family/job resettlement.

Transfer rule: If a ratio stays unchanged while one side’s total increases, then the other side’s total must increase proportionally too.
Error pattern: Success pattern—tracking ratio constraints correctly and inferring a necessary change in an unstated total.
Diagnostic check: Translate the claim into variables; hold the ratio constant, increase one variable, and verify whether the paired variable must also rise.
Use when: Relevant in must-be-true problems involving averages, rates, per-unit comparisons, or unchanged ratios across time.
Boundary: Ignore when the ratio could be offset by definitional shifts, hidden subgroup changes, or when the prompt asks what could happen rather than must happen.

Transfer rule: If a plan claims eradication by removing current carriers, then test whether a reservoir can recreate new carriers after the intervention.
Error pattern: Success came from checking for overlooked feedback loops that restore the original transmission vector.
Diagnostic check: Map the transmission cycle and ask, “After all present carriers are removed, can any remaining infected host regenerate the vector or pathway?”
Use when: Apply this to epidemiology, ecology, or system plans involving eradication, containment, or one-time elimination of intermediaries.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already blocks all reservoirs/reseeding routes or concerns only reduction rather than permanent eradication.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts groups by one factor and later compares outcomes, then choose the option stating that factor’s influence, not a stronger prescription or guarantee.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the conclusion’s strength to the evidence and avoiding causal overreach from correlation-like summaries.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rank choices by strength; eliminate any that add advice, absolute certainty, or broader claims not directly supported by the comparison.
Use when: Apply this to reading-comprehension items with survey/result narratives, grouped percentages, and a blank asking for the most justified takeaway.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly argues for action, gives a normative claim, or provides evidence establishing necessity or certainty.

Transfer rule: If asked for the EXCEPT supporter of a hypothesis, then eliminate choices that make the hypothesis more plausible and pick the one that is merely alternative, irrelevant, or non-supportive.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing direct evidential links from facts that explain the phenomenon in some other way.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “If this were true, would it increase belief in the specific storage location/mechanism, not just in oxygen needs or diving ability?”
Use when: Apply on strengthen/EXCEPT questions about a proposed mechanism, organ function, or causal explanation with several plausible-sounding facts.
Boundary: Ignore when choices require outside science knowledge or when the task is not to evaluate support for a specific hypothesis.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives examples from different eras and ends with a broad synthesis, then choose the option that captures the shared abstract theme across the examples.
Error pattern: Success came from integrating supporting details instead of fixating on one period, method, or causal claim not established by the text.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each example in 3–5 words and state the common relation linking all of them; match only the choice expressing that relation.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions built from multiple illustrations, comparisons across contexts, and a summarizing final sentence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, chronology, definition, or a cause-effect claim explicitly narrower than the whole passage.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers a permanent trend from a short run of record-setting observations, then check whether the passage says such runs can arise from ordinary fluctuation.
Error pattern: Strength is in resisting overgeneralization from limited evidence; temporary patterns may mimic lasting change.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does the evidence rule out chance variation as an explanation for this streak?” If no, reject permanence claims.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions about trends, records, streaks, averages, or causation versus randomness over limited time spans.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus provides long-term causal evidence, explicit exclusion of random variation, or direct proof of permanence.

Transfer rule: If a passage argues a current policy/action is inadvisable because supporting conditions are immature or flawed, then infer it advocates improving the underlying system, not merely distinguishing concepts.
Error pattern: Mistaking a premise or contrast for the author’s main claim instead of the normative takeaway.
Diagnostic check: Mark the conclusion words, list each reason, then ask which option best captures the recommendation implied by all reasons together.
Use when: Main-argument questions where the text contrasts reality with legal/formal procedure and gives multiple structural reasons.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a definition, direct paraphrase, or a specifically stated contrast rather than the central thesis.

Transfer rule: If examples show different immediate aims affecting the same facility/resource, then infer the shared higher-level goal around maximizing that facility’s use over time.
Error pattern: I fixated on the visible tactic and broad profit motive instead of abstracting the common target constrained by both examples.
Diagnostic check: List each example’s direct effect, identify the common object changed in both, and choose the option naming that object-level objective, not a generic business outcome.
Use when: A passage contrasts time-specific purposes, then asks for the unified underlying purpose behind them.
Boundary: Ignore this when the examples do not converge on one common object/resource or when the conclusion asks for a broader external motive.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “not judged best” to “therefore neglected,” then test whether it assumes no middle ground between top-ranked and ignored.
Error pattern: False dichotomy/equivocation on attention: treating lack of highest endorsement as equivalent to neglect.
Diagnostic check: Rephrase the conclusion using a weaker status (“not best”); if that no longer supports “neglected,” ask whether partial use, secondary value, or mixed attention is possible.
Use when: Rankings, surveys, or preferences are used to infer disregard, exclusion, or omission about alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises explicitly define anything not top-ranked as neglected or provide direct evidence of actual neglect.

Transfer rule: If a seating/position puzzle gives fixed gaps and adjacency, then enumerate every legal position pair from each constraint before combining them.
Error pattern: I made unsupported eliminations and shifted assumptions midstream instead of preserving all candidates consistently.
Diagnostic check: List all ordered pairs for each relation, intersect them, then build one full arrangement for each remaining target option to test feasibility.
Use when: Apply this to linear ordering problems with numbered slots, exact-distance phrases, adjacency, and comparative order constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is conceptual or probabilistic rather than a finite placement puzzle with explicit discrete positions.

Transfer rule: If something usually occurs and can happen only through one channel/location/group, then infer it sometimes uses that channel/location/group.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching a quantifier-plus-necessity structure, not surface topic similarity or stronger/weaker wording.
Diagnostic check: Abstract to variables: “Usually X are Y; only Z are Y; therefore some X are Z,” and verify both premises support an existential conclusion.
Use when: Relevant in parallel-reasoning questions with frequency terms like usually/most and restriction terms like only/allowed/only place.
Boundary: Ignore when premises use all/none, conclusions claim all rather than some, or the restriction points in the wrong direction.

Transfer rule: If an argument alleges contradiction between “has a legal/rightful power” and “ought not exercise it because of responsibilities,” then separate entitlement from moral or role-based constraints.
Error pattern: Treating different normative domains—ownership/authority versus duties to others—as if they were the same claim.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each statement as “can/is permitted” versus “should/has responsibility”; if both can be true together, there is no contradiction.
Use when: The stimulus mixes rights, permissions, obligations, harms to others, or stewardship duties in evaluating an action.
Boundary: Ignore this when both statements are in the same normative domain and use the same standard of permission or obligation.

Transfer rule: If a concept is based on category membership or intrinsic kind, then treat it as abstract; if based on observable qualities, then treat it as concrete.
Error pattern: Confusing sensory attributes with essential, class-defining properties.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: if the visible trait changed, would the item remain in the same class? Prefer the option whose grouping survives such changes.
Use when: The task contrasts intrinsic nature versus external features, or asks to separate classification by kind from description by appearance.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question defines “abstract” differently, such as in formal logic, linguistics, or everyday imageability.

Transfer rule: If a sentence says researchers mixed a substance-containing material with cells containing a cell type, then choose the underlying active substance and the contained cell type, not the carriers or markers.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating payloads from containers and distinguishing functional entities from measurement enzymes or structural materials.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the mixture as “carrier with X” + “cells with Y,” then strip away carrier words and marker words; see which option preserves only X and Y.
Use when: Relevant in biology passages describing extracts, particles, tissues, or cells that contain other components.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for the literal mixed materials, a detection marker, or a downstream product rather than the effective contents.

Transfer rule: If an act intentionally creates sensational controversy to attract public attention for personal gain, then classify it as public-opinion blackmail.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating genuine rights defense or complaint escalation from calculated publicity-seeking through outrageous behavior.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the controversy deliberately staged, is attention the immediate mechanism, and is profit or comeback the likely goal?
Use when: Apply in definition-matching questions involving media attention, scandal, petitions, disputes, or dramatic public behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the publicity is incidental to legitimate legal, safety, labor, or abuse-related reporting rather than the core strategy.

Transfer rule: If asked for a point at issue, then find a claim one speaker supports and the other denies, not merely a topic both mention.
Error pattern: Success came from matching each speaker’s stance on the same proposition instead of chasing side issues or strength of preference.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each speaker as yes/no on one candidate statement; accept only an option where one is yes and the other is no.
Use when: Relevant in dialogue, debate, disagreement, or “point at issue” questions with competing methods, objections, or rebuttals.
Boundary: Ignore when both speakers could agree, discuss different claims, or when the question asks for assumption, inference, or main point instead.

Transfer rule: If one group is entirely inside a chairman-received set and another group is entirely inside its complement, then conclude the two groups do not overlap; combine that with any existence claim.
Error pattern: Failed to translate universal statements into set relations and disjointness before testing the existential statement.
Diagnostic check: Draw three sets, mark subset/complement links, ask “Which intersections are impossible?” then apply the “there exists” statement to eliminate options.
Use when: Problems mix all/some/no language, especially with categories linked by subset, exclusion, or reception/status conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are causal, temporal, probabilistic, or use everyday plausibility rather than strict quantifier logic.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says a group originated in one region and later migrated to another, then prefer evidence showing the same group existed earlier in the proposed origin region.
Error pattern: Strong support comes from timeline-plus-location ancestry evidence, not from facts about success, competition, or broad relatedness that do not trace origin.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: does this option place the target group earlier outside the destination and thereby make migration the best explanation?
Use when: Arguments infer origin and migration from fossil records, evolutionary timing, geographic distribution, or absence of local precursors.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for weakening, resolving a paradox, or when chronology is irrelevant to the claim.

Transfer rule: If rankings depend on total goals across a round-robin with some fixed results, then compute each team’s goals for and against from all matches before comparing a single stat like goals conceded.
Error pattern: Success came from aggregating all match constraints instead of trusting rank order or one standout result to infer defense quality.
Diagnostic check: Build a per-team table with games, goals scored, and goals allowed; verify every stated draw and win/loss is entered once, then compare the target column only.
Use when: Use this for tournament word problems mixing overall rankings, individual match outcomes, and drawn games.
Boundary: Ignore this when the asked quantity follows directly from a stated rule or when not enough match information exists to total team stats.

Transfer rule: If a question asks to resolve a paradox, then prefer the choice that introduces a hidden behavioral difference making the surprising outcome expected.
Error pattern: Success comes from comparing incentives and oversight, not just the direct payoff structure stated in the setup.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it explain why the seemingly less cost-inflating arrangement ends up with more overruns by changing monitoring, incentives, or selection conditions?
Use when: Apply on strengthen-explain paradox questions involving contracts, incentives, principal-agent problems, or mismatched expected versus actual outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to weaken, calculate, define a term, or when an option merely restates background facts without linking them to the discrepancy.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers low influence from people not recognizing members, then require an assumption linking recognizability to influence.
Error pattern: Chose a tempting background explanation instead of the necessary bridge that makes the evidence support the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Remove the candidate assumption; if the evidence no longer has any bearing on the conclusion, keep it; if the argument could still stand, reject it.
Use when: Assumption questions where the argument moves from an observed sign, awareness, or familiarity measure to an evaluative judgment.
Boundary: Ignore when the option merely explains the observation, adds context, or concerns authority rather than connecting evidence to conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from endorsing a goal/state to claiming a specific action is needed, then require an assumption that the action is necessary for that goal.
Error pattern: I treated a helpful component as sufficient support, confusing “part of” or “contributes to” with “required for.”
Diagnostic check: Ask: if the action were not taken, could the stated goal still be achieved? If yes, the assumption is too weak.
Use when: Apply on strengthen/assumption questions where a broad value claim is used to justify one concrete policy or purchase.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only that the action helps, improves, or is one good option, not that it must be done.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a problem stops worsening because yearly additions have stabilized, then check whether total harm can still grow cumulatively.
Error pattern: Confusing a flat rate of increase with a flat overall burden; success came from separating new input from accumulated effect.
Diagnostic check: Ask: even if the amount added each period stays constant, does the total stock, damage, or exposure still rise over time?
Use when: Relevant in trend, rate-versus-level, accumulation, pollution, debt, inventory, or risk arguments.
Boundary: Ignore when the outcome depends only on the current period’s amount and past amounts do not persist or compound.

Transfer rule: If a correlation coexists with a denied causal link, then prefer an answer that explains the correlation via a third variable or reverse causation.
Error pattern: I treated an answer about prescribing behavior as relevant without showing how it connects immune strength to usage frequency.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, map both facts and ask: does this option explain why low use and stronger health co-occur while preserving that use itself is not harmful?
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/weaken or reconcile questions involving observational comparisons, especially health, behavior, and causation-versus-selection issues.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for a direct mechanism of harm/benefit, or when an option explicitly provides causal evidence.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts isolated, museum-like scholarship with the need to reconnect to real life, then choose the option that explicitly bridges old and new domains into practical, living use.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the author’s core remedy to the criticism, rather than grabbing a familiar slogan about preservation, selection, or origins.
Diagnostic check: Underline the stated problem and ask, “Which choice most directly fixes this problem?” Reject any option that is generic but does not address the contrast.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items where the author criticizes current study methods and implies a preferred reform.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a factual detail, definition, or a narrow inference without a problem-solution structure.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus gives a required threshold and says present capacity cannot reach it, then infer the requirement is impossible without changing that limiting condition.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining necessary conditions and a stated capacity limit, instead of adding unsupported claims about quality, past size, or sufficiency.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as facts: need at least X for outcome; current setup supports no more than below X; therefore ask what must change before outcome is possible.
Use when: Apply on must-be-true questions with minimum thresholds, capacity constraints, and conditional language about what is required.
Boundary: Ignore when choices add converse claims, historical comparisons, or causal details not explicitly linked by the premises.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives rankings and quantitative comparisons, then choose only the conclusion directly supported by those stated comparisons.
Error pattern: Success comes from preferring the weakest justified inference and rejecting exclusives or universals not evidenced by the text.
Diagnostic check: Underline every claim in the option; for each, point to an explicit sentence supporting it, and eliminate any option needing unstated scope expansion.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension or critical-reasoning items about reports, rankings, statistics, or “most appropriate corollary” wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for background knowledge, causal explanation, or normative judgment beyond the passage.

Transfer rule: If a statement says one subgroup all has property M, another subgroup with M sometimes has T, and some total members have neither M nor T, then infer those “neither” members must lie outside the all-M subgroup and thus lack T.
Error pattern: Successful partitioning by subgroup and quantifiers, instead of guessing from the “some” statement.
Diagnostic check: Define sets for subgroup, married, and traveled; place each premise on a mini Venn or list, then ask which group the “neither” cases can possibly belong to.
Use when: Relevant in categorical verbal-logic questions mixing all/some/none across overlapping groups.
Boundary: Ignore when terms are ambiguous, time-shifted, or premises are not about fixed group membership.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined as position-based, mandatory, and scope-limited, then choose the option that ties authority to role rather than personal traits or voluntary influence.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every clause in the definition and rejecting choices that swapped in general influence, guaranteed compliance, or broader mixed categories.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the definition’s necessary features and verify the option satisfies all of them with no extra contradiction.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about authority, rights, duties, organizational roles, or legally specified powers.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is explicitly about informal influence, interpersonal charisma, discretionary practice, or mixed sources of power.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a large shared portion with a small element that “negates” or redirects outcomes, then pick the option emphasizing that small decisive factor’s impact.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s contrast-and-conclusion structure instead of being distracted by setup details or broad background claims.
Diagnostic check: Mark shared-background statements, then underline the clause giving consequence or direction; choose the answer matching that consequence, not the comparison itself.
Use when: The text includes percentages, concession words, contrast terms, and a final claim about influence on future development or outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for a method, definition, or explicit comparison rather than the author’s main emphasized takeaway.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus argues from stated facts to “good journalism,” then choose the principle that makes those facts sufficient for that evaluation.
Error pattern: Success came from matching premises to a sufficient bridge rather than picking a merely related standard.
Diagnostic check: List each premise, paraphrase the conclusion, and verify one option says those premises guarantee that conclusion.
Use when: Relevant in principle-strengthen questions with a value judgment supported by factual traits like accuracy and public interest.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a necessary condition, a weakened claim, or an option that only condemns alternatives.

Transfer rule: If a passage reports changes in surrogate health markers from an intervention, then infer only a cautious “may reduce risk” claim, not treatment superiority or broad clinical effects.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching the conclusion’s strength to the evidence and avoiding overclaiming beyond measured outcomes.
Diagnostic check: List the exact measured outcomes and compare them word-for-word to each choice; reject any option adding unmeasured endpoints, comparisons, or guaranteed effects.
Use when: Relevant for small trials, placebo-controlled studies, and questions asking what can be inferred from biomarker or symptom changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the study directly measures the stronger outcome, explicitly compares groups on that point, or states a causal conclusion.

Transfer rule: If several conditional/equivalence predictions are all false, then translate each into logic and negate them systematically before counting possibilities.
Error pattern: Success comes from formalizing statements; failure usually comes from negating implications or “all same status” claims informally.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each claim as symbols, compute its false-condition directly, then verify one assignment satisfies every falsified claim simultaneously.
Use when: Apply this on election/selection puzzles where multiple people make statements about who is chosen and you are told which statements are false.
Boundary: Ignore this when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous in scope, or not all evaluated under the same final outcome.

Transfer rule: If a claim says a molecule may become a treatment, then prefer evidence showing that adding or using it in a disease model improves disease markers.
Error pattern: Strong support comes from intervention-based, causal evidence; background facts, novelty, or theory-building details are only weakly supportive.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does it test the proposed treatment itself and show a beneficial change in the target condition, not merely describe function or significance?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen-the-hypothesis questions about drug development, biomarkers, or gene/protein functions linked to disease.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for mechanism, definition, chronology, or broad context rather than the strongest supporting evidence.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives examples or applications after a broad claim, then choose the option that restates the broad claim plus recommendation, not a single example.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the main idea from supporting details and avoiding answer choices built around one vivid detail.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each sentence as claim, evidence, or implication; if one sentence governs the others, match the answer to that governing idea.
Use when: The paragraph has an opening general statement, then an invention/example, then a call for researchers to act.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, inference, tone, or the example itself is clearly the whole point.

Transfer rule: If a paradox says a preventable harm rises in one place but not comparable places, then prefer a choice showing weaker implementation of the stated preventions in that place.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the answer to the missing causal link between available prevention methods and worsening outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each prevention named and ask whether the option directly shows reduced vaccination, reduced regulation, or reduced education compared with peers.
Use when: Apply this on strengthen-explain questions involving cross-country trends, preventable conditions, and a gap between known remedies and observed outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices mainly address measurement differences, baseline prevalence, or unrelated risk factors unless the stem asks only about correlation.

Transfer rule: If an argument says someone can repeatedly permit extra effort because others respect their judgment, then test for a hidden cooperation condition enabling that permission.
Error pattern: I chose a statement about understanding quality instead of the operational assumption that respected directives will actually be followed.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Without this assumption, could the repeated action still occur?” If refusal or noncompliance breaks the claim, that compliance premise is presupposed.
Use when: Relevant in presupposition questions where authority, permission, prestige, or respect is used to explain repeated demanding actions by others.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already explicitly states willingness/compliance, or when the missing premise concerns only evaluation, not feasibility of the action.

Transfer rule: If an argument says popularity is not due to issue positions but to image traits, then prefer evidence showing voters do not know the positions.
Error pattern: I matched a choice to Jamie’s stated cause instead of testing which choice best weakens Tommy’s causal link.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option most directly disconnects the alleged cause from the observed effect by showing the audience lacks access to that cause?”
Use when: A stimulus debates why someone is popular, successful, or preferred, especially with competing causal explanations and polling-style evidence.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to prove the alternative cause itself, not to undermine the original cause.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers cross-species gene transfer from one genome study, then prefer evidence showing genes were inherited only from ancestors and no foreign-source sequences were found.
Error pattern: Success comes from targeting the claim’s core mechanism directly, not getting distracted by facts about resilience or unusual traits.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option deny external-origin genetic material or the transfer process itself?” If not, it is weak.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about biological causation, ancestry, genome evidence, or claims that a trait came from outside sources.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to support the hypothesis or when options attack study reliability rather than the transfer claim.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by reframing an example as a broader “social problem,” then choose the option stating the larger social diagnosis, not the immediate moral exhortation.
Error pattern: Mistaking illustrative anecdotes and rhetorical questions for the main purpose, while missing the author’s evaluative shift to societal critique.
Diagnostic check: Underline the final sentence’s function; ask whether it calls for action, explains a trait, or labels a wider condition beyond the example.
Use when: The passage praises or blames individuals, then generalizes from one case to comments about present society or public morality.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion gives a direct recommendation or policy goal without broad societal assessment.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts valid criticism with missing positive elements, then choose the option naming imbalance or negativity, not a total rejection of realism.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s concession-then-critique structure and separating “insufficient positivity” from broader, unsupported accusations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the praised baseline, then underline the specific “however” complaint; verify the option matches that narrow defect only.
Use when: Apply this on passage-main-criticism questions with contrast words, mixed evaluation, and discussion of both exposing problems and affirming humane or hopeful values.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage attacks the whole approach, focuses on technique or tradition, or gives evidence for complete detachment from life.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from poll results about what people believe to a factual policy conclusion, then verify that independent evidence supports the claimed real-world condition.
Error pattern: Treating public perception or concern as proof that the underlying situation actually exists.
Diagnostic check: Mark each premise as belief-report or fact-report; if the conclusion needs a fact but premises give only beliefs, flag a belief-to-fact gap.
Use when: Polls, surveys, or opinion data are used to justify claims about trends, causes, or states of the world.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about opinions, political support, or perceptions themselves, not external facts.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends increasing a behavior because groups at higher levels do better, then check for the assumption that the increase itself does not create offsetting harm.
Error pattern: Mistaking a motivation or implementation issue for a required causal safety assumption in a prescriptive argument.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “If people moved from the lower level into the recommended range, could that very change worsen the targeted outcome?” If yes, the conclusion needs a no-harm assumption.
Use when: Advice is drawn from comparative outcome data and concludes that changing behavior will improve health or performance.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is only descriptive, or when safety of the change is explicitly established.

Transfer rule: If an argument says “imagine having to include X, Y, Z” to attack a proposal, then classify it as reductio via absurd consequences, not analogy, unless a separate parallel case is used to infer matching treatment.
Error pattern: Mistaking an illustrative extension of the same proposal for a true analogy.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the speaker comparing two cases, or showing the original rule becomes unreasonable when applied strictly?” If only the latter, choose absurd-consequence reasoning.
Use when: The stimulus criticizes a policy by expanding what compliance would require and emphasizing impractical or ridiculous results.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument depends on shared features between distinct situations to transfer a judgment.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined by a thinking process, then choose the option that directly matches that process rather than an example of inspiration or invention.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the definition’s structure to the choice instead of chasing vivid anecdotal examples.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it explicitly describe generating ideas from multiple directions or only a single trigger leading to one insight?
Use when: Apply this on definition-to-example multiple-choice questions, especially where one abstract description competes with several story-like cases.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term includes analogy, biomimicry, or insight-based invention as part of its formal definition.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one model is most competitive, then prefer evidence showing a direct mechanism linking its features to superior market performance.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning targets the conclusion’s comparative claim; weak reasoning settles for background conditions, generic necessity, or side effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option explain how the model’s stated structure produces faster, stronger, or more adaptive results than alternatives?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about business models, alliances, organizational forms, or strategies justified by speed, flexibility, and uncertainty handling.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for assumptions, weakeners, definitions, or when options mainly address feasibility rather than competitive advantage.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers faster growth from similar size plus shorter lifespan, then test whether the compared species reach maturity or key size at similar ages.
Error pattern: Confusing total lifespan with growth rate; success comes from targeting the hidden link between longevity and growth speed.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does the evidence compare age-to-size or age-at-maturity directly?” If not, look for a choice showing equal developmental timing despite different lifespans.
Use when: Comparative biology claims, life-history reasoning, or arguments equating shorter life expectancy with quicker growth.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim already uses direct growth measurements, or when lifespan is itself the stated outcome rather than support.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects restoration because unexamined evidence may be destroyed, then choose the principle that prioritizes preserving potential future evidence over present display or reconstruction benefits.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the stated objection to a value tradeoff rather than being distracted by motives, ownership, or a separate historical preference.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list premise and conclusion, then ask: what bridge rule makes “possible evidence loss” sufficient to defeat the proposed benefits?
Use when: Relevant in justify-the-argument questions involving preservation versus access, display, funding, or reconstruction based on current theories.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the objection concerns who funds or controls the project, authenticity standards, or which historical period should be represented.

Transfer rule: If an argument says choosing X would cause outcome Y, and the agent will avoid Y or maximize the opposite, then infer the agent will not choose X.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching a conditional prediction plus a stated decision priority, rather than matching topic or surface wording.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “If do X, then worse by goal G; agent prioritizes G; therefore not X,” and confirm the choice has the same deny-the-trigger structure.
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions featuring incentives, preferences, optimization, or comparative outcomes tied to a decision.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion evaluates fairness, credit, probability, or uses converse/inverse/contrapositive shifts not anchored to the agent’s goal.

Transfer rule: If a passage states necessary conditions for perception, then choose the option that restates that condition without adding strength, degree, or causation claims.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the text’s explicit condition and rejecting tempting extrapolations beyond what was stated.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether every claim is directly supported by a sentence; reject any option containing a new comparison, intensity rule, or generalized mechanism.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension questions about scientific descriptions, definitions, sensory conditions, or filtered/limited perception.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for inference, main purpose, author attitude, or external domain knowledge rather than literal support.

Transfer rule: If a passage balances benefits with risks and ends by urging measures or oversight, then choose the option combining development with supervision.
Error pattern: I overfocused on the most alarming subtopic and mistook a supporting warning for the author’s overall purpose.
Diagnostic check: List the text’s structure in order—benefit, risk, highlighted example, final recommendation—and match the answer to the final recommendation’s full scope.
Use when: Apply this to purpose/main-idea questions where one example is emphasized but the closing sentence broadens to policy or governance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific concern, example, or implied detail rather than the author’s overall aim.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers objectivity from similarity across times or groups, then test whether later judgments were shaped by earlier examples rather than independently matching them.
Error pattern: Missed a causal-dependence alternative and treated lack of exposure by some people as more damaging than influence on the standard itself.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the observed agreement arise because one side inherited, learned, or copied the other standard?” If yes, that weakens the inference.
Use when: The claim moves from cross-cultural or historical similarity to a universal, mind-independent standard.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already establishes independent formation of each judgment standard.

Transfer rule: If a claim says a new method will control or replace an outcome, then favor evidence showing key external conditions still dominate that outcome.
Error pattern: Strength is in attacking the conclusion’s core causal/control assumption, not side issues like convenience, inconsistency, or secondary tradeoffs.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this fact show the method cannot reliably produce the promised result under the needed real-world conditions?”
Use when: Apply to weaken questions about technologies, interventions, or causal tools claimed to make events happen predictably or better than existing methods.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only compare costs, ethics, ease, or partial limitations unless the conclusion itself is specifically about those factors.

Transfer rule: If totals are compared with a cause removed, then compute each group’s removed-cause contribution by subtracting the “without-cause” rate from the total rate.
Error pattern: I inferred an unproven explanation about people or equipment instead of choosing the conclusion directly forced by the arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Write total = excluded-cause + all-other-causes for each group, solve both excluded-cause amounts, and pick only the option matching that difference.
Use when: Relevant for word problems comparing rates or counts across two groups, especially when one scenario excludes a category.
Boundary: Ignore when answer choices require causal mechanisms, intentions, or abilities not explicitly measured by the given data.

Transfer rule: If a strategy reuses the firm’s existing core technology/market strengths to launch related new products with different uses, then treat it as concentric diversification.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definition clause; failures come from accepting growth, acquisition, vertical integration, or unrelated expansion as “diversification.”
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify three boxes: same core capability retained, new product category added, and products remain commercially/technologically related rather than merely upstream, downstream, or unrelated.
Use when: Apply this on management-definition questions contrasting related diversification with mergers, integration along the supply chain, or conglomerate expansion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns branding only, ownership structure, market entry mode, or pure process-chain expansion without a related new product line.

Transfer rule: If a passage shows two different methods both achieve the same goal, then infer a flexible, context-dependent combined approach, not an absolute claim about one model.
Error pattern: Success comes from generalizing cautiously from parallel evidence instead of jumping to broad value judgments or hidden costs.
Diagnostic check: List each stated method and its shared effect; choose only an option that preserves both and adds no new mechanism, motive, or impossibility claim.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions contrasting centralized and natural or alternative processes with comparable outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly ranks one method, gives causal tradeoff evidence, or asks for recommendation beyond what is stated.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives indicators and then draws a broad takeaway, then choose the option that restates that takeaway, not one that prescribes actions or overstates scope.
Error pattern: Success came from separating descriptive criteria and final conclusion, then rejecting options that turned correlation into purpose, universality, or causation.
Diagnostic check: Mark the passage’s measure, what each side signals, and the final claim; verify the option preserves direction and strength without adding “mainly,” “everyone,” or “if choose X, then Y.”
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items with contrasts, ratio/sign indicators, and a concluding “therefore” statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an unstated implication, a detail retrieval, or a directly quoted definition.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires processing one’s own application for approval, then exclude cases that are merely complaint reporting or enforcement feedback.
Error pattern: Mistaking any online government interaction and reply for an approval process, instead of checking for applicant-initiated licensing/certification review.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: who is applying, what approval/document is sought, what materials are examined, and is the reply an approval result rather than a report outcome?
Use when: Relevant for classification questions about e-government, administrative approval, permits, licenses, certificates, or online submission workflows.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept includes public reporting, consultation, supervision, or any online service beyond approval/examination.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires long-lasting unsatisfactory sleep quality, then pick the case with persistent difficulty sleeping plus ongoing daytime impairment, not merely short sleep time.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every clause in the definition and rejecting tempting cases that satisfy only duration or only reduced hours.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes: chronic course, poor/unsatisfying sleep, and functional harm; choose only an option that clearly checks all required boxes.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about disorders, conditions, or classifications with multiple necessary criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the rule uses alternative criteria, exclusions, or sufficient examples rather than a strict all-elements definition.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts an earlier ethically constrained state with a later trend toward neutrality or amorality, then infer weakening constraints, not that the earlier period already had the later trait.
Error pattern: I collapsed chronology and projected the described current trend backward onto the historical starting point.
Diagnostic check: Mark time phases and descriptors, then test each option by matching whether it states an early condition, a later development, or an unsupported causal leap.
Use when: Apply to comparative passages with “however,” trend language, historical-vs-current framing, and shifts from ethical limits to instrumental methods.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly states continuity across periods or directly gives a causal claim rather than a contrastive evolution.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires focusing on part of a stimulus while neglecting other parts, then choose the option showing simultaneous selection and neglect within the same situation.
Error pattern: I matched a case of mere busyness or distraction, not true selective filtering of aspects of one ongoing stimulus.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: what is the target stimulus, which aspect is attended, and which competing aspect is ignored at the same time?
Use when: Apply this on psychology-definition items about attention, perception, filtering, or choosing among aspects of a scene/event.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is about memory, emotion, motivation, consequences, or simple lack of time/exposure rather than attentional selection.

Transfer rule: If a circular seating puzzle mixes left/right, opposite, and genders, then draw all seats and propagate each clue stepwise before judging adjacency.
Error pattern: Chose too early from partial local fits instead of enforcing all constraints globally until only one couple-status remains possible.
Diagnostic check: Mark clockwise direction, assign every clue on a seat diagram, track genders/partners, then verify exactly one nonadjacent pair and no clue contradictions.
Use when: Round-table arrangement problems with relational terms like left, right, opposite, spouse, and uniqueness conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when orientation is undefined or clues are probabilistic, non-positional, or do not require a full consistent seating layout.

Transfer rule: If a policy argument says a relabeling will improve behavior, then test whether the people deterred by the old label currently choose options that are already better on the stated goal.
Error pattern: I focused on the speaker’s motives instead of the causal assumption linking the proposed wording change to healthier consumer choices.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “For the target consumers, compared with their current substitute, would the renamed product move them toward or away from the advocated outcome?”
Use when: An argument recommends changing names, framing, or labels to influence choices for health, safety, or welfare reasons.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns honesty, legality, or intent rather than predicted comparative effects on behavior.

Transfer rule: If a passage praises localization but warns against surface imitation without respect or understanding, then choose the option making deep cultural understanding the prerequisite.
Error pattern: Success pattern: prioritize the author’s central condition or warning over broader, merely related statements about strategy, aesthetics, or frequency.
Diagnostic check: Identify the contrast pivot; ask, “What requirement is said to determine success, and what is criticized as insufficient?”
Use when: Apply this to main-idea questions where examples support a caution about using cultural symbols, branding, or localized messaging.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, attitude strength, or a comparison rather than the passage’s governing prerequisite.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion applies a property from a cited theory/model to reality, then require that the property actually holds in that theory/model.
Error pattern: Success pattern: spotting a hidden bridge assumption linking “this framework describes reality” to “reality has feature F.”
Diagnostic check: Replace the theory name with “framework” and ask: “Without assuming framework has feature F, can the conclusion still follow?” If no, that assumption is required.
Use when: An argument moves from endorsement of a descriptive system by experts or evidence to a claim about what exists or does not exist.
Boundary: Ignore when the missing assumption concerns expert credibility, survey counts, or sufficiency of endorsement rather than transfer of a specific property.

Transfer rule: If conditional statements form a loop leading from a condition to its negation, then infer the negation of every loop member by contradiction.
Error pattern: I treated a cyclic chain as support for affirming a statement, ignoring that one link denied a later consequence in the same cycle.
Diagnostic check: Rename propositions, chain them symbolically, and test whether assuming any node makes both that node and not-that-node follow.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice logic items with only if-then links, especially when terms repeat and one clause negates a repeated outcome.
Boundary: Ignore this when premises are probabilistic, causal without strict implication, or when no closed loop with a negating link exists.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “not real” from “would vanish if belief vanished,” then require the bridge that real things do not depend on universal belief for their existence.
Error pattern: Mistook a sufficient-condition statement about belief creating existence for the needed necessary-condition statement about existence persisting without belief.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the conclusion and premise as a conditional chain, then test each option by negating it; pick the one whose negation breaks the move from dependence-on-belief to nonexistence.
Use when: Necessary-assumption questions where the stimulus argues from social acceptance, perception, or belief dependence to claims about what exists.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about knowledge, value, legitimacy, or practical effects rather than existence itself.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a food or treatment caused better health from a study, then require that the compared groups not differ in other major health-improving behaviors.
