Transfer rule: If a stimulus contrasts a newer priority with reduced attention to fundamentals, then choose the option stating that adopting the new trend can sideline basic skills.
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting the general principle from the example instead of matching surface wording or overclaiming inevitability.
Diagnostic check: Identify the “new emphasis,” the “reduced traditional area,” and test whether the option preserves a possible-result relation rather than a universal or value judgment.
Use when: Relevant in principle-illustration questions built from tradeoffs, especially education, policy, or resource-allocation examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus supports necessity, exclusivity, or comparative worth rather than a tradeoff-based cautionary pattern.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says a warning system leaves little usable time, then add the premise linking warning lead time to the event’s dangerous cases being too short.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the missing premise to the gap between mechanism description and the practical conclusion about limited usefulness.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the conclusion in plain words and ask, “What unstated fact makes this practical limitation follow from the earlier causal chain?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/necessary-premise questions where science/process facts are given and the conclusion shifts to real-world feasibility or effectiveness.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only restate background, add vivid examples, or discuss frequency/timing details that do not connect the mechanism to the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “only when,” then treat the stated condition as necessary, not enough by itself to infer the result.
Error pattern: Confusing a one-way conditional by reversing it or promoting a required condition into a guaranteeing condition.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each statement as “result → required condition”; then test whether the argument later uses “required condition → result.”
Use when: Relevant in conditional-logic questions using words like only, only if, requires, depends on, or must be.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument explicitly provides the converse, a biconditional, or an independent premise that makes the result follow.

Transfer rule: If a definition asks for the attitude’s object, then identify what the feeling targets and reject any option that switches object with subject or mislabels the target.
Error pattern: Confusing the experiencer, the target, and a related attribute/service instead of mapping the definition to the sentence structure.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Who has the attitude?” “What are they reacting to?” “Does the explanation name that target, not the person?”
Use when: A concept is defined by roles in a relation, especially attitude/emotion questions with paraphrases of everyday statements.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when options hinge on factual truth, causation, or word meaning rather than role assignment from a definition.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “not all X at all times,” then translate it as “for every time, at least one X is not affected,” and test options against that form.
Error pattern: I confused quantifier scope, treating a time-based universal restriction as if it allowed a time when everyone could still be affected.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim with symbols or plain logic using “for every” and “there exists,” then negate each option carefully to see which contradicts the original.
Use when: This applies to multiple-choice items built from claims with all/some/no, time words, or nested quantifiers.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem depends on factual knowledge, causal inference, or ordinary wording without quantifier ambiguity.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends with a therefore-thesis after giving background concessions, then choose the option that restates that final claim most directly.
Error pattern: Success came from separating supporting context from the author’s main conclusion instead of chasing earlier descriptive details.
Diagnostic check: Mark premise indicators and the conclusion indicator; paraphrase the last claim in 8–12 words, then match the option closest in scope and force.
Use when: Relevant for main-point or “directly addresses” questions with multiple related statements, examples, and a concluding summary.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, attitude, or strongest support rather than the central claim.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined as a reversible transitional stage before disease, then choose the case showing functional disturbance from ongoing strain without confirmed pathology or acute injury.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every definitional clause instead of fixating on hidden illness, absence of symptoms, or recovery status.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it between normal and disease, caused by accumulated stress, mainly functional, and still potentially reversible?
Use when: Apply this on classification questions about intermediate states, especially where some choices describe diagnosed disease, trauma recovery, or structural abnormalities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category includes established disease, permanent lesions, emergency harm, or mere asymptomatic diagnosis without a transitional functional phase.

Transfer rule: If an argument goes from “All A are B” plus “X is B” to “X is A,” then reject it and seek an analogy with the same reversed conditional.
Error pattern: Confusing a sufficient condition with a necessary one; affirming the consequent by treating a shared trait as proof of category membership.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the form symbolically as A→B; B; therefore A, and test whether many non-A cases could still be B.
Use when: The stimulus classifies things by a property and then infers identity, status, or membership from having that property.
Boundary: Ignore when the second premise actually states A, or when the conclusion only validly goes from A to B.

Transfer rule: If an argument says someone dislikes or tends toward one option, then treat that only as evidence, not as proof that alternatives are impossible.
Error pattern: Conflating a preference, habit, or likelihood with necessity; ruling out another available action without support.
Diagnostic check: List every action still logically available after the stated constraints, and ask whether any was excluded by fact or only by attitude.
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions about plans, choices, schedules, or practical constraints involving words like hates, prefers, likely, usually, or tends.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument explicitly states the alternative cannot occur or gives a strict rule eliminating it.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives signs and what each sign indicates, then choose the option capturing the overall function or message of those sign-to-result links.
Error pattern: Success comes from prioritizing the author’s main claim over vivid setup details or reversed cause-effect wording.
Diagnostic check: List the subject, the observed change, and the inferred result; if the answer matches that full chain best, keep it.
Use when: Apply to short expository passages with examples, contrasts, or clues showing what observations are used to infer.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a detail, tone, or causal mechanism rather than the passage’s main point.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from one industry or case to another by comparison, then test whether the compared harms are relevantly similar in kind and severity before accepting the policy inference.
Error pattern: Correctly identified a weak-analogy challenge rather than a dispute about definitions, facts, or source credibility.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does the reply target the comparison itself by highlighting a key disanalogy between the two cases?”
Use when: Relevant for argument-role questions where one speaker answers another by contrasting consequences, harms, or contexts across compared cases.
Boundary: Ignore when the response instead denies a premise, redefines a term, or questions who reported the information.

Transfer rule: If a term is defined by events being near in time or place, then choose the example linked by co-occurrence, not by similarity, category, or personal memory.
Error pattern: Confusing contiguity-based association with resemblance-based, thematic, or autobiographical association.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: do the two items usually happen together or nearby in the world; if separated in time/space, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for psychology items contrasting associative mechanisms, especially examples involving perception, recall, and paired events.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is about similarity, contrast, cause inference, symbolism, or learned personal triggers rather than proximity.

Transfer rule: If a passage argues current dependence yields little control or value because key technology and brands stay external, then infer the need to build domestic core technology and competitive brands.
Error pattern: I chose a broad problem-fixing statement instead of the stronger, text-grounded necessity the evidence specifically supports.
Diagnostic check: List each concrete deficiency mentioned; pick the option that directly reverses most of them, not one that merely calls for improvement.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions contrasting specific structural lacks with general policy or process-oriented responses.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly limits claims to harm reduction, feasibility, or a narrower short-term policy change.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion compares totals across subsets, then translate each statement into category counts and combine them before choosing.
Error pattern: I treated a local property of one subset as sufficient, instead of checking whether the whole-population comparison follows.
Diagnostic check: Let total = pinned + flat; carving = all pinned + some flat; non-carving = remaining flat. Test each option by symbolic counts to see whether carving must exceed non-carving.
Use when: Relevant for partitioned-set arguments with universal and existential claims that end in “more/fewer than” conclusions.
Boundary: Ignore when choices hinge on wording, causality, or definitions rather than count relationships across exhaustive categories.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires people working below the surface through excavated underground passages, then reject any option lacking subsurface entry and tunnel-like channels.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every clause of the definition instead of keying on a single word like “construction” or “maintenance.”
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: below ground, entered by workers, at depth from surface, via excavated passage, for production/maintenance purpose? Eliminate any “no.”
Use when: Apply this to category-definition multiple choice items about work environments, methods, or legal/safety classifications.
Boundary: Ignore when the definition is metaphorical, abbreviated, or the options hinge on exceptions, time limits, or jurisdiction-specific inclusions.

Transfer rule: If a second speaker adds a new causal reason that by itself favors the same recommendation, then classify it as independent support for the conclusion, not a required missing premise.
Error pattern: Mistaking corroborating evidence for a necessary assumption or indispensable premise.
Diagnostic check: Remove the added statement and ask: does the first argument still reach its conclusion from its own stated reason? If yes, the addition is independent support.
Use when: One argument is followed by an “indeed/in fact” remark giving another mechanism, effect, or consideration pointing to the same policy or claim.
Boundary: Ignore when the added statement is needed to link an existing premise to the conclusion or explains a premise rather than separately backing the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a proposal aims to restore behavior by removing one suspected cause, then check whether alternative causes in the same system would still produce the problem.
Error pattern: I focused on measuring effect size at the named target instead of testing whether the target is uniquely causally relevant.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If this intervention is fully implemented, what other sources could still trigger the same unwanted outcome?”
Use when: Necessary-assumption or evaluate-the-plan questions about causal fixes, especially when one location, factor, or actor is singled out.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out competing causes or when the question asks for impact magnitude rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If a statement lists benefits to two different parties, then choose the option that restates a joint benefit and reject options claiming harm, uselessness, or reversal.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning from explicit positive consequences to the least stronger paraphrase covering all named beneficiaries.
Diagnostic check: Underline each stated effect, map each to who gains, then verify the choice preserves all effects without adding stronger claims or contradictions.
Use when: The prompt gives a causal claim with clearly positive outcomes and asks what must be true.
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes are conditional, mixed, ironic, or when choices hinge on quantity, exclusivity, or unstated causal assumptions.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires bottom-up, mutual member influence plus shared decision/responsibility/benefit, then choose the option showing ongoing peer collaboration independent of formal rank.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all core conditions instead of overvaluing a single active person, rotation, or mere process reorganization.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the option has peer-to-peer influence, broad internal participation, shared authority/responsibility, and collaboration; reject any missing one.
Use when: Apply this to concepts about distributed, shared, collective, or horizontal leadership/team processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept is individual initiative, formal delegation, task reassignment, or simple role rotation without real shared influence.

Transfer rule: If a claim contrasts per-item performance with total category contribution, then look for a difference in the number of items across categories.
Error pattern: Success came from separating average or typical outcome from aggregate outcome and asking what hidden quantity could bridge them.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rewrite the statements as “per unit” versus “sum over all units,” then test whether changing only category counts could remove the tension.
Use when: Apply this on resolve-the-discrepancy questions involving rates, averages, percentages, or typical returns versus overall totals.
Boundary: Ignore this when totals are fixed equal, the issue is causal rather than arithmetic, or the answer must explain a mechanism instead of aggregation.

Transfer rule: If every subgroup’s average rises but the overall average falls, then check for changes in subgroup sizes or composition that shift weight toward lower-average groups.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a weighted-average/composition effect rather than treating the overall average as a simple summary of subgroup trends.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Could more cases have moved into lower-paying groups, enough to drag down the national average despite within-group increases?”
Use when: Relevant in paradox questions comparing regional, sectoral, demographic, or time-based subgroup averages with an aggregate average.
Boundary: Ignore when subgroup shares are fixed or when the issue is causal policy impact without any averaging or aggregation conflict.

Transfer rule: If asked what cannot be directly derived, then eliminate choices explicitly supported or paraphrased and reject any option adding a new comparison, subgroup claim, or extra premise.
Error pattern: Mistaking a broad relational claim for an unsupported leap, while overlooking that comparative statements usually need evidence not stated.
Diagnostic check: For each option, underline every key element and match it to exact text; if any element introduces ranking, age groups, quantities, or causation absent from the passage, mark it unsupported.
Use when: Short reading-inference questions asking for the statement not directly implied by a general argument.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the best extension, main idea, or a claim requiring outside common knowledge.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires acts by governmental organs or officials under legal authority, then first verify the actor has formal administrative status and rulemaking power.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every definition element instead of focusing only on topic, public benefit, or policy seriousness.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark actor, legal authority source, decision form, and public-administration role; eliminate any case led by social, trade, or private organizations.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about administrative acts, government decisions, regulatory measures, or exercises of public power.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept includes non-government self-regulation, delegated private enforcement, or mixed bodies explicitly treated as administrative by the prompt.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers present scientific legitimacy from past acceptance by brilliant thinkers, then test whether changes in evidence or theory over time break that inference.
Error pattern: Mistaking historical endorsement or authority for timeless scientific support; ignoring that scientific status is time-sensitive.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could this claim have fit the best evidence then but conflict with later evidence or theories now?” If yes, the reasoning is weak.
Use when: The support cites respected people, earlier eras, tradition, or former consensus to defend a current scientific conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already compares past and present evidence directly rather than relying on acceptance alone.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the wrong understanding, then match each option to explicit claims and reject choices that add one-sided value judgments not stated.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing neutral, mixed influence in the passage from an option that exaggerated it into purely negative influence.
Diagnostic check: Underline each effect named in the passage; if both enabling and limiting effects appear, eliminate any option claiming only harm or only benefit.
Use when: Apply this to reading-comprehension items about an author's context, influence, atmosphere, causes, or effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage itself clearly makes an evaluative claim or asks for an inference beyond literal paraphrase.

Transfer rule: If an objection relies on a distance or containment limit, then prefer evidence showing a mechanism that extends exposure beyond that limit.  
Error pattern: I chose evidence about harm in the accepted zone instead of attacking the objection’s key assumption about who could be exposed.  
Diagnostic check: Underline the objection’s hinge claim, ask “what must be false for this objection to fail?”, then pick the option that directly falsifies that claim.  
Use when: Relevant in weaken/refute questions where one side explains away causation using range, timing, or physical spread constraints.  
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for supporting evidence, or when an option only shows the hazard is harmful without changing exposure feasibility.

Transfer rule: If a rebuttal adds a new causal factor that can offset an argument’s effect without disproving its premise, then classify it as weakening support, not refutation.
Error pattern: Confusing a partial underminer with a direct contradiction or a counterexample.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does the response deny the original evidence, or introduce an independent consideration showing the conclusion may not follow strongly?
Use when: Competing causes, offsetting effects, or tradeoffs are introduced in strengthen/weaken or method-of-reasoning questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the reply gives a concrete case contradicting the claim, attacks an assumption directly, or proves the conclusion independently.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires initiating a civil court case in one’s own name to protect civil rights, then choose only the option that starts such a civil action.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definitional element and rejecting lookalikes from criminal reporting, appeals, or procedural moves inside an existing case.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark for each option: initiator, forum, case type, timing, and purpose; accept only if all five fit the definition.
Use when: Apply this to legal-definition multiple choice where several options involve authorities or courts but differ by procedure, stage, or branch of law.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept is broader than first-instance civil filing or expressly includes appeals, complaints, or counterclaims.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts tools by function and asks what is reasonable, then choose the option matching the stated goal with the tool’s described capability.
Error pattern: Success came from aligning mission requirements with explicit functional differences instead of reacting to dramatic or unsupported alternatives.
Diagnostic check: List the goal, list each tool’s stated abilities, eliminate any option requiring unstated capabilities or adding a new strategy not supported by the passage.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions that compare categories, roles, or technologies and ask for the best deployment or recommendation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for moral judgment, outside knowledge, or when multiple options are equally supported by the text.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists social interaction and a relatively fixed gathering space without explicitly requiring the internet, then test both online and offline groups before choosing.
Error pattern: I over-literalized a familiar term and anchored on a prototypical internet example instead of the exact stated criteria.
Diagnostic check: Underline each necessary condition, then verify for every option whether each condition is explicitly met; reject choices that fit only by association with the label.
Use when: This applies to concept-definition multiple choice items where everyday terminology may differ from the definition provided in the stem.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem explicitly restricts the domain or gives an unambiguous technical definition.

Transfer rule: If a warranty lists different remedies by time window and service type, then match each option to the specific promised remedy and time limit separately.
Error pattern: I conflated any product defect with the earliest, strongest remedy instead of checking whether the requested service fit the stated window.
Diagnostic check: Make a mini table: issue cause, elapsed time, requested remedy, and compare each column against every clause; reject any option failing one clause.
Use when: Relevant for consumer-policy, contract, warranty, or rule-application questions with multiple deadlines, exceptions, and remedies.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for moral judgment, best practice, or unstated assumptions rather than strict policy matching.

Transfer rule: If a passage presents evidence and mechanisms supporting one central claim, then choose the option stating that broad claim, not a supporting detail.
Error pattern: Main-idea success comes from separating the thesis from explanatory mechanisms and background description.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a five-word summary of the whole passage; confirm the option matches that summary better than any detail-level statement.
Use when: The text has one headline claim followed by examples, processes, or reasons showing how it could happen.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific function, detail, inference, or the author’s attitude instead of overall content.

Transfer rule: If a passage compares systems and states one wins under competition, then choose the option summarizing comparative superiority, not merely its benefits.
Error pattern: I collapsed a comparative main claim into a weaker causal/support claim by focusing on effects instead of the passage’s verdict.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the author mainly saying this helps, or that this is better than alternatives?” Match the answer choice to that scope.
Use when: Relevant for summary/main-idea questions featuring contrast words, competition between models, or explicit winner/stronger suitability language.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage only explains functions or consequences without comparing alternatives or making an overall preference judgment.

Transfer rule: If a passage predicts warming from absorbed solar energy, then choose the follow-up that states an equal or balancing energy loss from the whole Earth system.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the causal gap and selecting the statement that directly counteracts it, not one that merely redistributes, interrupts briefly, or restates internal heat.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option reduce net energy gain over time globally, rather than move energy around or describe a short-lived event?”
Use when: Relevant in climate, radiation, or energy-budget questions asking what prevents continual heating, cooling, or runaway change.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about regional effects, transient phenomena, or internal structure rather than long-term global balance.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both a social public-issue focus and analytical depth, then choose the option showing systematic investigation plus explanation of causes/impacts.  
Error pattern: Success comes from matching all necessary criteria, not being distracted by timeliness, prominence, repetition, or promotional tone.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the candidate addresses a broad social problem, uses investigation/analysis, and goes beyond event narration; reject any missing one item.  
Use when: Apply this to category-definition questions about journalistic forms, especially when several options are ordinary reports, follow-ups, official activities, or publicity pieces.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target category is defined mainly by medium, length, speed, or audience format rather than purpose and method.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what most supports a claimed cause, then choose the fact that links the cited feature to a motive affecting the outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the proposed cause to an employee-valued mechanism, not from picking a merely plausible alternative explanation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this statement make the named feature directly increase retention, rather than just describe the industry or another factor?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/causal explanation items where one distinctive workplace trait is offered to explain unusually strong retention or similar outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is to weaken, resolve a paradox, or compare broad background conditions unrelated to the claimed causal trait.

Transfer rule: If an argument dismisses anecdotes by analogy to selective memory, then require that analogous misses are less likely to be remembered than hits.
Error pattern: Necessary-assumption questions often hinge on an unstated memory or sampling bias that makes the anecdotal evidence look stronger than it is.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected assumption; if the analogy no longer explains why the anecdotes are unreliable, that assumption is required.
Use when: Apply this to arguments comparing one anecdotal claim to another rumor where observers recall confirming cases more vividly than nonconfirming cases.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument instead relies on causation, base rates, or representativeness rather than recall bias.

Transfer rule: If a passage links a specific setting or sensory detail to ideas arising, then choose the option stating that direct link, not a broader environmental generalization.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a concrete travel-image claim to an abstract claim about all thinking being shaped by environment.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the subject, trigger, and result in the passage; verify the option preserves all three at the same specificity.
Use when: The prompt asks for the main point or intended explanation and the passage gives a concrete cause-effect example from travel or scenery.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly broadens from the example to a universal principle or emphasizes character growth rather than thought generation.

Transfer rule: If a statement offers alternatives with pros/cons but no ranking, then infer only the logical relation between options, not a preference or priority.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating disjunction-based commitments from evaluative comparisons unsupported by the wording.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim in logic form; mark whether it asserts exclusivity/inclusivity/necessity, then ask whether any answer adds a value judgment absent from that form.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items built from “either/or,” conditionals, and descriptive attributes of alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly states a recommendation standard, preference ordering, decision rule, or comparative conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers anxiety from delayed replies, then require an assumption that immediate replying is normally feasible and expected, not an alternative reason for delay.
Error pattern: I chose a distractor that explains delayed response instead of the background norm that makes delay seem suspicious.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “If this statement were false, would the suspicious/anxious reaction lose its basis?” Prefer the option establishing expectation, not merely giving another cause.
Use when: Necessary-assumption questions about emotional reactions, social expectations, technology-enabled timing, or unmet response norms.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a weakening explanation, a sufficient cause, or a direct reason someone did not respond.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires perception without external stimulation, then reject cases that start from a real object being misidentified and prefer cases with no sensory trigger present.
Error pattern: I confused illusion with hallucination by focusing on fear-based misinterpretation instead of checking whether any external stimulus existed.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “What physical stimulus is acting on that sense right now?” If one exists, it is not hallucination under this definition.
Use when: Relevant in classification questions contrasting hallucination, illusion, imagination, or ordinary perceptual bias using definitional wording about objective stimulation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target category explicitly includes distortion of real stimuli or when the prompt asks for illusion rather than hallucination.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a conditional limit on when to stop resisting failure, then preserve that limit; don’t strengthen it into “never.”
Error pattern: Overgeneralized a qualified principle by dropping necessary conditions and converting a bounded claim into an absolute one.
Diagnostic check: Compare the option’s strength to the stem: underline qualifiers like “until,” “when still,” or “unless,” and reject any choice that removes them.
Use when: Applicable in verbal logic questions where persistence, exceptions, or acceptance depends on whether a final condition has been reached.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the stem itself states an unconditional rule with no exception, threshold, or timing qualifier.

Transfer rule: If a forecast about a seller’s decline is based on trouble among local buyers, then check that the seller is not mainly supported by customers from elsewhere.
Error pattern: I focused on an extra condition about reduced activity among remaining buyers instead of testing whether the cited customer group actually drives most sales.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the conclusion still fail if the affected local market shrinks, because outside demand or other customer segments dominate?”
Use when: The argument infers sales or revenue changes for one business from changes in one named customer base, region, or sector.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise already states that this customer group provides most sales or when the conclusion concerns only that subgroup.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives evidence against one common remedy and ends with a broader recommendation, then choose the option matching the overall takeaway, not a side point.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s main conclusion instead of latching onto supporting facts, comparisons, or intermediate claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, paraphrase the final sentence in 8–12 words and see which option most closely matches that paraphrase.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items with experimental evidence, a rejection of one practice, and a concluding advice statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, purpose of one example, or an unstated implication rather than the central message.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires estimating restoration to basic normal status plus needed time/resources before emergency management ends, then choose the option that evaluates recovery duration or restoration requirements.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every clause of the definition instead of picking any emergency-related action.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it an evaluation, not an intervention/order, and does it estimate return-to-normal time or resources during the emergency?
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about emergency management stages, recovery, restoration, or assessment versus response actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept concerns prevention, immediate rescue, command decisions, or post-event long-term reconstruction rather than recoverability assessment.

Transfer rule: If a ranking problem mixes pairwise inequalities with a threshold count, then convert the threshold into person-by-person status constraints before ordering anyone.
Error pattern: I overused relative comparisons and failed to enforce the global count condition, allowing an impossible placement to survive.
Diagnostic check: Mark each person as forced above, below, or uncertain relative to the cutoff; count how many can be nonqualifying, then verify every adjacent ranking pair respects all inequalities.
Use when: Apply this to logic questions with score ordering, cutoff categories, and statements comparing sums or relative performance.
Boundary: Ignore when no global count/category constraint exists, or when the task is pure arithmetic rather than consistency-based ranking.

Transfer rule: If asked for the most accurate summary, then choose the option matching the passage’s main claim, not a prerequisite, method, or hoped-for result.
Error pattern: I elevated a supporting condition and implied benefit over the author’s central topic and conclusion.
Diagnostic check: In 10 words or fewer, state the passage’s thesis; eliminate any option that captures only one reason, step, or consequence.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea/summary questions with argumentative structure, especially when the text includes premises, dialogue conditions, and a final evaluative statement.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an assumption, inference, purpose of a detail, or a specifically named subclaim.

Transfer rule: If two speakers debate causation versus voluntary choice, then isolate the exact disputed link: whether the policy itself would produce the behavior.
Error pattern: Success pattern: separating a shared background claim from the single premise one speaker denies.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase each speaker as “X says policy change would/would not cause outcome Y”; pick the answer matching that yes/no clash, not side remarks.
Use when: Apply on “point at issue” questions with short dialogues where one side challenges another’s because-premise or causal explanation.
Boundary: Ignore when the disagreement is about facts both discuss independently, definitions, or predicted compliance without a causal dispute.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires migration because residence has become uninhabitable from environmental deterioration, then choose the option showing direct forced displacement by that change.
Error pattern: I matched a broad environmental hardship example instead of checking for strongest fit to every definitional element.
Diagnostic check: Verify three boxes: environmental change worsens the place itself, people cannot continue living there, and relocation is compelled rather than planned or seasonal.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching items about migration, causation, or necessary conditions among several plausible environmental scenarios.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept allows voluntary, temporary, policy-driven, or merely economically motivated movement without loss of habitability.

Transfer rule: If a study infers X causes Y from a questionnaire/correlation, then look for evidence that Y could instead drive X or that both share a cause.
Error pattern: Causal-inference success pattern—testing for reverse causation and confounding rather than accepting the authors’ preferred mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does any option make the observed association likely even if the proposed direction of cause is false?”
Use when: Survey, observational, or cross-sectional designs report “the more X, the more Y” and then offer a causal explanation.
Boundary: Ignore when the design randomly manipulates X or an option only explains how X might cause Y without challenging direction or third variables.

Transfer rule: If a definition bans averages only for extreme values, ambiguous data, or different-quality measurements, then accept grouped but precise data and reject datasets with outliers, estimates, or mixed populations.
Error pattern: I overtreated demographic variety as “different quality data” instead of separating valid subgroup differences from invalid measurement inconsistency or ambiguity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three flags only: extreme outlier present, data not accurately observed, or measurements combined across incomparable standards; choose an option with zero flags.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items asking whether an arithmetic mean is applicable under definition-based exclusions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about representativeness, usefulness, or interpretation of a mean rather than mere calculability.

Transfer rule: If an argument says lower price explains stronger sales, then check it assumes non-price factors—especially quality—are roughly comparable.
Error pattern: Mistook a background or opposite-side fact for the needed hidden premise linking price advantage to consumer choice.
Diagnostic check: Ask: if product quality were much worse, would low price alone still explain the sales gap? If not, comparable quality is required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions about market demand, where one cited advantage is claimed to be the main cause of higher sales.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes quality equivalence or when the claim concerns cost changes, legality, or distribution instead of purchase preference.

Transfer rule: If an ad says a substitute gives the benefits of a recommended item, then check whether it contains the specific property that produces those benefits.
Error pattern: Success pattern: tested the link between a recommendation’s stated benefit and the product’s actual capacity to deliver it, not just its appeal.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What is the causal reason experts recommend the broader category?” Then verify whether the featured item has that benefit-conferring trait.
Use when: Claims infer health, performance, or expert-endorsed benefits from category membership plus a nonessential attractive feature.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is only about taste, convenience, or preference, not about preserving the recommended benefit.

Transfer rule: If an argument relies on an imagined idealized setup to derive a law, then require that the imagined setup match the target system’s actual governing laws.
Error pattern: I chose a feature of creative imagination instead of the necessary validity condition linking the thought experiment to reality.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the conclusion still follow if the imagined scenario were unrealistic?” If no, select the option asserting correspondence between the model and the real law.
Use when: Relevant in questions about thought experiments, idealization, hidden premises, necessary conditions, or deriving laws under removed interference.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for historical evidence, who could perform it, or merely helpful but nonessential background details.

Transfer rule: If a charge merely reimburses direct production/administrative cost without profit and is tied to a public/educational function, then treat it as outside business-taxable operating revenue.
Error pattern: Success came from separating true operating turnover from incidental cost recovery attached to noncommercial duties.
Diagnostic check: Ask: is this activity a commercial service/asset transfer/property sale for consideration, or just pass-through reimbursement with no business margin?
Use when: Relevant for tax questions contrasting commercial entities or entertainment/property transactions with schools, agencies, or institutions collecting nominal fees.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the fee is bundled into paid services, exceeds cost, is profit-oriented, or the activity is plainly a taxable business category.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires a loosely organized online crowd reacting to a shared trigger through network spread, then choose the option showing spontaneous mass netizen action.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every clause of the definition instead of being distracted by anything merely involving the internet.
Diagnostic check: Verify four boxes: many participants, relatively unorganized, common stimulus, and behavior occurring through online propagation or response.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about collective online behavior, public reactions, viral events, or network-driven group actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the group is formally organized, mainly offline, individual investigation, or routine institutional/technical internet use.

Transfer rule: If post-event pollution seems lower than after a major disaster, then test whether the baseline before the event was already unusually high.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a mechanism that speeds cleanup instead of comparing wartime observations to preexisting contamination sources.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this option resolve the paradox by raising the earlier baseline, not by changing decay rate, damage severity, or impact?”
Use when: Relevant in discrepancy questions comparing before/after levels, especially when the later period seems surprisingly less severe than expected.
Boundary: Ignore when the puzzle is about measurement error, timing lag, or causal process after the event rather than baseline conditions.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a real-life post-event effect from cells reacting under lab conditions, then require a premise linking the event to the triggering conditions.
Error pattern: Strength was spotting a missing bridge between experimental activation and the natural situation the conclusion is about.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected bridge premise; if the event would no longer produce the triggering condition, the conclusion loses support, so that bridge is necessary.
Use when: Apply to necessary-assumption questions involving physiology, experiments, mechanisms, or causal chains from observed response to everyday behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when the gap concerns cross-species generalization, mere background biology, or details not required to connect event to trigger.

Transfer rule: If a one-to-one assignment has a conditional, then test both branches of the condition and eliminate the branch that makes any item impossible or duplicated.
Error pattern: Prematurely assumed the antecedent of a conditional without proving it, then propagated unsupported assignments.
Diagnostic check: Build each person’s allowed set, try “condition true” and “condition false,” and verify every branch can still assign all distinct foods exactly once.
Use when: Apply to logic-grid or matching problems with exclusivity plus statements like “if not X, then Y not Z.”
Boundary: Ignore when choices are not mutually exclusive, items can repeat, or the statement is causal rather than a strict logical constraint.

Transfer rule: If a boldface statement is what one group infers from evidence and the author then questions that inference, then treat it as an intermediate conclusion, not mere evidence.
Error pattern: Confusing a reported reasoner’s inferred claim with the raw evidence that supported it.
Diagnostic check: Reconstruct the chain as evidence → inferred claim → final author judgment; ask whether the first boldface is something concluded from prior facts and whether the second is the author’s takeaway.
Use when: Boldface-role questions where the passage reports others’ reasoning and then offers a skeptical or corrective evaluation.
Boundary: Ignore when the first boldface is directly observed data or when the second boldface is only supporting evidence, not the passage’s endpoint.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a familiar intermediary prevents disturbance, then require that the intermediary’s altered, goal-directed behavior remains within the target’s normal expectations.
Error pattern: Success pattern: identify the hidden bridge between “familiar presence” and “no change in observed behavior.”
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption and ask whether the conclusion collapses because the target would treat the setup as novel or abnormal.
Use when: Apply to assumption questions involving observation methods, proxies, camouflage, or substitutions meant to avoid affecting natural behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not depend on preserving normal reactions, or when the disputed choice concerns side details like equipment awareness, range, or unrelated effects.

Transfer rule: If asked which statement cannot support a prediction, then test whether it blocks the key application condition rather than merely changing cost, scale, or degree.
Error pattern: Success came from separating direct feasibility requirements from attractive but nonessential advantages.
Diagnostic check: List the prediction’s necessary conditions; if an option negates any one requirement, mark it as the non-supporting choice.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/weaken or support-except questions about adopting a new material, technology, or method for a specific use.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is comparative without fixed requirements, or when every option affects only magnitude, not feasibility.

Transfer rule: If an argument says “only X has feature-set F, so only X suits goal G,” then test whether rivals can meet G through different features or mechanisms.
Error pattern: Mistaking a claim about one named implementation as if it established exclusivity of the underlying benefit.
Diagnostic check: List the exact safety benefits cited, then ask: could another product deliver each benefit without the advertised proprietary add-on?
Use when: Ads or arguments infer “only choice” from a branded feature bundle or from one way of achieving a valued outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns the specific branded feature itself, not the broader benefit or suitability.

Transfer rule: If a rule restricts an organization or government entity, then do not automatically extend it to individual members unless the text explicitly bridges entity-to-person scope.
Error pattern: Mistaking an institution-level waiver/prohibition for a person-level waiver/prohibition; scope shift from collective subject to individual subject.
Diagnostic check: Identify the actor named in the premise and the actor targeted in the conclusion; if they are different types, require an explicit transfer principle before accepting.
Use when: A prompt involves declarations, policies, rights, duties, or bans stated for states, agencies, schools, companies, or groups, but concluded about individuals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the premise itself explicitly binds members, agents, representatives, or personal claims/acts.

Transfer rule: If a policy removes an intermediate host/vector’s preferred target, then test whether the vector will switch to humans and raise transmission.
Error pattern: I focused on a true-but-irrelevant fact about direct spread instead of the causal mechanism linking the intervention to worse outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Map the chain intervention → animal availability → vector behavior → human exposure; choose the option that makes human bites increase after host reduction.
Use when: Relevant in ecology/public health questions about vectors, reservoirs, host substitution, or claims that reducing one species could backfire.
Boundary: Ignore when transmission is direct, vector behavior is fixed, or the option only states background facts without affecting the intervention’s causal chain.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects one of two choices because it has a bad effect, then check whether the remaining choice may also have serious bad effects before accepting the conclusion.
Error pattern: I focused on whether the chosen option achieves a positive goal, instead of testing the hidden assumption that it is acceptable overall.
Diagnostic check: List the stated alternatives, note why one is dismissed, then ask: “What downside of the adopted alternative would undermine ‘must choose it’?”
Use when: Relevant in forced-choice, elimination, or “must adopt” arguments that compare policies, plans, or actions using one cited drawback.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only comparative on one metric, or when other consequences are explicitly ruled out or irrelevant.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “only if X, then Y,” then challenge it by finding a clear Y-without-X case, not merely an X-without-Y case.
Error pattern: I attacked a necessary-condition claim with a counterexample to sufficiency instead of negating the stated necessity.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the statement as “Y requires X”; before answering, test whether each option shows Y occurring despite no X.
Use when: Relevant for assumption, weaken, or challenge questions using cues like “only,” “must,” “requires,” “cannot unless,” or similar necessity language.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the claim is probabilistic, comparative, or about honesty/quality rather than a strict condition.

Transfer rule: If one speaker says “at most k” and another says that claim is wrong, then infer the true count is greater than k before testing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from translating nested disagreement into a strict numerical consequence instead of chasing each option’s wording.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite statements symbolically, negate carefully (“wrong” means the whole claim is false), derive the allowable count range, then eliminate any choice incompatible with that range.
Use when: Apply to logic items with quantities, participation/existence counts, and second-order claims about another person’s statement being mistaken.
Boundary: Ignore when “wrong” is not standard logical negation, or when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous, or use everyday exaggeration.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires demonstrated talent plus fitting placement and prompt promotion/reuse, then choose the case where observed strengths are quickly matched to a higher-impact role.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking every required element and rejecting choices driven by example-setting, personal favoritism, or reassignment that wastes strengths.
Diagnostic check: Underline each criterion in the definition, map each to facts in the option, and eliminate any option missing even one required element.
Use when: A concept is defined by multiple necessary conditions about personnel selection, promotion, role fit, and timing.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the term describes broad leadership style, team action, or outcomes without explicit personnel-placement criteria.

Transfer rule: If an argument says an event is misclassified, yet praises the resulting discussion because that topic matters independently, then choose the parallel with the same misattribution-plus-welcome-discussion structure.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the author’s attitude toward the mistaken interpretation, not the surface subject matter.
Diagnostic check: Mark three parts: actual cause, mistaken attributed cause, and whether discussion of the attributed issue is endorsed despite the mistake.
Use when: Relevant in principle/parallel questions where a bad inference or false attribution still leads to a beneficial conversation about an important issue.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument condemns the misattribution, lacks explicit endorsement of the discussion, or shifts from discussing effects to justifying the event itself.

Transfer rule: If a rebuttal relies on a per-capita outcome trend, then test whether changes in survival/measurement distort that outcome without improving prevention.
Error pattern: I focused on reporting bias, but reporting cannot create completed-offense counts; I missed a causal factor that breaks the link between outcome rates and prevention ability.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the same attacks have produced fewer recorded deaths now because of outside improvements?” If yes, the rebuttal is weakened.
Use when: The argument compares rates across years and infers institutional effectiveness from deaths, injuries, or other downstream outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the disputed metric is not affected by survivability, recording practices, or other external conversion factors.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives examples after a broad claim, then choose the option that captures the overarching theme linking them, not a narrower effect.
Error pattern: Success comes from hierarchical summarizing: separate central thesis from supporting illustrations and avoid overcommitting to absolute wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 6–10 word gist for each sentence, identify the shared umbrella idea, then reject options covering only one sentence or adding absolutes.
Use when: Apply this to main-idea questions with topic sentences plus examples, especially about social or technological change across regions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, author attitude, or the passage contrasts multiple equally weighted claims.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts old labor-driven growth with costly information/technology infrastructure, then infer dependence on advanced technology, not merely on spending level.
Error pattern: Mistaking supporting evidence about investment scale for the main inferred claim about what now drives economic development.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What is the author’s core contrast or thesis?” Then test each option for direct support versus a narrower byproduct of the evidence.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions where examples and costs illustrate a broader shift from one development driver to another.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly asks about financing structure, labor costs specifically, or comparative national outcomes.

Transfer rule: If a role-in-argument question asks about a factual clause that helps the main claim, then classify it as support, not the conclusion or a target.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the author’s main takeaway from a premise that explains why the proposal would work in practice.
Diagnostic check: Identify the conclusion first, then ask whether the statement gives a reason for it, restates it, or presents an opposing view.
Use when: Relevant in short arguments about evidence, feasibility, or effectiveness where one sentence supplies a practical link.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement is merely background, a definition, or the author’s final claim itself.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one improved skill frees resources for another, then prefer evidence that greater gains in the first track greater gains in the second within the same period.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the answer to the stated causal mechanism rather than to background facts or reverse-direction associations.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice directly connect change in the proposed cause to change in the proposed effect, instead of only describing initial levels, representativeness, or the effect predicting the cause?
Use when: Strengthen questions with a causal explanation based on correlated improvements after training or intervention.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about sampling, definition, or a different causal direction than improvement-to-improvement linkage.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats high spending on fixes or improvements as proof of adequacy, then ask whether high spending could instead indicate a severe underlying problem.
Error pattern: I accepted a choice about issue relevance instead of attacking the link between the cited evidence and the claimed condition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, test: if true, does it make the same evidence more expected when the claim is false than when it is true?
Use when: Apply this to arguments inferring quality, safety, or sufficiency from unusually large repair, maintenance, or improvement expenditures.
Boundary: Ignore this when spending level is independently validated as a reliable outcome measure, not merely a symptom.

Transfer rule: If a rule says “must report when injury or high damage, unless incapable” and a driver is not required, then infer either the trigger failed or the exception applies; if a trigger is separately assumed, conclude the exception.
Error pattern: I treated one person’s lack of duty as creating another person’s duty instead of analyzing the conditional with its exception.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “required if (trigger and capable)” and test each choice by contraposition or by adding a stated trigger to see whether incapacity follows.
Use when: A legal or formal rule has thresholds, exceptions, and a statement that someone is not obligated.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for causal explanation, moral blame, or facts beyond the rule’s logical scope.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a fixed day-by-day schedule from total days worked plus one exception, then check for an unstated capacity/schedule rule that makes the remaining days necessary.
Error pattern: I filled the gap with irrelevant calendar exclusion instead of the premise linking the workplace’s allowed number of workdays to the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List the stated facts, then ask: “What extra rule forces the remaining days/slots to be exactly these, not merely possible?”
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions about schedules, allocations, counting, “other days,” and conclusions claiming necessity from partial timing information.
Boundary: Ignore when the missing step is causal, definitional, or about weekend attendance unless the conclusion explicitly depends on those facts.

Transfer rule: If a passage traces sensing in one organ but says recognition/impression forms after brain processing, then choose the brain-centered main idea, not a step-specific detail.
Error pattern: I overfocused on one intermediate mechanism and missed the broader author emphasis spanning the full pathway.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 5-word gist of each paragraph/sentence chain; if most clauses describe process-to-brain and final perception, prefer the overarching summary.
Use when: Apply to main-idea questions about biological or cognitive processes with multiple stages, locations, and functions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific function, stage, structure, or explicitly requests a detail rather than the passage’s main point.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers a broad deficiency from one narrow preference indicator, then attack the link by showing the indicator does not validly measure the broader trait.
Error pattern: I treated supporting examples as weakening, instead of challenging whether the cited evidence is relevant to the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the evidence directly define, represent, or reliably proxy the conclusion?” If not, prefer the option that breaks that proxy assumption.
Use when: An argument generalizes from one survey item, behavior, taste, or metric to a wider ability, knowledge base, or cultural condition.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence is explicitly established as a valid measure of the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires linking culture-level conditions to individual psychological traits or mechanisms, then choose the option explicitly about how a cultural environment shapes personality or character.
Error pattern: I matched a broad cultural change topic instead of requiring an individual-level psychological variable connected to a wider cultural context.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline one phrase naming a culture/social environment and one phrase naming a psychological trait; reject choices missing either element.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions in social science where disciplines are distinguished by level of analysis and type of variable.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target field studies texts, discourse, history, or aesthetics without any claim about psychological traits or mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a criterion because it includes a problematic subclass, then choose the principle that says that subclass must be excluded from the target category.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the objection’s flaw to a bridge principle, rather than picking a tempting restatement of the original criterion.
Diagnostic check: Identify the broad rule, the cited bad cases it would admit, and test each option for “these cases should not count,” not merely “good cases do count.”
Use when: Necessary-assumption or principle questions attack a proposed standard by citing items admitted under it.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus supports a standard directly or asks for a sufficient principle.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses a past case to support a prediction about a current belief, then identify the cited case’s function as an analogy or precedent, not just topic background.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking argumentative role; failure comes from choosing an option that merely restates subject matter instead of evidential function.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: remove the historical reference—does the conclusion lose support, context, or coherence? Match the option to that specific loss.
Use when: Relevant in role-of-a-statement questions featuring historical examples, comparisons across eras, or claims that one situation mirrors another.
Boundary: Ignore this when the cited material only defines terms, gives neutral background, or is rhetorically decorative without supporting an inference.

Transfer rule: If a claim says one product is best, then verify the evidence compares it against relevant alternatives, not merely against nonuse or a baseline.
Error pattern: Strength in spotting a comparison-gap flaw: the conclusion outruns the study because the test omits head-to-head competitors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list conclusion target and tested conditions; ask, “Was every needed comparison directly evaluated?”
Use when: Relevant for ads, experiments, or surveys that infer superiority, ranking, or “most effective” from limited preference data.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion only claims advantage over the specific baseline actually tested, not over all alternatives.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “all X cannot occur without Y,” then translate it as “every X requires Y,” and keep any “some X may not Z” as possibility only.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting awkward negatives/modals into clear quantifiers without strengthening “may not” into “must not” or weakening “all” into “some.”
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each clause in simple form: “all X -> Y” and “some X -> possibly not Z”; accept only an option preserving both exactly.
Use when: Relevant for quantified verbal-logic items using all, some, may, cannot, necessarily, or double-negative phrasing.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on real-world causality, probability beyond modality, or added claims about unrelated categories.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a claim because disconfirming evidence came from poor conditions, then infer only that the stated implication is unsupported, not broader counterfactual claims.
Error pattern: Overextended the critique by adding a stronger “even under good conditions” judgment not licensed by the premises.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What exact conclusion is denied?” Then remove any answer that introduces hypotheticals, stronger quantifiers, or claims about total worthlessness absent explicit support.
Use when: A speaker attacks an inference from recent observations by citing flawed methodology, bad conditions, or weak evidence quality.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus explicitly evaluates what would happen under better conditions or gives enough facts for a stronger modal conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one delivery route explains how something reached Earth, then prefer evidence for an alternative route carrying the same material over points about later survival or rarity.
Error pattern: I attacked the downstream “forming life” step instead of the specific causal link about transport to Earth.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, state the conclusion in one clause and ask, “Does this option challenge that route/source, or only what happens after arrival?”
Use when: Relevant for causal, origin, or pathway questions that infer one messenger, source, or mechanism from observational buildup.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about viability after arrival, quantity thresholds, or a claim explicitly about life’s emergence rather than delivery.

Transfer rule: If the stimulus has the form “All A are B; x is A; therefore x is B,” then choose the option with the same categorical syllogism.
Error pattern: I matched on topical plausibility or causal feel instead of exact logical form and quantifier structure.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each argument as variables; verify it uses a universal premise plus category membership, not probability, advice, necessity, or causal prediction.
Use when: Relevant for analogy questions asking which argument is most similar in reasoning, especially with words like all, any, is, therefore.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task compares content, truth, or strength rather than formal inference pattern.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires missed perceptual change in immediately viewed external features, then reject choices about later memory or source confusion.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating real-time perception failures from post-event remembering, attribution, or identity-belief errors.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: was there an actual visible change, was it brief/immediate, and was the miss due to perception rather than later recall?
Use when: Apply this to definition-based multiple-choice items contrasting attention/perception phenomena with memory, inference, or narrative confusion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept itself concerns memory distortion, source monitoring, delayed recall, or mistaken ownership of experiences.

Transfer rule: If a case features failure, insecurity, or blocked desire followed by a face-saving explanation, then choose it as rationalization.  
Error pattern: Mistaking deliberate deception or external factual analysis for a self-protective reinterpretation of one’s own motives.  
Diagnostic check: Ask: Did the person first face an ego threat, then give a socially acceptable reason that hides the real motive from self or others?  
Use when: Relevant in definition matching about defense mechanisms, excuses after not achieving a goal, or post hoc justifications of embarrassing behavior.  
Boundary: Ignore when the explanation is a genuine causal investigation, coercive lying for punishment avoidance, or action without a later justificatory story.

Transfer rule: If an argument attributes changed survey responses to altered question order across two times, then require that time-related factors are ruled out.
Error pattern: I chose an irrelevant memory assumption instead of testing for a competing cause behind the observed difference.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If the order had stayed the same, could the later group still differ because of timing, season, or external events?”
Use when: Comparing different samples measured at different dates while claiming wording/order effects explain response changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the same respondents are compared immediately, or when timing effects are already controlled or shown irrelevant.

Transfer rule: If a definition says external reasons replace internal motives, then require evidence of an original internal motive being overridden by an external one.
Error pattern: I matched any incentive-driven behavior to the concept without checking whether the behavior initially came from internal control.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark (1) initial motive, (2) added external reason, (3) replacement of the initial motive, and reject any case missing step 1 or 3.
Use when: The concept hinges on a shift in motivation source, especially in psychology or behavior-definition multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns simple reinforcement, coercion, or outcomes without a before-and-after motive transition.

Transfer rule: If a plan infers “best past performer” will guarantee future abundance, then test whether concentrating on that winner creates a new vulnerability that can defeat the goal.
Error pattern: Success pattern—look for hidden-risk assumptions where optimization on one metric is mistaken for robustness over time.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could following this proposal make the system less resilient by reducing diversity or increasing exposure to a single failure mode?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken arguments about selecting one top option based on historical outcomes to ensure future success.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already addresses resilience/diversity tradeoffs or when the choice does not increase concentration risk.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus redefines an old category using a new criterion, then pick the choice stating that the new criterion is replacing the old basis.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the argument’s abstract shift in definition, not getting distracted by predictions, preferences, or side effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “old basis → new basis” in 3–6 words and verify one option mirrors that replacement exactly.
Use when: Relevant for questions about changing definitions, classifications, or distinctions, especially when examples contrast former and revised standards.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus argues causes, consequences, values, or trends without explicitly substituting one defining criterion for another.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists examples and background, then choose the option that states the author’s overall purpose or takeaway, not a supporting detail.
Error pattern: Success came from separating evidence and context from the main intended message.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each sentence in 3–5 words, then write one line covering all of them; match the choice to that line only.
Use when: The text mixes scandals, examples, value claims, and policy mentions while asking what the passage is intended to explain.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific fact, cause, inference, or the role of a single sentence.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a method is inefficient from producing fewer total results, then compare results per unit time before accepting the claim.
Error pattern: I treated a superficially similar counterexample as relevant instead of attacking the efficiency metric the conclusion actually required.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the lower total output be explained solely by much less time spent on that method?” If yes, the argument is weak.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about learning, productivity, or effectiveness where evidence reports totals, frequencies, or shares but concludes relative efficiency.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already controls for time, effort, exposure, or uses a different standard than efficiency.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists an industry’s problems and then presents a model as the needed remedy, then choose the option stating that model’s importance/significance to the industry.
Error pattern: Mistaking an argument about value or necessity for a neutral description of combination, application, or coexistence.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does the text mainly describe a relationship, or does it argue that one approach solves key problems and is therefore important?”
Use when: The passage has a problem-to-solution structure, with need words like “need,” “change,” “implement,” “integrate,” or “through.”
Boundary: Ignore this when the text only defines terms, reports trends, or compares models without endorsing one as especially useful.

Transfer rule: If an argument blames a specific standards violation for a failure, then prefer evidence that an external load exceeded what the standards were designed to handle.
Error pattern: I focused on an irrelevant detail about occupancy/load instead of testing whether the cited violation was actually causally responsible.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the failure likely occur even if every code requirement had been met?” If yes, that option strongly weakens the claim.
Use when: Causal weakening questions link a bad outcome to one defect while background conditions, design limits, or abnormal stresses are discussed.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices only affect severity, aftermath, or unrelated features rather than the causal link.

Transfer rule: If a case shows a strong risk factor without the usual outcome, then prefer an explanation naming a local protective mechanism that blocks the causal pathway from risk to disease.
Error pattern: Success comes from explaining the exception directly; failure comes from picking choices about background prevalence, weaker contributors, or effects that do not neutralize the main risk.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option identify why these people avoid the disease despite having the risk, by interrupting the risk-to-outcome mechanism?”
Use when: Relevant for paradox, exception, or “most helps explain” questions involving correlation, causation, and a subgroup that defies the trend.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to weaken, quantify association, or compare rates without needing a causal explanation for an anomaly.

Transfer rule: If an argument says an input-cost increase won’t much affect retail price because that input is a small cost share, then test for indirect supply effects that can raise price anyway.
Error pattern: Success came from looking beyond direct cost pass-through and spotting a hidden causal path through producer exit and reduced output.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could this higher input cost change participation, capacity, or supply enough to move final prices even if per-unit cost share is small?”
Use when: Relevant in pricing, markets, production chains, or “small component of total cost” arguments.
Boundary: Ignore when supply is fixed or buffered, or when the claim is only about immediate accounting effects.

Transfer rule: If a question defines a process as requiring a nervous system or specific organ, then first eliminate any option from organisms or systems lacking that structure.
Error pattern: Success came from matching each option against the formal definition instead of choosing by surface similarity to “response.”
Diagnostic check: For every option, ask: does this organism have the required system, and is that system participating in the response?
Use when: Relevant in biology items that mix animal, human, and plant responses or contrast reflexes, tropisms, taxis, instincts, and conditioned behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is defined behaviorally without requiring a particular anatomical system.

Transfer rule: If premises give “some X are Y” and all Y have Z, then infer “some X are Z,” not the reverse “all Z are Y.”
Error pattern: Mistook a one-way conditional for its converse and ignored a valid existential chain from overlap plus subset.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map sets and test each claim with arrows and at least one witness; reject any option that reverses an arrow.
Use when: Relevant in quantified logic items using some/most/all language, category overlap, and trait inheritance through class inclusion.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are causal, temporal, or comparative rather than set-membership/quantifier relations.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives only negative screens and bonus factors, then eliminate choices hitting the screens and treat bonuses as optional, not required.
Error pattern: Success came from separating necessary disqualifiers from merely helpful traits instead of assuming every mentioned advantage must appear.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark “fails screen?”, “has any relevant experience?”, and “has bonus skill?”; reject any failing a screen before comparing bonuses.
Use when: Apply to verbal logic items with phrases like least likely, more likely, increases possibility, especially in hiring or selection scenarios.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt gives sufficient conditions, exact requirements, or exclusivity words like only, must, iff, guaranteed.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a global trend from evidence centered on a few major regions or markets, then require a premise that conditions elsewhere are at least not worsening.
Error pattern: Mistook a background/detail statement about cited evidence for a bridging assumption needed to generalize from local indicators to a worldwide conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List the covered areas; ask, “What uncovered areas must be true for this broader claim to hold?” Choose the option that fills that geographic/scope gap.
