Use when: Relevant in assumption/premise questions where evidence is regional, sector-specific, or partial but the conclusion is broad, worldwide, or system-level.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about the cited regions, or when an option directly states a necessary causal link rather than a missing scope bridge.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts two groups across parallel behaviors, then choose the option summarizing the shared comparison, not one side’s detail.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking structure and selecting the broader comparative theme instead of a narrower example or moral slogan.
Diagnostic check: List the subjects, mark each described behavior, and ask whether the main point is contrast, praise, blame, or advice.
Use when: Apply this to main-idea questions with repeated “not only...but also...” or explicit side-by-side descriptions of two categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an inference, attitude, cause, or a specific supporting detail rather than the central theme.

Transfer rule: If boldface asks for roles, then identify the argument’s main conclusion first and classify each bold part by its relation to that conclusion.
Error pattern: Treated a cited supporting consideration as the author’s own evaluation instead of separating others’ evidence from the argument’s conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the structure as “Some people say X because Y; however, author says Z because W” and map each bold clause to Y, Z, or W.
Use when: Relevant in role-of-statement questions with contrast words, reported beliefs, and an author rebutting another group’s reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore when the text lacks competing viewpoints or when bold parts are merely premises within a single speaker’s argument.

Transfer rule: If a currency seems abundant in raw form, then check whether only a processed, restricted, or socially certified subset actually functions as money.
Error pattern: Success pattern: resolve an apparent contradiction by distinguishing the plentiful material from the scarce money-qualifying version.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What exact feature makes an item acceptable in exchange, and is that feature itself limited by labor, access, skill, or approval?”
Use when: One statement gives a general principle, and the other cites a seeming counterexample involving widespread physical availability of the item.
Boundary: Ignore when the dispute is about spending habits, symbolism, persistence over time, or unrelated valuables rather than what confers exchange value.

Transfer rule: If named people are included in a group with a stated property, and that property excludes another trait, then infer each named person lacks that excluded trait.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: chaining membership into a universal condition and then applying the stated exclusion correctly.
Diagnostic check: Write the chain “named person ∈ group; all in group have property; property rules out trait,” then verify the conclusion mentions only those named people.
Use when: Relevant for syllogism questions with group inclusion, universal statements, and a prohibition or incompatibility.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion adds uniqueness, total population claims, or stronger facts not forced by the premises.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts current progress with a remaining gap and ends with a “must” recommendation, then choose the option stating the unmet need, not the background or cause.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions often tempt with partial truths: context, effect, or inferred cause instead of the author’s central takeaway.
Diagnostic check: Mark topic, gap, and final prescription; if one option matches all three, prefer it over choices covering only one or two.
Use when: Apply to expository passages that summarize a trend, acknowledge improvement, note insufficiency, and call for further action.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a specific cause, detail, attitude, or best title rather than the passage’s main point.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends targeting a large high-demand group, then test whether the provider has enough capacity to serve that group effectively.
Error pattern: I attacked general effectiveness claims instead of the operational assumption linking demand concentration to feasible service delivery.
Diagnostic check: List the conclusion’s required conditions; if one is staffing, supply, or scalability, prefer the option that blocks fulfillment rather than one adding vague uncertainty.
Use when: The stimulus moves from “many promising customers need help” to “this firm should focus there” or assumes personalized service can cover many people.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about desirability, price, or proven efficacy, not implementation capacity.

Transfer rule: If a statement says small habitual actions reflect inner traits and changing habits changes those traits, then infer a start-from-small-habits principle, not stronger necessity or difficulty claims.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning from reflection-plus-modification premises to a cautious, process-based inference about habit formation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each option as supported, merely plausible, or too strong; reject any option adding exclusivity, necessity, value judgment, or difficulty not stated.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions linking minor behaviors, habits, character, consciousness, or temperament through reflection or change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt provides causal, comparative, or mandatory language that directly justifies stronger conclusions.

Transfer rule: If premises say community life centers on interactions and life focus shifts toward community, then infer a broader effect of interpersonal relations, not moral duties or absolute predictions.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: choosing the option that restates the causal implication at the same scope; avoiding overreach, exclusivity, and unsupported value judgments.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each choice as paraphrase, stronger claim, normative claim, or unrelated extension; keep only a supported paraphrase.
Use when: Apply to conclusion questions built from social trends, role shifts, or essence/constitutes statements that imply practical impact.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for policy, attitude, prediction with new evidence, or when answer choices require external facts.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “factor X is necessary for harm” to “reduce Y to block harm,” then require a premise linking Y to X’s functioning.
Error pattern: Success pattern: identified the missing bridge between a biological target and the proposed intervention, rather than judging safety, availability, or side effects.
Diagnostic check: State the conclusion as target action → reduced outcome; then ask, “What causal dependency must hold for this action to disable the named necessary factor?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/premise questions involving biomedical mechanisms, necessary conditions, and treatment claims based on lab findings.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns feasibility, ethics, approval, or comparative benefits instead of mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a statement asserts a comparative or linked fact between entities that cannot be split into independent single-entity attributes, then classify it as a relational judgment.
Error pattern: Mistaking a conjunction of separate property claims about multiple entities for a true relation between them.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the sentence as isolated “X has property P” claims; if meaning is preserved, it is essential, but if a cross-entity link is lost, it is relational.
Use when: Apply this on classification questions contrasting object nature, compound property statements, and inter-object relations.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the sentence contains hidden quantifiers, causal structure, or definitions that require extra logical analysis beyond property-vs-relation.

Transfer rule: If a claim states only a one-way condition about a specific subgroup, then infer only its contrapositive for violations, not a broader converse or generalization.
Error pattern: Overextended a limited sufficient condition by treating a correlated feature as universally predictive.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each premise as “If X, then Y,” note subgroup limits, then test each choice by contraposition only and reject any answer adding new scope.
Use when: Necessary-assumption or must-be-true questions with quantifiers, subgroup restrictions, and tempting size/causal explanations.
Boundary: Ignore this when premises explicitly give biconditionals, all-group coverage, or independent rules supporting the broader generalization.

Transfer rule: If a concept chain is meant to show inverse connotation–extension, then each step must add attributes while narrowing the set under the same genus-species hierarchy.
Error pattern: I accepted a sequence with role/status labels that did not consistently form nested species by accumulating defining features.
Diagnostic check: For each adjacent pair, ask: “Does the later concept equal the earlier one plus one extra essential qualifier, and is every instance of the later also an instance of the earlier?”
Use when: Options present ordered terms that may be hierarchical, categorical, geographic, or individual, and you must verify true connotation-extension inversion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when relations are part-whole, location containment, rank/institution naming, or individual-example links rather than species subdivision.

Transfer rule: If a definition stresses bounded information, limited time/cost, and satisficing through partial-result comparison, then choose the option explicitly using a satisfactory-not-optimal standard under incomplete foresight.
Error pattern: I overweighted practicality and gradual improvement, while missing the core bounded-rationality mechanism required by the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the definition’s mandatory elements and verify the choice contains incomplete information, constrained resources, and satisfactory selection rather than optimal or emotional choice.
Use when: Relevant for concept-definition questions contrasting rational optimization, intuition/emotion, and bounded or incremental decision processes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition centers on long-term implementation, moral judgment, or outcomes rather than the decision rule itself.

Transfer rule: If a plan changes who makes decisions to raise productivity, then prefer evidence showing the change directly frees time or resources for productive work.
Error pattern: Success came from linking the proposal’s mechanism to the stated goal, rather than being distracted by attitudes, staffing side effects, or facts about irrelevant task types.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this option make the proposed change causally increase the target outcome, not merely make the change acceptable or possible?”
Use when: Apply on strengthen questions about organizational plans, delegation, process redesign, or technology-enabled workflow changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a flaw, assumption, weaken point, or when outcomes depend mainly on costs, morale, legality, or feasibility instead of productivity.

Transfer rule: If a passage first lists strong achievements then contrasts them with weaker underlying indicators, then choose the option that preserves both progress and remaining gap.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s overall contrast rather than overfocusing on either praise or one specific deficiency.
Diagnostic check: Mark positive evidence and negative evidence, count both sides, and reject any choice that mentions only one side or narrows the contrast to a single cause.
Use when: Apply to main-message questions built around “however,” “but,” or other pivot words after comparative statistics.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a detail, cause, inference, or policy recommendation instead of the passage’s central takeaway.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a ban is unreasonable because a similar unbanned item also has side effects, then check whether it assumes the harms are comparable in severity.
Error pattern: I chose a broad policy principle instead of the specific comparability assumption linking the example to the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Remove the claim that the two items’ side effects are similarly serious; if the analogy no longer supports the conclusion, that claim is required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions built on analogies, parity arguments, or claims of inconsistent treatment by regulators.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes matched risk levels or when the conclusion rests on authority, legality, or definitions instead of comparison.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a hiring preference from traits common among top performers, then test whether those traits were already common in the overall hired pool.
Error pattern: Base-rate neglect—treating a trait’s frequency among successes as evidence of causal advantage without comparing it to its frequency among all selected cases.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Would this fact show the admired trait was prevalent across hires generally, making the success rate uninformative?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions about recruiting, admissions, or selection where evidence cites the backgrounds of the best members.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus already compares success rates across groups or gives controlled performance data.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines an educational ideal through inner freedom, non-instrumental learning, and transcendence of self, then map it to the broad philosophical tradition it describes, not a narrower outcome-based label.
Error pattern: I matched vivid moral/life-value language to a thematic subset instead of identifying the higher-level concept unifying all listed traits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s core features and ask whether the choice names the overarching educational philosophy or merely one consequence, goal, or component.
Use when: The prompt describes education via aims, spirit, human development, freedom, and meaning rather than curriculum details or practical skills.
Boundary: Ignore this when the options are direct synonyms, explicitly defined in the passage, or distinguished by concrete institutional or curricular criteria.

Transfer rule: If a category is defined as after completion/use plus comprehensive retrospective learning, then exclude actions done during implementation for ongoing monitoring or control.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every option to all required timing-and-purpose conditions instead of relying on surface similarity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Did it occur after completion? Is it retrospective? Is the aim broad evaluation for lessons, not real-time supervision, audit, or control?
Use when: Relevant in definition-matching questions with necessary conditions about stage, scope, and purpose, especially evaluation vs monitoring distinctions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition allows ongoing/process evaluation or when a single qualifying feature is sufficient.

Transfer rule: If a policy change directly raises buyers’ costs, then infer the prior alternative was cheaper than the post-change source.
Error pattern: Success pattern—draw the weakest necessary economic comparison from stated causal effects, not speculative motives or trade relationships.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What must have been true immediately before the change for this reported cost increase to occur?”
Use when: Relevant in inference questions about bans, tariffs, substitution, or supply shifts with explicit before/after cost consequences.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives offsetting factors, changing demand, subsidies, quality changes, or only discusses goals without observed effects.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts how to address children versus adults, then choose the criterion explicitly contrasted, not a broader social quality.
Error pattern: I generalized from tone/politeness language and missed the concrete comparison that determined the rule.
Diagnostic check: Underline every direct contrast or example pair; ask, “Which answer names this exact split?” and reject options that only describe consequences.
Use when: A reading question asks what factor should be considered and the passage gives examples of different wording for different kinds of people.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text states multiple equal factors or when examples are illustrative rather than rule-setting.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a policy affects few directly, then test for indirect ripple effects on related pay, prices, or incentives.
Error pattern: I focused on background facts about where wages are higher instead of mechanisms that spread the policy’s impact beyond the initially affected group.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Could this fact force adjustments for workers or costs above the new floor even when few are below it now?”
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about economic policies, thresholds, minimums, or regulations where direct coverage is used to claim negligible overall impact.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only describe unaffected sectors, static demographics, or facts with no causal path from the policy to broader costs.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion relies on “no observed instances,” then test whether the observation method was capable of detecting those instances.
Error pattern: I treated a premise-weakening fact as decisive and ignored an alternative explanation that blocks the move from no detection to nonexistence.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Would this option show the evidence could be absent because of limits in measurement, access, or technology rather than actual absence?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/required-reconsider questions where someone infers “none exist” or “the theory is false” from failed observation.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence comes from a genuinely exhaustive search or the option does not affect detectability.

Transfer rule: If testing full scheduling options with conditionals, then verify every option by direct rule-checking and treat “if” rules as one-way only.
Error pattern: Success comes from constraint-by-constraint elimination; failure usually comes from inventing extra requirements or reversing implications.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate, make a four-item checklist: paired-together rule, forbidden-pair rule, trigger-1, trigger-2; mark each satisfied/violated before choosing.
Use when: Apply this to small assignment or timetable problems with fixed slots, exclusivity, and conditional placement constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when rules are probabilistic, preferences rather than hard constraints, or when multiple answers can satisfy the setup.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts workers will leave for higher pay, then check whether it assumes no nonsalary advantages offset the pay gap.
Error pattern: I focused on comparative quantities instead of required compensation assumptions linking incentives to behavior.
Diagnostic check: Negate each candidate assumption; if better conditions or benefits could reasonably balance lower pay, the departure prediction weakens.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/assumption questions about job choice, retention, migration, or incentives comparing sectors, firms, or roles.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion already measures total compensation/preferences directly, or when headcount comparisons are the argument’s main hinge.

Transfer rule: If an argument says removing a constraint worsened quality, then prefer an inference that the constraint could sometimes help rather than a stronger “must” remedy.
Error pattern: Overreaching from criticism of one cause into a necessary prescription not stated by the premises.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compare each option’s strength to the evidence; reject any answer adding necessity, exclusivity, or future requirements absent from the claims.
Use when: The stimulus contrasts effects before and after a barrier, rule, or limitation and asks what is most strongly supported.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument explicitly states a required fix, sole cause, or unconditional principle.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a conclusion by attacking the arguer’s mindset or tone, then check whether it ever addresses the supporting reasons.
Error pattern: Dismissing a claim via source-psychology or rhetoric instead of evaluating the evidence offered for it.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What premises for the disputed conclusion were answered?” If none were examined, flag the flaw.
Use when: The stimulus mentions anxious, biased, emotional, or otherwise suspect speakers and then treats that as enough to reject their view.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument independently evaluates the evidence or when the issue is explicitly about credibility, not the claim itself.

Transfer rule: If a passage says people were “brought out by” a writer’s specific works within a genre, then infer the writer authored works in that genre, not that allegations are proven.
Error pattern: Mistaking reported accusations, publicity, or court acceptance for established facts, while missing the weaker authorship/classification inference directly licensed by wording.
Diagnostic check: Mark each clause as fact, allegation, or background; only derive statements supported by fact clauses, and reject any choice that upgrades an allegation into a confirmed event.
Use when: The stimulus mixes genre descriptions, legal disputes, media attention, and references to named works by an author.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage explicitly states a court finding, admission, or other confirmed determination.

Transfer rule: If an argument judges a defense as not worth the cost from low direct success, then test whether it still improves final outcomes by deterrence or reduced losses.
Error pattern: Cost-benefit claims often fail by using a narrow performance metric and ignoring the intervention’s broader payoff.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the stated metric and ask, “What downstream result actually matters, and is there comparative evidence on that result?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/undermine questions about effectiveness, value, or policy based on percentages, hit rates, or one operational measure.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion already evaluates the true end outcome directly or comparative outcome evidence is unavailable.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “if P, then must Q,” then the strongest inconsistency is an option asserting P while denying Q.
Error pattern: Success came from testing contradiction structure directly instead of getting distracted by unrelated claims or inverses.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the core claim as P → Q; mark each choice as affirms/denies P and Q, then prefer the one matching P and not Q.
Use when: Apply this to conditional-logic questions asking for the statement most inconsistent with a quoted principle, rule, or obligation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for entailment, weakest support, causal explanation, or when the source claim is not conditional.

Transfer rule: If an option adds a new causal claim, then verify the passage explicitly states that cause-and-effect link rather than merely mentioning both facts.
Error pattern: I treated a supported superlative/paraphrase as suspect and overlooked an option that smuggled in an unsupported causal interpretation.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, mark whether it is restatement, scope shift, or causal inference; reject any choice whose causation or impact wording cannot be directly traced to the text.
Use when: Apply this on “does not conform to the original meaning” questions, especially when options paraphrase facts but one adds explanation, consequence, or motive.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for implication, best inference, or author’s likely view rather than strict textual correspondence.

Transfer rule: If a statement says something is “higher/greater than any other,” then treat it as strictly exceeding every peer, so ties are not allowed.
Error pattern: Quantifier/comparative misread—turning a strict superlative claim into a non-strict “at least as high as” claim.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each key comparison in symbols or plain logic; ask, “Does this permit equality, or must every other case be lower?”
Use when: Relevant in could-be-true/except questions with superlatives, exclusivity, rankings, or comparisons across all members of a group.
Boundary: Ignore when the wording explicitly allows ties, uses non-strict terms, or the comparison is only about some subset rather than every other case.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists examples after a thesis sentence, then choose the option that restates the shared central claim, not a narrower attribute of the examples.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying overall main-idea structure and resisting tempting detail-focused summaries.
Diagnostic check: Mark the topic sentence, label each later detail as support/example, then ask which option can cover every example without adding a new claim.
Use when: Relevant for short reading-comprehension items with vivid examples, brand/item lists, and one broad evaluative or summary statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, inference, author attitude nuance, or comparison rather than the passage’s main content.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one local practice caused better outcomes, then prefer evidence comparing participants with similar nonparticipants in the same setting.
Error pattern: Success came from using a controlled comparison that isolates the proposed cause rather than discussing alternative causes abstractly.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice show the target group outperformed a matched group lacking only the proposed factor?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about causal attribution, especially when several rival explanations are mentioned.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not causal, or when the option lacks a reasonably comparable control group or outcome contrast.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “no effect” from “no change during removal/absence,” then require that the observation window would have shown a change if the cause really mattered.
Error pattern: I chose a statement about explaining past trends instead of the needed bridge connecting the temporary shortage evidence to the no-effect conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption; if the argument can no longer treat the no-change period as informative, it is likely required.
Use when: Relevant in causal arguments using a natural experiment, interruption, or shortage to deny efficacy from unchanged outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about correlation/history, not about what absence of the factor should have produced.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a one-way condition (“if qualified, then receive benefit”), then infer only that sufficient-direction result, not its converse or extra usage rights.
Error pattern: Mistaking possession/effect for proof of the qualifying cause, and importing assumptions about what the benefit allows.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the premise as Qualified → Benefit; test each choice by asking whether it states this direction, reverses it, or adds unstated consequences.
Use when: Conditional language links a criterion to a reward, status, or action, especially in multiple-choice inference questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly says “only if,” “iff,” defines the benefit’s properties, or states all beneficiaries and acquisition routes exhaustively.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists image, duty, professionalism, and legal/service identity, then choose the option capturing internal awareness/quality rather than operational effects or social impact.
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting the author’s main value claim instead of chasing a vivid but secondary phrase.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as motive, effect, or example; select the option matching the dominant motive repeated across the passage.
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions where several choices paraphrase details but only one summarizes the passage’s underlying rationale.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, direct consequence, or the best paraphrase of one sentence.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives one product example plus percentages/margins to support a broad claim, then choose the option stating the broader structural point, not the example-specific detail.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward abstraction from evidence to thesis; the reliable pattern here was correctly separating illustration from emphasized conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as evidence or claim, then pick the choice matching the claim that the evidence is used to prove.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension items with statistics, case studies, or named products used to argue about an industry, country, or system.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference about the example itself, or a directly stated factual relationship.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses conditional or tentative wording, then preserve that uncertainty and avoid upgrading it to certainty, exclusivity, or strongest-effect claims.
Error pattern: I overstrengthened a limited possibility statement into a definitive recommendation, adding force not supported by the text.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, replace key verbs with modal tags—may/can/will/must—and reject any option that is stronger than the passage on certainty or scope.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items comparing paraphrases of causal, conditional, or probabilistic claims about effects or benefits.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage itself explicitly states necessity, superiority, universality, or a proven best method.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists physical features but emphasizes the overall mood, symbolism, and viewer experience they create, then choose the option about artistic conception over mere layout or style.
Error pattern: I focused on concrete spatial details and ignored that they were presented mainly as devices for building a sacred atmosphere.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each descriptive detail as structure-only or atmosphere/symbolism-building; if most details support an experiential effect, prefer the theme about conceived mood.
Use when: This applies to architecture or art passages mixing forms, symbols, plants, sounds, and viewer perspective.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text chiefly explains plan, dimensions, sequence, or technical design without discussing emotional or symbolic effect.

Transfer rule: If an argument links an intervention to a health benefit through a chain of effects, then verify each causal bridge, especially the unstated middle link.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping premises to conclusion and spotting the missing necessary connection rather than choosing a tempting side claim.
Diagnostic check: Write the chain as A → B → C; if one arrow is unstated, negate it and see whether the conclusion collapses.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions involving causal reasoning, therapeutic value claims, or evidence about stress, biology, or behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a strengthen/weaken answer or when the missing statement is merely sufficient, not required.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts case-level unfair outcomes with long-term procedural/legal-order benefits, then choose the option that preserves procedure over immediate substantive justice.
Error pattern: Success comes from identifying the author’s main tradeoff and selecting the broader normative claim, not literal side remarks or exaggerated oppositions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state in one sentence what is being prioritized over what; reject options that flip, narrow, or absolutize that priority.
Use when: Apply this to argument-interpretation questions about law, institutions, process, neutrality, and long-term versus short-term values.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly defines concepts, reports facts without endorsement, or asks for a detail rather than the central viewpoint.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several concrete mechanisms after a broad claim, then choose the option emphasizing methods/channels rather than a general effect.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the passage’s focus level: specific implementation routes, not merely overall importance or policy considerations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the thesis and count mechanism cues like “through,” “via,” or parallel actions; if multiple appear, prefer a “ways/how” summary.
Use when: The stem asks what is highlighted and the text names distinct policy tools, steps, or channels supporting one goal.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly argues necessity, impact magnitude, or recommendations without enumerating concrete mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If two speakers discuss the same method and one calls it best while the other proposes a supplement or alternative due to a limitation, then infer disagreement about that method’s optimality, not its total usefulness.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating “best” from “sometimes useful” and tracking each speaker’s stance precisely.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each speaker’s claim as strongest endorsed level: best, acceptable, limited, supplement, alternative, or reject; choose the option matching the clash in levels.
Use when: Apply in dialogue questions asking what two people disagree about, especially when one gives praise and the other gives a timing or evidence-based critique.
Boundary: Ignore when the issue is factual agreement about background details rather than comparative evaluation or recommendation.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats “not praising/not mentioning positives” as “harmful/violating a ban,” then check for an unjustified shift from absence of benefit to presence of harm.  
Error pattern: Confusing a missing compliment or neutral omission with active damage; overlooking a required bridge principle.  
Diagnostic check: Restate the premise and conclusion in polarity terms: does the proof go from “not positive” to “negative”? If yes, ask whether a rule explicitly connects them.  
Use when: A condition forbids harm, offense, or detriment, but the evidence only shows silence, omission, or failure to endorse.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus states that omission itself counts as harm or that praise is explicitly required.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined by suppressing diverse views within group decisions, then choose the option that actively gathers information and encourages dissent as the exception.
Error pattern: I overfocused on one mechanism of conformity and missed the broader definition-based contrast between restrictive and open decision processes.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether it restricts expression, pressures dissenters, or channels discussion into one framework; the one lacking these markers is the answer.
Use when: Apply this on “which is not” questions about groupthink, conformity, discussion failure, or decision environments shaped by pressure or authority.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept concerns only individual bias, factual procedure, or outcomes unrelated to group discussion dynamics.

Transfer rule: If a response introduces delayed or missing evidence, then treat it as weakening the argument’s support, not directly disproving the conclusion.
Error pattern: Correctly distinguished an attack on evidential sufficiency from an attack claiming the conclusion is false.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does the objection show the premise sample is incomplete, time-limited, or unable to detect the relevant phenomenon?
Use when: Relevant in argument-role questions where evidence comes from surveys, observations, or reports taken before all outcomes would appear.
Boundary: Ignore when the response supplies independent proof, states the conclusion is impossible, or targets circular reasoning instead.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires borrowing an idea or method from another field, then reject cases based on direct observation within the same investigation field.
Error pattern: I confused cross-domain transfer with ordinary discovery and misread a clear analogy case as not fitting.
Diagnostic check: For each option, name source domain and target domain; if you cannot state two distinct domains and a transferred method/idea, mark it as not using lateral thinking.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about analogy, inspiration, transfer, invention, or methods crossing domains.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is about experimentation, induction, or discovery without any requirement of cross-field borrowing.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion attacks an argument by adding a missing necessary condition, then choose the option that denies that condition under the argument’s stated setting.
Error pattern: I preferred a statement about what hinders progress instead of one that directly blocks the premise-to-conclusion link.
Diagnostic check: Map the argument as setting + claimed cause + extra required condition; then test which option says that required condition is absent whenever the setting holds.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/infer questions where the passage says “X leads to Y, but Y also requires Z, so the pro-X argument fails.”
Boundary: Ignore when choices compare strength, give examples, or discuss effects without asserting absence of the needed condition.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires long-term work stress causing exhaustion, then reject cases driven by short duration, external coercion, or simple unwillingness before calling it burnout.
Error pattern: I overmatched surface fatigue/disengagement and missed necessary conditions, especially duration and stress-origin within the job itself.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each required element from the definition and verify every option satisfies all of them; eliminate any option missing even one element.
Use when: Apply this on definition-based multiple-choice items where several choices share symptoms but differ in cause, timespan, or domain.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is graded by degree rather than strict criteria, or when the prompt asks for best fit instead of necessary-fit screening.

Transfer rule: If a passage repeatedly links complex tasks to needing “professional counterparts” or specialized response capacity, then choose the option about building professional talent, not broader cooperation or expansion.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions are solved well by tracking the author’s repeated causal driver rather than attractive background details.
Diagnostic check: Underline repeated need-words and ask, “What missing ingredient is said to enable all listed functions?”; match the answer to that recurring requirement.
Use when: The text lists many service duties, mentions complexity changes, and repeatedly cites specialized ability across institutions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage evaluates outcomes, compares models, or centers on coordination mechanisms rather than personnel capacity.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers product quality from survey preference, then test whether preference could be driven by non-quality factors.
Error pattern: Spot or avoid the flaw of treating popularity, intention to buy, or stated preference as direct evidence of the claimed property.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Would the survey result still occur if buyers favored price, style, habit, availability, or advertising instead of quality?”
Use when: Apply to ads or arguments that cite surveys, customer preferences, rankings, or purchase intent to prove superiority or excellence.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence directly measures the claimed trait itself or explicitly rules out alternative causes.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a present harmful-cause claim by saying the alleged cause existed before, then test whether it could still have been harmful all along.
Error pattern: Treating long-standing or unchanged presence of a factor as evidence that it cannot undermine outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the rebuttal rule out ongoing negative effects, or only show the factor is not new?”
Use when: A stimulus argues “not a cause now” because the condition historically existed, persisted, or was stronger earlier.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument provides evidence the factor is harmless, offset by stronger improvements, or causally disconnected from the outcome.

Transfer rule: If a status term is defined by formal legal appointment, inclusion in the state establishment, and state-funded pay, then choose only the option showing an actual official post within that establishment.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every definitional element instead of relying on workplace, longevity, or government affiliation alone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark for each option: legal public authority role, establishment staffing status, and state salary/benefits; reject any option missing one.
Use when: Apply this to classification questions about legal employment status, especially when distractors involve contractors, support staff, or public institutions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about broad public-sector workers rather than a narrowly defined legal civil-service category.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires unlawful use of public authority causing harm to a private party and a payout by the state, then choose the option matching all three elements.
Error pattern: Success comes from element-by-element matching instead of picking any government payment or public-benefit spending.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: actor is a state organ/staff? act is illegal in official power? victim is a private rights-holder? payment is compensatory for that harm?
Use when: Relevant for legal-definition multiple choice with several government-related scenarios that can be confused with subsidies, honors, welfare, or private liability.
Boundary: Ignore when the concept does not hinge on illegality, official authority, causation of damage, and compensation to an injured non-state party.

Transfer rule: If a passage argues information is filtered to fit superiors’ expectations, then choose the option about preserving a superior’s preferred earlier view, not one requiring extra unseen knowledge.
Error pattern: I overreached beyond the text, inventing what the superior knew instead of matching the stated motive of expectation-driven suppression.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option follow directly from the described filtering motive, or does it assume additional facts about awareness or decisions?”
Use when: Apply to completion/inference questions about bureaucracy, message screening, distorted reporting, or withholding updates to match prior beliefs.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly states the superior’s knowledge, decision status, or another concrete reason for withholding information.

Transfer rule: If a passage asks for the main point and begins with a phenomenon plus “why,” then choose the option that states the author’s overall causal explanation.
Error pattern: Success came from separating supporting illustrations about preferences and reactions from the broader claim explaining the trend.
Diagnostic check: Identify the first sentence’s claim, then ask whether each option paraphrases that claim rather than a reason, example, or side comment.
Use when: Relevant in main-point questions where later sentences provide motivations, attitudes, or examples to support an opening explanatory thesis.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a detail, inference, attitude, or when the thesis appears only at the end or is heavily qualified.

Transfer rule: If evidence targets people overhearing one side of a conversation, then prefer conclusions about bystanders’ distraction, not the speaker’s own risk.
Error pattern: I shifted the effect from the described listener to a different actor and added an unsupported causal outcome.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label who experiences the stated effect and ask whether the option keeps the same subject, mechanism, and level of claim.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/must-be-supported questions with multiple actors, indirect effects, or tempting real-world assumptions beyond the passage.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus explicitly generalizes across roles or provides direct evidence about the broader causal consequence.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what explains opposite outcomes from the same treatment, then prefer a common alternative cause that can account for both cases without extra assumptions.
Error pattern: I overfit to a subgroup difference and grabbed a tempting detail instead of testing whether it explains both experiences.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: could this alone plausibly produce improvement in one person and worsening in another under the same regimen?
Use when: Two anecdotes report conflicting effects from one intervention, especially in causal-reasoning multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt provides controlled evidence or explicitly asks for a moderator variable distinguishing the people.

Transfer rule: If several statements are linked by “only one is true,” then translate each into a precise truth condition and test every option by counting truths.
Error pattern: I succeeded by using consistency across all claims, but I nearly treated vague-looking statements informally instead of as exact logical propositions.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate outcome, mark each prediction True/False, especially conditionals as false only when antecedent is true and consequent is false, then verify the total true count equals one.
Use when: Relevant in ranking or assignment problems with multiple predictions, exclusivity constraints, and at least one “only one correct” condition.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous in scope, or multiple answers could satisfy the truth-count rule equally.

Transfer rule: If asked which option does not match a passage, then map each choice to a direct claim or necessary implication and reject the one that weakens, reverses, or overqualifies the author’s stance.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing the passage’s overall endorsement/caution structure from a tempting paraphrase that subtly changed force.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label it support / possible / contradiction; if it adds “not necessarily,” “only,” or another scope shift absent from the passage, treat it as suspect.
Use when: Apply to reading-comprehension items with attitude, implication, or “except/not match” wording and mixed literal-versus-inferred choices.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on outside facts, technical definitions, or quantitative detail rather than passage logic.

Transfer rule: If a scenario shows deliberate practice with a clear goal and attention-demanding effort, then classify it as explicit learning.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating intentional, rule-guided study from skill pickup through repeated exposure or immersion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the person had a stated objective, consciously practiced, and invested focused mental effort; require all three.
Use when: Apply this on questions contrasting conscious learning versus automatic acquisition from environment, family background, or incidental repetition.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the example mixes both processes equally or lacks enough detail about intention and attention.

Transfer rule: If a legal definition requires negligent traffic-law violation plus serious harm, then choose the scenario showing both a rule breach by the driver and accidental, not intentional, harmful results.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every element of the definition and separating negligence from intent and from pure mechanical failure without fault.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes: traffic-rule violation, negligent mental state, serious injury/death/property loss; accept only if all three are clearly satisfied.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about offenses with required conduct, causation, harm threshold, and specified culpability.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the offense allows intent, strict liability, attempted conduct, or no underlying traffic-management violation is required.

Transfer rule: If an argument equates a rare disaster’s initiating human error with errors said to be nearly inevitable in similar systems, then infer the disaster becomes nearly inevitable over continued operation.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by chaining analogy plus long-run inevitability from cause frequency to event likelihood.
Diagnostic check: List the causal link, the comparison class, and the inevitability claim; verify the answer preserves all three without adding stronger claims about impossibility, complexity, or policy futility.
Use when: Apply in strengthen/support questions involving analogies, human error, and repeated-operation or long-run language.
Boundary: Ignore when the comparison is disputed, the event needs extra missing conditions, or choices generalize beyond the stated causal scope.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists harmful consequences after a policy/setup, then choose the option that states the author’s implied evaluative conclusion about that policy.
Error pattern: Success came from synthesizing examples into the passage’s main claim instead of chasing background explanations or general facts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, summarize each example in 3–6 words; if they all point in one direction, pick the option matching that shared direction.
Use when: Relevant for completion/inference questions built from multiple concrete cases, contrast words, and a clearly cautionary or supportive tone.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for a direct fact, definition, purpose statement explicitly given, or a neutral principle rather than the passage’s takeaway.

Transfer rule: If a question contrasts “structure” with “matter,” then map “structure” to organization/arrangement and “matter” to the constituent entities themselves.
Error pattern: I narrowed a general concept to a specific scale instead of separating relation-level description from object-level items.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rewrite each term as “how parts are organized” versus “what the parts are”; reject any choice that treats both as the same kind of thing.
Use when: Apply this on terminology questions distinguishing pattern, composition, hierarchy, or arrangement from the particles/components composing a system.
Boundary: Ignore this when the terms are explicitly defined as synonyms or the question asks about a specific level only.

Transfer rule: If asked which statement cannot support a conclusion, then test each option for direct relevance to the exact claim and reject options that shift to another product, use case, or comparison target.
Error pattern: I favored a superficially weaker-seeming benefit instead of checking whether the evidence was actually about the conclusion’s subject.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this give a reason this technology would replace the named incumbent in the stated domain?” If it mainly discusses a different domain, mark it non-support.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken EXCEPT questions with broad conclusions and answer choices mixing direct evidence with off-domain facts.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion itself explicitly generalizes across domains or products.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims two opposite conditions are equally serious, then choose evidence showing both cause comparable harm to the same target.
Error pattern: I favored a mechanism that continues the causal story instead of evidence that directly supports the comparative conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conclusion, identify the compared outcomes, and ask which option gives parallel damage evidence rather than background process details.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions with analogies, comparisons, or claims of equal severity across different causes or states.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is about timing, reversibility, or causal mechanism rather than comparative impact.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion infers a hidden trait from observed behavior, then choose the assumption that makes that behavior a valid indicator of the trait.
Error pattern: I matched a tempting cause/background statement instead of the bridge linking evidence to the claimed generalization.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If the observed behavior were not a reliable sign of the claimed trait, would the argument collapse?” If yes, that bridge is required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where evidence is attendance, choices, or reactions, and the conclusion is about interest, belief, ability, or attitude.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for explanation, strengthening by cause, or when the conclusion already directly describes the observed behavior.

Transfer rule: If a passage blames poor outcomes on missing oversight or guarantees, then infer the remedy is stronger supervision/enforcement, not creating more institutions.
Error pattern: I overfocused on an intermediate cause and chose a structural fix instead of the directly targeted mechanism named in the argument.
Diagnostic check: Underline each stated cause; ask which option most precisely reverses that cause with the fewest added assumptions.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions about policy, management, law, or administration that contrast issuing rules with ensuring execution.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly argues that organizational capacity or new institutions, rather than oversight, is the primary missing factor.

Transfer rule: If a behavior is only a personal habit or preference without a role-based social norm, ritual, or rule, then treat it as not institutionalized.
Error pattern: Distinguishing collective, role-governed patterns from repeated private behavior is the key success pattern.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this behavior attach to a social role and persist because of shared norms, customs, or formal rules beyond the individuals involved?
Use when: Relevant for choices mixing customs, ceremonies, official procedures, obligations, and ordinary recurring personal actions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns mere frequency, coordination, or natural timing rather than socially enforced conduct.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle mixes identities, locations, and family comparisons, then build a table mapping each person to each referenced role before ordering ages.
Error pattern: Misassigned relational statements across categories, causing one “sister in [place]” to be treated as the wrong person.
Diagnostic check: List every comparison as ordered pairs, substitute using the location-person mapping, then verify the final ranking satisfies all inequalities with no contradiction.
Use when: Relevant for word problems with three or more entities linked by attributes like place, kinship, and comparative terms such as older or younger.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are already directly matched or the task is simple arithmetic rather than cross-referenced constraint tracking.

Transfer rule: If an argument attacks reasoning by comparing it to another case with the same sampling flaw, then classify it as using an analogous flawed inference, not offering an alternative conclusion.
Error pattern: Mistaking critique-by-analogy for drawing a better inference from the evidence.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does the second case share the structure and expose the same defect, or does it generate a new conclusion from the data?”
Use when: The stimulus includes “it would be like...” or a parallel example meant to show biased selection, circular support, or other matching reasoning errors.
Boundary: Ignore when the comparison is a literal counterexample, a contradiction test, or evidence for a separate, more plausible inference.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a risky intervention should be avoided, then ask how many harms attributed to the intervention would have occurred anyway from the underlying condition.
Error pattern: I focused on comparing overall outcomes across groups instead of testing whether the cited intervention-caused deaths are net additions versus substituted timing/causes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, identify the argument’s counted harm, then ask: “Among those harmed this way, what fraction would still die without the intervention?”
Use when: Relevant for recommendation/causal arguments about treatment, safety, or policy where subjects already face substantial baseline risk from an illness or hazard.
Boundary: Ignore when the issue is purely prevalence, trend, or patient-controlled prevention, not whether the intervention changes total mortality beyond baseline.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts intense concern for distant events with neglect of nearby people, then infer the author is urging renewed attention to the immediate human environment.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions hinge on the contrast and evaluative tone, not on surface topics like technology or broad-mindedness.
Diagnostic check: List the praised and criticized behaviors; if criticism targets neglect of family or local strangers, choose the option addressing nearby care.
Use when: Relevant for rhetorical passages using examples, irony, or contrast between “far away” matters and everyday relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage explicitly praises global awareness without criticizing local neglect.

Transfer rule: If a logic setup has one-to-one assignments plus conditionals, then fix the given assumption, eliminate impossible roles person-by-person, and test each option against all remaining valid cases.
Error pattern: I treated a conditional as triggered by an unrelated role and jumped to a single placement without exhausting alternatives.
Diagnostic check: Under the stated assumption, make a grid of allowed roles; for each option, try to build one consistent counterexample—if none exist after full elimination, infer it.
Use when: Relevant in assignment puzzles with exclusive categories, “if…then” clues, and a temporary assumption about one person’s role.
Boundary: Ignore when clues are probabilistic, non-exclusive, or an option asks for likelihood rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If a passage links several traits to a final sentence naming a broader topic, then choose the option describing it as an introduction to that topic, not a mid-level detail.
Error pattern: Mistook supporting imagery and repeated metaphors for the main idea instead of tracking the passage’s rhetorical destination.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the concluding sentence, ask “What earlier points are building toward this?”, and match the option at that same level of scope.
Use when: The passage is abstract, uses many analogies, and ends by connecting them to a larger theme or upcoming discussion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, or when the passage fully develops one claim without signaling a broader frame.

Transfer rule: If asked which act is not ultra vires, then first verify whether it is an administrative licensing act at all before comparing authority, level, subject matter, or territory.
Error pattern: I matched on obvious overreach facts but ignored the threshold classification of the government action type.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is this a license/approval decision? If no, exclude ultra vires analysis; if yes, test the four jurisdiction limits.
Use when: Relevant in administrative-law multiple choice that defines a doctrine narrowly and mixes examples from different state powers or procedures.
Boundary: Ignore this when the doctrine applies to all administrative acts generally, not specifically to licensing decisions.

Transfer rule: If an argument concedes severe harm yet rejects prohibition because of liberty or markets, then infer it prioritizes those principles over reducing harm.
Error pattern: Success pattern: reading the conclusion as a value-ranking claim, not as an absolute rights claim or an unsupported causal prediction.
Diagnostic check: State the harm premise and policy conclusion separately; ask, “What principle explains allowing the harmful behavior anyway?”
Use when: Relevant in passages balancing public health, safety, or welfare against freedom, autonomy, or market freedom.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives practical limits only, or when answer choices add absolute language or new causal assumptions.

Transfer rule: If cues point in opposite directions, then prefer the option that explains both as ambivalence or neutrality before inferring a hidden test or strong intent.
Error pattern: Overinterpreting mixed evidence by inventing a motive beyond what the observable facts support.
Diagnostic check: List each cue, mark whether it supports permission, prohibition, or uncertainty; if evidence splits and no extra motive is stated, choose the least-committal interpretation.
Use when: A scenario contains conflicting signals, policies versus accommodations, or behavior that can plausibly support more than one attitude.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives explicit intentions, a clear hierarchy of rules, or strong contextual evidence for irony, deception, or testing.

Transfer rule: If a work is created by a member of an organization as part of an assigned job task, then classify it as a duty work.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definitional element, especially organizational role plus task assignment, not mere employment or personal expertise.
Diagnostic check: Verify three boxes: creator belongs to the organization, creation arose from official duties or a direct assignment, and the output serves the organization’s work.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about whether a creation belongs to an employer, institution, or organized entity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rule concerns independent hobby projects, personal publications, or works unrelated to assigned organizational duties.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “something discourages entry” from low representation in a profession, then test whether differential exit or retention could explain the pattern instead.
Error pattern: I accepted an upstream-pipeline explanation and missed a stronger alternative cause at a later stage that breaks the entry-specific conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, list the exact causal claim; ask whether each option attacks entry, selection, popularity, or attrition, and prefer one that explains the evidence while denying the claimed cause.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions involving population percentages, career funnels, and conclusions about why a group is underrepresented.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about overall prevalence or when no alternative stage in the process is plausible.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a group can be effectively treated only by one method because of an underlying cause, then check for the assumption that alternatives cannot address that cause.
Error pattern: Success pattern: identifying a hidden exclusivity bridge from causal explanation to exclusive treatment.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could any rejected option still affect, reduce, or correct the stated cause?” If yes, the “only” claim is unsupported.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions with causal language, subgroup claims, and a conclusion that one intervention alone can work.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is comparative, probabilistic, or about speed, symptoms alone, or prevalence rather than exclusive effectiveness.

Transfer rule: If an option includes systematic data collection plus organizing/analyzing results about a target group, then classify it as statistical work.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking for the full workflow; failures come from accepting casual observation, a decision to study, or public solicitation as enough.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is there a defined population/question, a method for gathering data, and an explicit step of sorting or analysis that yields summarized data?
Use when: Apply this on items asking whether an activity counts as statistics, surveys, investigations, or data analysis.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is about policy choice, publicity, complaint handling, or idea collection without data processing.

Transfer rule: If premises give a conditional necessity plus a separate cause of that necessary factor, then infer the cause might establish a precondition, not the final outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining implications conservatively and distinguishing necessary conditions from sufficient ones.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as necessary or sufficient; test whether the candidate conclusion asserts only a prerequisite reached through the chain, not growth itself.
Use when: Apply this to argument-completion items with conditionals, causal triggers, and wording like “without,” “any,” or “might.”
Boundary: Ignore this when premises include biconditionals, explicit sufficiency for the end state, or normative terms requiring value judgments.

Transfer rule: If asked to explain a stable difference between common and rare groups, then prefer a choice naming a mechanism tied to abundance that directly affects the target outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the answer’s causal variable to the observed contrast instead of choosing facts that are merely related or beneficial.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Does this option create a direct chain from being more common/rarer to the stated difference, and does it work no matter which group fills each role?”
Use when: Relevant for explain-the-pattern questions comparing high-frequency versus low-frequency members across changing identities.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for methodology critique, prediction, or an effect unrelated to the compared trait.

Transfer rule: If an argument applies a general definition to a case because one stated feature matches, then check whether all required elements of that definition are actually established.
Error pattern: Illicit full-definition transfer from partial similarity; treating a case as fully covered by a concept after showing only one component.
Diagnostic check: List the definition’s necessary conditions and mark each as explicitly supported; if any are missing, reject answers that say the definition fully applies.
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions where premises cite a definition, criterion, or principle and then classify a specific case under it.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus independently proves every condition or the issue is about policy, causation, or ambiguity rather than definitional fit.

Transfer rule: If premises say “most/all” across overlapping groups, then infer only guaranteed overlap/existence from subset chains, not a universal converse about the whole class.
Error pattern: Treated strong premises about many members as if they justified an all-members conclusion; confused subset direction and overgeneralized.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each statement as set links, then test each choice with a small counterexample model satisfying the premises; reject any choice falsified there.
Use when: Quantifiers like most, all, some, certain appear, especially in chained category statements about traits, results, and training.
Boundary: Ignore when the task uses definitions, biconditionals, or explicit equivalence that legitimately supports reversing or universalizing a relation.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts improvement from increased resources, then look for high-demand side effects that independently worsen the outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from checking for a countervailing cause instead of accepting the stated causal chain at face value.
Diagnostic check: List the argument’s main cause, intended effect, and one plausible accompanying change; ask whether that change could reverse the effect.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken causal questions comparing two conditions, especially when one condition brings added staffing, workload, speed, or complexity.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only restate the benefit, are irrelevant background, or do not occur specifically in the condition being evaluated.

Transfer rule: If an argument compares counts from two groups to infer many members of one are also in the other, then check overlap before accepting it.
Error pattern: Treating similar-sized populations as substantially intersecting without evidence about membership overlap.
Diagnostic check: Define the two sets and ask: could they be mostly disjoint while all stated numbers remain true? If yes, reject the overlap claim.
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions using two population totals, percentages, or headcounts to conclude “few,” “many,” or “most” are shared.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus directly gives intersection data, subset relations, or mutually exclusive categories.

Transfer rule: If one group is wholly contained in another and at least one member of the smaller group is given, then infer existence in the larger group, not reversed training or origin claims.
Error pattern: Illicit conversion/quantifier shift—turning “most institutions train X” into “most X come from those institutions.”
Diagnostic check: Translate statements into set arrows and quantifiers; ask whether the conclusion is existential, universal, or about source distribution, and whether direction is preserved.
Use when: Premises mix category inclusion, named individuals, and “most” statements about institutions producing or training people.
Boundary: Ignore this when premises explicitly state graduates’ origins, bidirectional equivalence, or exact counts supporting reverse-frequency claims.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one seller wins mainly because its prices are lower, then require an assumption linking buyers’ choice in that product category to price.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from market competitiveness to a broad business principle instead of the specific consumer decision driver needed by the claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option state that customers in this purchase actually choose based chiefly on price, rather than naming a general factor or extra feature?”
Use when: Apply in assumption questions comparing two channels or sellers where one cited advantage is lower price and the conclusion is about popularity or performance.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states buyer priorities, or when another premise directly explains preference without relying on price sensitivity.

Transfer rule: If a principle question asks what justifies someone’s refusal based on prior praise, then pick the rule that forbids inconsistent treatment of the same kind of conduct across cases.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the stated ground to a consistency principle rather than drifting to broader policy or institutional duties.
Diagnostic check: Identify the actor’s explicit reason, abstract it in one sentence, and test each option by asking whether it directly links the earlier approval to the present refusal.
Use when: Relevant when facts emphasize prior endorsement, current objection, and a claim about fairness or hypocrisy.
Boundary: Ignore when the justification turns on outcomes, expertise, legality, or duties instead of consistency between past and present evaluations.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why protection is needed only briefly despite a longer vulnerability window, then prefer a choice that limits when the threat exists, not one about other requirements.
Error pattern: I matched a tempting detail about incubation conditions instead of resolving the timing mismatch between danger duration and guarding duration.
Diagnostic check: State the paradox in two timelines—how long harm is possible vs. how long guarding occurs—and eliminate any option that does not explicitly narrow the threat period.
Use when: Apply to strengthen/explain questions involving temporary guarding, protection, monitoring, or intervention despite an apparently ongoing risk.
Boundary: Ignore when the gap is explained by an alternative protective mechanism that continuously prevents harm after guarding ends.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why a harmed party avoids enforcement, then prefer a choice showing the violation also creates future customers or strategic benefits.
Error pattern: Success came from reconciling the paradox by finding an incentive that makes inaction rational, not by comparing severity or unrelated industry behavior.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the harm, the omitted action, and one concrete benefit of not acting; choose the option that supplies that benefit.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen-explain paradox questions involving lost sales, illegal copying, nonenforcement, or seemingly self-defeating business decisions.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to judge legality, ethics, or direct causal effects rather than explain an apparent contradiction.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “if you want X, then you must do Y,” then treat Y as necessary for X only; do not infer what holds when X is not wanted.
Error pattern: Conditional-direction control succeeded: avoid reversing or negating a one-way requirement.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each statement as Want(X) → Must(Y); test options by contraposition only, and reject any that infer ¬Want(X) → ¬Must(Y) or force a false either/or.
Use when: Arguments use “if you want,” “must,” “only if,” or similar necessity language tied to goals or outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage states biconditionals, explicit sufficiency, or independent reasons for Y unrelated to wanting X.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers higher incidence from a rise in case counts, then test whether the underlying population size also rose.
Error pattern: Confusing absolute numbers with rates; strong weakening often comes from a denominator shift, not a direct medical rebuttal.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the trend still look alarming after converting counts to per-capita prevalence within the same age group?”
Use when: Relevant for surveys or reports comparing more people, more patients, or more cases over time across a demographic group.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already uses rates/proportions, holds population constant, or the option does not affect the comparison base.

Transfer rule: If an argument questions predictive value by comparing signal frequency at event times versus ordinary times, then prioritize base-rate and observability questions over cross-category similarity.
Error pattern: I overvalued extra pattern-matching evidence and undervalued whether the cited cue is distinctive, prevalent, or selectively noticed.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, sort each option by whether it tests discrimination (event vs normal), prevalence before events, or reporting bias; mark least important any option only about resemblance across groups.
Use when: Relevant for causal or predictive arguments about anecdotal warning signs, especially when the critique invokes coincidence, subjectivity, or constant background occurrence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the claim specifically requires a shared mechanism across groups or compares categories as the core evidence.

Transfer rule: If asked to explain rapid adoption of a paid learning service, then prefer the option linking the service’s core mechanism to a broad user need and the stated trend.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched population-level growth with a general causal driver, not a niche feature, subgroup motive, or merely compatible benefit.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it explain why many people would newly adopt this service now, across users, better than the others?
Use when: Relevant for “best explain the phenomenon” questions about market growth, acceptance, or behavior shifts with several plausible causes.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for necessary assumptions, predictions, exceptions, or when a narrow subgroup/mechanism is explicitly the phenomenon.

Transfer rule: If clues compare ages to roles, then convert each clue into person–role exclusions/ordering facts and test every remaining assignment against all clues.
Error pattern: I treated “different age” as if it created an ordering/equality consequence, inventing a restriction not stated.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each clue in plain logic form, then for the chosen assignment verify each clause one by one without adding assumptions.
Use when: Apply this on matching/logic-grid problems with unique roles and relational clues about age, order, or attributes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem requires numerical calculation or when a clue explicitly defines stronger relations than simple inequality/exclusion.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives what did not yet exist at an earlier time, then infer only what earlier instances lacked, not global “first/earliest” rankings.
Error pattern: Overgeneralized from one ancient example to an unsupported superlative about all members of a class.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list each claim as timeline fact, absence fact, or ranking claim; reject any option needing a ranking not explicitly stated.
Use when: Relevant in chronology questions comparing what existed and what did not exist at a past time.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt directly provides comparative priority, exclusivity, or a complete inventory of all categories.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers what policymakers believe from equal legal penalties, then strengthen it by adding a rule linking penalty size to policymakers’ beliefs about harm.
Error pattern: Success pattern: identify and reinforce the hidden bridge from observed policy equivalence to inferred evaluative judgment.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What assumption lets equal punishment imply equal perceived harm?” Then choose the option that states that assumption most directly and generally.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions where conclusions about beliefs, values, or intentions are drawn from enacted rules, sanctions, prices, or classifications.
Boundary: Ignore when choices discuss actual outcomes, unusual exceptions, victim-level comparisons, or deterrence instead of the decision-maker’s general penalty-setting principle.

Transfer rule: If a passage criticizes a dominant framing throughout, then choose the option that states the author’s broader alternative perspective, not just a harmful consequence.
