Diagnostic check: Underline conclusion markers and compare each option by tense/scope; choose the one matching the passage’s final inferred direction, not just listed instances.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension items with many supporting examples, a limitation statement, and a concluding sentence about future development.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a directly stated fact, definition, or example rather than the author’s overall takeaway.

Transfer rule: If an argument uses a special feature to claim high value but states value depends on rarity plus another met condition, then assume that feature guarantees rarity.
Error pattern: Success pattern: bridge a stated indicator to the decision criterion instead of choosing a choice that merely restates, compares, or limits factors.
Diagnostic check: List each premise-supported criterion for the conclusion; verify the missing criterion is supplied by the assumption and that removing it breaks the inference.
Use when: Relevant in necessary-assumption questions where the conclusion depends on a standard and one cited fact must connect to that standard.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for sufficient support, flaw identification, or when the link to the criterion is already explicitly given.

Transfer rule: If one agent explicitly adopts a screening or policing standard and another does not, then prefer a principle tying blame to that self-imposed commitment.  
Error pattern: I chose a broad duty principle that applied to both actors, failing to explain the asymmetry in judgments.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking whether it justifies blaming one actor while excusing the otherwise similar other.  
Use when: The stimulus contrasts similar actions but highlights a difference in stated policy, role commitment, or assumed obligation.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks who acted best overall, or when both actors share the same explicit duty.

Transfer rule: If a statement defines a fund’s management and intended uses, then choose the option that paraphrases the fund’s overall purpose/effect, not one that shifts management onto the beneficiaries.
Error pattern: Confused the manager of the fund with the object being funded; matched a surface phrase instead of the sentence’s actor-action-target structure.
Diagnostic check: Mark three roles—who is entrusted, what is managed, and who receives support—and reject any option that swaps these roles or upgrades means into guarantees.
Use when: Relevant for definition, policy, or announcement questions describing institutions, entrusted management, funding flows, and intended support outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for implied causation, evaluation strength, or facts beyond the stated management-purpose relationship.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires judging one feature and then projecting or masking other traits, then reject choices that only state a broad sameness or category-level generalization without feature-to-feature inference.
Error pattern: I confused stereotyping or universal-category claims with a halo-style spillover from one salient attribute to other attributes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is one observed positive/negative trait causing assumptions about different unobserved traits, or merely summarizing a group/object as generally the same?”
Use when: Relevant for concept questions about impression formation, trait spillover, masking effects, or inferring multiple qualities from one salient cue.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the statement is only about preference, direct observation, or simple group generalization with no cross-trait inference.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists transmission channels and enabling device features, then infer a broad risk/exposure claim directly supported by them.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: combine repeated mechanism details into the safest generalization, instead of choosing broader evaluation or policy claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each option as direct restatement, supported summary, or added judgment; choose the strongest supported summary only.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions built from causes, channels, technical features, or repeated evidence about how something spreads or operates.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for attitude, recommendation, comparison beyond the text, or a specific unstated consequence.

Transfer rule: If a definition is for enterprise inventory, then require goods owned/managed by firms and currently on transport or awaiting transport, not consumer parcel-tracking states.
Error pattern: I matched a surface cue (“at a transit station”) while ignoring scope and ownership constraints in the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list required attributes: business inventory, destination not yet reached, physically in or queued for transport, not sitting in a regular warehouse.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about logistics categories, inventory stages, or supply-chain status.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category is about end-customer delivery experience, generic location labels, or warehouse stock ready for shipment.

Transfer rule: If asked which option does not support a criticism, then test whether each option attacks the experiment’s validity or merely adds an irrelevant detail.
Error pattern: I favored a superficially strong objection instead of separating methodological critiques from statements that do not bear on the experts’ claim.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Does this weaken the experiment-to-conclusion link?” If yes, mark support; if it discusses a side issue, mark non-support.
Use when: Applicable in strengthen/weaken/support-except questions about experimental design, causation, and inference from evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for the best improvement, a direct conclusion, or when every option clearly addresses the same flaw.

Transfer rule: If a claim says buyers resist producer influence, then prefer evidence that directly links producer actions to buyer behavior over evidence about confusion or habits.
Error pattern: I chose an option about decision difficulty, not the one that most directly undermined the core causal claim about susceptibility.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which choice, if true, most strongly shows sellers can systematically change purchases?” Reject choices that only describe preferences, routine, or social context.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/irrationality questions about autonomy, persuasion, advertising, manipulation, or independence of consumer choice.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument concerns product availability, search costs, peer coordination, or nonpersuasive causes of purchasing.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends with prescriptions after brief background, then choose the option capturing the main recommended course of action.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating setup and critique from the author’s central proposal, rather than overweighting context.
Diagnostic check: Mark background, problem statement, and recommendation; if one section tells what should be done, test whether the choice summarizes that directive.
Use when: The text contrasts past/current conditions, mentions practical constraints, and concludes with advice about attention, promotion, survival, or expansion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage is mainly definitional, historical, or comparative without any clear action-oriented takeaway.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several roles or values of a subject, then choose the option capturing the broad shared attribute, not one example.
Error pattern: I narrowed from a multi-point argument to a single supporting detail instead of extracting the main thesis.
Diagnostic check: Underline every claim, group them into theme vs examples, and reject any choice covering only one subgroup.
Use when: The paragraph defines significance, gives multiple functions, and ends with an illustrative case or city-level example.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, example, or the author’s final emphasized case rather than the overall summary.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends expanding a subgroup because its observed rate is lower, then test whether the subgroup operates in safer conditions rather than being inherently better.
Error pattern: Confusing correlation from selective exposure with causal superiority; success comes from spotting a hidden confound between group type and operating context.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the rate advantage likely remain if both groups faced the same routes, environments, trip lengths, and restrictions?”
Use when: A policy claim extrapolates from subgroup performance data to predict systemwide improvement after wider adoption.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already controls for operating conditions or directly compares outcomes under matched exposure.

Transfer rule: If two speakers cite different salary statistics while arguing over a complaint, then identify the disagreement as the evaluative claim those facts are meant to support, not a side condition.
Error pattern: Mistaking evidence or a conditional premise for the actual contested issue.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state each speaker’s bottom-line claim in one clause and choose the option matching the clash between those claims, not the numbers mentioned.
Use when: One speaker gives a judgment, another challenges it using factual data, averages, or distributions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an unstated assumption, cause, or whether a stated condition is true.

Transfer rule: If an argument needs a specific causal link, then prefer choices that directly fill a missing step over broad statements that merely sound related.
Error pattern: I treated a generally relevant consequence as support and missed that one option failed to connect to any required premise in the chain.
Diagnostic check: Map the argument into steps; for each option, point to the exact step it strengthens. If no step gains support, mark it as the non-supporter.
Use when: Apply this on strengthen/weaken/support questions with multi-step causal reasoning and subconscious, preference, perception, or behavior links.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for assumptions about wording, definitions, or evidence quality rather than support within the causal chain.

Transfer rule: If asked which option cannot explain a belief-versus-survey contradiction, then reject choices that merely reinforce one side without bridging the gap.
Error pattern: Success came from separating “explains the discrepancy” from “supports either the public belief or the measured result.”
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it create a reason public impressions differ from anonymous reports, or does it only describe subgroup burden with no mechanism for the mismatch?
Use when: Relevant in weaken/explain-exception questions contrasting public perception, self-reporting conditions, social desirability, anonymity, or sampling frames.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks which statement best supports the belief/result itself rather than explains their inconsistency.

Transfer rule: If a set has category counts and a selected subset must be from different categories, then test each answer by distributing the selected items across categories and examining the leftover counts.
Error pattern: I treated a merely possible arrangement as a necessary inference instead of checking all valid category allocations.
Diagnostic check: List category totals, place the constrained selected items in every allowed category pairing, then see which category must still appear among the unselected items in every case.
Use when: Apply to grouping problems with small fixed counts, subset-selection constraints, and words like “must” or “can be inferred.”
Boundary: Ignore when extra conditions identify individuals directly or when the claim is only about possibility, not necessity.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers permanent vaccine immunity from isolating an antibody-triggering fragment, then ask whether prior real-world exposure fails to produce lasting immunity.
Error pattern: Success pattern: attacked the hidden assumption that antibody stimulation alone guarantees durable protection.
Diagnostic check: Compare the claim’s required immunity duration with evidence from natural exposure; if people are likely exposed earlier yet still get the disease later, mark the permanence link unsupported.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions about vaccines, immunity, or causal claims moving from lab mechanism to long-term population outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about short-term response, isolation feasibility, or strain coverage rather than lasting immunity.

Transfer rule: If an argument says increased choice or new media destroys shared interests, then prefer evidence showing a mechanism that recreates shared interests despite diversification.
Error pattern: Success came from targeting the causal link, not getting distracted by background descriptions of technology or interaction patterns.
Diagnostic check: State the claim as cause → effect, then ask which option most directly blocks the effect or weakens that causal step with an alternative pathway.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/refute questions built on social change, technology, diversification, and claims about declining common behavior or preferences.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices only restate trends, strengthen the premise, or the question asks for explanation rather than refutation.

Transfer rule: If an item is generated by a living thing or productive property through its ordinary natural growth before separation, then treat it as a natural fruit.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every clause of the definition and rejecting items that were merely found, unearthed, gifted, or otherwise not naturally produced.
Diagnostic check: Ask: What is the original thing, did this item arise from its regular biological/productive process, and was it simply separated from that original?
Use when: Apply this to legal-definition multiple choice about fruits, yields, offspring, ownership, or things derived from another thing.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item comes from discovery, human transfer, manufacture, excavation, or accidental possession rather than natural generation.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle says exactly one statement is false, then test each speaker as the sole liar and enforce all remaining statements simultaneously.
Error pattern: I jumped from one contradiction to a preferred option without exhausting all one-liar cases or chaining conditional statements.
Diagnostic check: Build a truth table or case list; for each person, assume “this is the only false statement,” propagate consequences, and discard any case violating uniqueness.
Use when: Apply to short verbal logic problems with exclusive counts, self-reports, and if-then claims about participation or outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous in scope/time, or the task is not constrained by an exact number of falsehoods.

Transfer rule: If a claim says climate caused a cultural replacement, then prefer evidence linking each group’s way of life to stable climate/environment requirements.
Error pattern: I chose a proximate trigger for one group instead of a broader mechanism that explains both departure and arrival under the same cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice strengthen the causal bridge from environmental shift to population movement/replacement for all groups mentioned, not just one symptom?
Use when: Applicable in strengthen questions about migrations, cultural succession, or social change attributed to ecology, climate, or resources.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument needs timing, authenticity, or direct factual confirmation rather than a general causal principle.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion attributes an outcome difference to one added treatment component, then require baseline equivalence on that component across groups.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a hidden confounder and matching the needed assumption to causal attribution in a comparative experiment.
Diagnostic check: List the only systematic difference intended between groups; ask whether any preexisting imbalance in that same factor could also explain the outcome gap.
Use when: Apply this to randomized trials, control-versus-added-treatment setups, and “prerequisite/assumption” questions about causation.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only descriptive, or when baseline equivalence is already established or irrelevant to the added factor.

Transfer rule: If a behavior is claimed to show avoidance conditioning, then verify it is an immediate action that removes or prevents contact with a present aversive stimulus.
Error pattern: Success came from separating concrete stimulus-driven escape/avoidance from broad fear, trait anxiety, or socially generalized withdrawal.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: What exact unpleasant stimulus is encountered now, what action follows, and how does that action reduce exposure?
Use when: Apply this to psychology items about avoidance, escape, negative reinforcement, or learned reactions to unpleasant sensory or situational cues.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the item concerns long-term phobias, attitudes, beliefs, or motivations without a specific immediate aversive trigger-action link.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers motive or purpose from a behavior’s byproduct alone, then flag effect-to-purpose reasoning.
Error pattern: Treating a helpful consequence of an action as proof that producing that consequence was one aim of the action.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What independent evidence shows the agent’s goal, beyond the fact that others benefit or a result occurs?”
Use when: The conclusion is about intent, function, altruism, or purpose, and the premises mainly describe outcomes or side effects.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises include direct evidence of aims, selection history, signaling design, or explicit reasons linking behavior to purpose.

Transfer rule: If a statement only fixes who is recommended or selected from a group, then infer bounds on that chosen set, not on the underlying trait of the whole group.
Error pattern: Treated praise/background as evidence about actual winners, instead of separating qualifications, recommendations, and final outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each predicate and entity set, then mark whether the conclusion is about candidates, recommendations, or confirmed awardees.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic items with role shifts such as worker quality, nomination, recommendation, selection, or award status.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly equates the stages or states that recommendation guarantees the later status.

Transfer rule: If a claim says reduced supply will raise price, then require an assumption that demand stays roughly constant or does not drop enough to offset the supply shift.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching a supply-side conclusion with the missing demand-side stability condition.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could demand fall enough after the change that price would stay flat or drop?” If yes, the needed assumption blocks that possibility.
Use when: Relevant in supply-and-demand arguments predicting price effects from quotas, bans, ceilings, shortages, or production limits.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already gives demand behavior, or when the conclusion concerns quantity, welfare, or substitutes rather than the item’s own price.

Transfer rule: If a principle says lower-quality substitutes crowd out higher-quality ones under similar use, then choose the option showing cheap/inferior goods displacing better ones in the same market.
Error pattern: Mistook a competitive "best wins" scenario for a displacement-by-inferior-substitutes scenario.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Are there two substitute goods, unequal quality, treated similarly by users, with the worse one spreading while the better one retreats?
Use when: Relevant for analogies about markets, circulation, selection pressures, or social adoption where inferior and superior versions coexist.
Boundary: Ignore when the case is about rank, excellence standing out, broad availability, or winners being strongest rather than worse alternatives crowding out better ones.

Transfer rule: If a use fits an expressly listed fair-use category and all listed conditions match, then choose it; otherwise reject it.
Error pattern: Success comes from strict element-matching to statutory categories instead of relying on broad “noncommercial” intuition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, verify publication status, purpose, user, act type, and whether any distribution/publication goes beyond the listed exception.
Use when: The rule text gives a closed list of exceptions with specific conditions such as study/research, public art copying, performance, or translation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the law uses open-ended balancing factors or when facts depend on extra jurisdiction-specific exceptions not listed.

Transfer rule: If evidence rules out specific cues yet shows preserved performance, then choose the broader hypothesis that explains the remaining ability.
Error pattern: Success came from eliminating cue-specific explanations and matching the answer’s scope to what the experiment actually supports.
Diagnostic check: List each manipulated cue, note what ability remained unchanged, and reject any option requiring a disabled cue or adding unsupported mechanisms.
Use when: Relevant for experiment-based inference questions comparing broad capacity claims against narrower cause claims.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a precise mechanism directly tested, not the best-supported general hypothesis.

Transfer rule: If two analyses date an object differently because a material is present, then check whether the material comes from a later-added layer rather than the original object.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning resolves a contradiction by separating original composition from later restoration, contamination, or modification.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does the new evidence specify where the material was found, and could that location reflect a nonoriginal addition?
Use when: Relevant in chronology, provenance, archaeology, or forensics questions involving layered materials, repairs, overpainting, or mixed-time evidence.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence is known to come from the original layer or when the dispute is about detection sensitivity alone.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a monotonic relation directly, then choose the option that restates only that relation without adding strength or scope.
Error pattern: Success came from matching an explicit textual claim and rejecting choices that introduced absolutes, unsupported causation, or broader claims.
Diagnostic check: Underline each option’s key claim and verify every term appears in the passage or follows immediately from one stated relation.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items about scientific descriptions, instrument behavior, or variable relationships stated in comparative language.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question requires outside knowledge, multi-step inference, or evaluating assumptions not explicitly discussed.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which assumption is unnecessary, then test each option by adding it to the premises and checking whether the target conclusion follows.
Error pattern: Success came from using transitive ordering constraints rather than judging options by plausibility or contradiction alone.
Diagnostic check: Draw a rank graph; for each option, ask “without this link, is there still a forced path from premise items to the conclusion item?”
Use when: Apply this to comparison, ranking, inequality, or “except/necessary assumption” problems with chained relations between entities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about causes, definitions, or evidence strength rather than formal order relations.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what explains a shift between two time periods, then choose the option that introduces a causal event occurring between those periods and matching the changed subgroup.
Error pattern: Success came from aligning timeline, mechanism, and affected population rather than being distracted by broad background trends.
Diagnostic check: Verify the choice answers all three: when did it happen, how could it cause the later change, and does it target the same kind of cases highlighted.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/explain questions involving before-vs-after data, delayed effects, and emphasis on a particular offender or victim group.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is purely descriptive, asks for prediction, or the best option lacks any temporal or subgroup connection.

Transfer rule: If a claim is justified only by restating the conclusion in different words, then flag circular reasoning.
Error pattern: Mistaking vivid language or weak support for the core flaw, while missing a premise that assumes what it must prove.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the argument as premises and conclusion; if a premise already asserts the conclusion’s truth or an equivalent status, mark it circular.
Use when: Relevant in arguments that infer a universal evaluation from an identity claim, slogan, or self-awarded title.
Boundary: Ignore when the supporting premise can be independently verified without presupposing the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a concept, lists traits, then emphasizes worth and uses outside actions only as support, then choose the option stating the central value claim.
Error pattern: Overweighting a concluding example or consequence and mistaking supporting evidence for the author’s main explanatory purpose.
Diagnostic check: Strip the final illustrative sentence; if the core paragraph still primarily answers “why it matters” rather than “who competes” or “what is hard,” select the value-focused theme.
Use when: Expository reading questions with definition-plus-features structure followed by one example, policy reaction, or real-world proof.
Boundary: Ignore when most sentences analyze competition, leadership, or technical obstacles in detail rather than using them briefly as evidence.

Transfer rule: If a statement appears first and later sentences provide reasons for it, then treat that first statement as the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing a headline claim being argued for from background contrast or mere topic framing.
Diagnostic check: Mark each claim and ask, “Which claim do the later premises most directly support?” and “Could the argument still work without this sentence?”
Use when: Apply on role-in-argument questions with contrast words, an initial surprising thesis, and subsequent factual support.
Boundary: Ignore when the opening sentence only sets context, defines terms, or is unsupported by later premises.

Transfer rule: If a choice says someone matches all items liked by a person who likes two constrained items, then verify whether any rule forbids any single other person from having both.
Error pattern: Success came from translating “none ... both” into a per-person impossibility and testing options against that hard constraint, not against what is merely unstated.
Diagnostic check: List each subject, mark required likes and forbidden combinations, then ask of each option: contradiction, allowed possibility, or irrelevant add-on?
Use when: Apply on logic questions with quantifiers like all/none/some, shared attributes, and “could be true EXCEPT” wording.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on external facts, probabilities, or meanings beyond explicit set-membership constraints.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a broad, diverse market makes varied messaging smart, then prefer support showing a single targeted style can repel non-target groups.
Error pattern: Mistook a possibility of broader spillover appeal for evidence about the downside of uniform targeting; chose weak compatibility over stronger causal support.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this choice explain why diversity of audience makes one-style branding risky by identifying a cost of narrow demographic targeting?
Use when: Strengthen questions compare varied-vs-uniform strategies, especially where the conclusion depends on audience heterogeneity.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about message quality, overall ad effectiveness, or broad appeal without any tradeoff from targeting.

Transfer rule: If a rebuttal says a desired substance is too dilute to motivate behavior, then test whether the agent can concentrate or delay use of the source before consumption.
Error pattern: I accepted a comparative preference clue instead of attacking the rebuttal’s key assumption about effective intake at the moment of use.
Diagnostic check: Identify the objection’s bottleneck variable, then ask, “Could timing, evaporation, processing, or accumulation change that variable enough to remove the bottleneck?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/strengthen arguments about low concentration, low yield, inefficiency, or “too much input for too little payoff.”
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already fixes consumption conditions or no plausible mechanism could alter concentration before use.

Transfer rule: If a passage reports an observed feature directly, then prefer the option that restates that observation over a broader exclusivity claim.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a comparison group’s absence finding into a universal “only these have it” conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark each answer as direct restatement, necessary implication, or stronger extrapolation; choose the strongest supported category only.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions built from observed differences between two groups and a proposed causal explanation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly quantifies all groups, states exclusivity, or asks for the best hypothesis rather than a strict inference.

Transfer rule: If an argument concludes “only X investigates Y” from “not Z,” then look for evidence ruling out other possible investigators.
Error pattern: I treated support for the usefulness/existence of Y as strengthening, instead of strengthening the exclusivity link in the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, list every unstated alternative source/actor; prefer the option that closes those gaps rather than one that adds background benefits.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions where premises discuss one sponsor’s incentives and the conclusion says a different sponsor is, for the most part, the only one.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument’s weakness is about whether Y works or exists, not about who else could do it.

Transfer rule: If testing whether one diet/environment causes a nutrition difference, then hold breed/quality constant and vary only that factor between otherwise matched groups.
Error pattern: Success comes from isolating the claimed cause; failures compare mixed changes or measure inputs instead of the outcome.
Diagnostic check: List all possible confounders; ask whether exactly one differs across groups and whether the measured result is the target trait.
Use when: A claim links product quality to feed, habitat, treatment, or upbringing and asks for the most reliable experiment.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for observational evidence only, or when random assignment/control is impossible or unethical.

Transfer rule: If a premise says every thing has internal contradiction as the source of change, then infer universal motion and development, not permanence or uniform rates.
Error pattern: Success pattern: mapping a universal contradiction principle to a universal process claim while rejecting extra specifics not supported by the premise.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the conclusion only restate “all things contain change-driving tension,” or does it add limits, exceptions, speed claims, or special cases?
Use when: Apply this on philosophy or logic questions moving from a broad dialectical principle to the most general consequence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem gives empirical conditions, comparative data, or a theory where contradiction does not imply development.

Transfer rule: If an argument applies one standard in one case and condemns the same standard in a parallel case, then classify the critique as exposing inconsistency.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching the author’s move by comparing two judgments for tension rather than chasing facts, assumptions, or alternate conclusions.
Diagnostic check: Identify the two compared cases, state the principle used in each, and ask whether both can stand together without an explicit differentiator.
Use when: The passage contrasts treatment of similar groups, actions, or policies across contexts and notes missing justification for the difference.
Boundary: Ignore this when the author mainly denies evidence, derives a new claim, or attacks a hidden premise instead of comparing standards.

Transfer rule: If asked whether something is a public good, then test both non-rivalry and non-excludability; if either fails, reject it as a public good.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the defining criteria instead of relying on social usefulness or government involvement.
Diagnostic check: Ask: can one person’s use reduce others’ use, and can access realistically be restricted to payers or selected users?
Use when: This fits classification questions about goods, services, externalities, collective consumption, or government-provided items.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category depends on legal ownership, production method, funding source, or a special textbook definition overriding standard criteria.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts having abundant resources with not yet realizing their value, then choose the option urging development of that potential, not the explanatory mechanism alone.
Error pattern: I fixated on the key causal concept in the middle and missed the author’s main persuasive takeaway directed at the focal subject.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What is the author trying to get the focal actor to do or recognize overall?” Then compare that with any narrower supporting claim.
Use when: The passage centers on one country, firm, or actor, praises its assets, notes a gap, and uses a concept to justify a broader recommendation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a defined mechanism, not the passage’s main emphasis or practical implication.

Transfer rule: If a term names a profession-specific vocabulary set rather than a group-based speech variety, then exclude it from social dialect.
Error pattern: I conflated social prestige/class labels with dialecthood and missed the category difference between full language variety and technical lexicon.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this refer to how a social group broadly speaks, or mainly to specialized terms used for a task or field?
Use when: Relevant in classification questions contrasting social groups, regional varieties, accents, class speech, and occupation-related language.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition explicitly includes jargon/registers as dialects or when the option clearly denotes an entire community speech system.

Transfer rule: If an outcome depends on two contributors, then prefer the choice where increasing one contributor can indirectly worsen the other and thereby reduce the outcome overall.
Error pattern: Success came from matching causal structure, not surface topic; the key pattern is a tradeoff within a two-factor formula.
Diagnostic check: Identify the stated determinants, then test whether the conclusion says “more of factor X can lower result Y because X sometimes decreases factor Z.”
Use when: Apply on parallel-reasoning questions featuring deterrence, success, effectiveness, or attractiveness defined by multiple variables.
Boundary: Ignore when the option merely adds risk, shifts priorities, or compares categories without one factor undermining another determinant.

Transfer rule: If a claim about someone’s reliability in one context is inferred from a single different-context incident, then flag an overgeneralization from weakly relevant evidence.
Error pattern: Treating one possibly irrelevant example as enough to support a broad judgment about honesty or trustworthiness.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the cited incident from the same domain and same kind of stake, and is one case enough to justify the broad conclusion?”
Use when: Arguments attack or defend a person’s credibility using an anecdote from another situation, especially to assess testimony.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple directly relevant cases show a consistent pattern or when the task is about expertise, not general trustworthiness.

Transfer rule: If a passage stresses effects beyond the household, imitation by others, and society-wide teaching value, then choose the option about broader social function.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the main emphasis of consequences and scope, not getting distracted by background mentions.
Diagnostic check: Underline phrases naming scope, audience, and effects; if most point to society/public influence rather than origin or family-only education, select the social-function framing.
Use when: The stem asks what the passage is mainly describing and choices contrast function, origin, influence, or educational role.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage chiefly explains chronology, authorship, or private household instruction without wider social reach.

Transfer rule: If a passage says the minimum viable population was revised upward while habitat cannot support growth beyond the current level, then infer present inability to survive the specified shock.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: chain comparative constraints across time and capacity instead of choosing broader causal or trend claims not directly stated.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the required threshold now above current size, and is expansion blocked by an explicit capacity limit? If both yes, pick the short-term vulnerability conclusion.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/must-be-true questions involving revised minimums, current levels, and environmental carrying-capacity limits.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus provides a recovery mechanism, surplus habitat elsewhere, uncertain revision direction, or asks for the main cause rather than an immediate implication.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined by necessary components, then choose the option that preserves all core components without adding unsupported specifics or reducing it to one effect.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the full definition rather than being distracted by examples, leaders, or partial manifestations.
Diagnostic check: Underline the definition’s required elements, then test each option for omission, overreach, or substitution of example for definition.
Use when: Apply this to definitional multiple-choice questions asking which statement is true according to a provided description.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an application, causal explanation, or best example rather than strict definition matching.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a general claim and then one example supporting it, then choose the option that restates the modest general claim, not a broader recommendation.
Error pattern: Turning an argument about limited exceptions into a normative or strategic principle that goes beyond what the premises establish.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, strip the example away and paraphrase the conclusion in one sentence; reject any option adding “should,” exclusivity, or new criteria.
Use when: Main-conclusion questions where evidence shows some actions in a common category fail to achieve the actor’s long-term interest.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for the best policy advice, implication, or strengthened interpretation rather than the stated conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is impossible from conditional statements, then test each option against every relevant rule and look for a direct contradiction, not merely something unsupported.  
Error pattern: I matched one statement too locally and ignored combining time, road-use, and light-status conditions across multiple premises.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, write the needed facts, chain all implications/contrapositives, and ask: “Can any model satisfy all premises plus this option?”  
Use when: Relevant for logic problems with universal claims, time qualifiers, categories, and behavior conditions that must be integrated.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task depends on outside knowledge, ambiguous language, or probabilistic rather than strict logical possibility.

Transfer rule: If a pairing puzzle has sequential swaps, then track every person’s current partner after each swap in a two-column state table and update only the named participants.
Error pattern: Mis-updating state across chained exchanges; treating a later swap as if earlier pairings still held or swapping the wrong side of a couple.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list pairings after step 1, step 2, and step 3, then verify each person appears exactly once and all swaps conserve the full set of partners.
Use when: Partner, seat, object, or assignment problems involve multiple sequential exchanges or substitutions among a fixed group.
Boundary: Ignore when the question depends on independent clues, probabilities, or one-step direct matching without evolving state.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives multiple causes and one offsetting factor for an observed total, then infer that the size of any one cause cannot be determined from the total alone.
Error pattern: Success came from separating net outcome from component contributions instead of treating the observed effect as a direct measure of one source.
Diagnostic check: List every stated contributor and subtractor; ask, “Would the same total be possible with different values for this one component?”
Use when: Relevant in inference questions about totals, rates, or changes produced by several interacting processes.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage states only one operative cause or gives enough constraints to isolate a component exactly.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a cause from better outcomes in a selected group, then test whether the selector chose cases using the very traits credited as alternative causes.
Error pattern: Confusing a broad background statistic with a direct challenge to the causal link; missed a selection-effect/confounding explanation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the financing source be screening for stronger founders, plans, or structures rather than producing success itself?”
Use when: Comparative outcome claims argue one factor matters more, especially where gatekeepers, admissions, investors, or lenders decide who enters the favored group.
Boundary: Ignore when group assignment is random or controlled, or when evidence already isolates the factor’s independent effect.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus gives a conditional chain from a policy change to a broad result, then link the stated effects and infer a weaker guaranteed outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining premises carefully and translating “many would improve” into the minimal must-true claim that at least some improve.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the chain in arrows, then ask which choice is directly entailed by weakening quantity claims rather than adding new assumptions.
Use when: Apply this on must-be-true questions with causal or conditional statements, especially when answer choices vary by strength.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for explanation, probability, or best support rather than strict logical necessity.

Transfer rule: If a statement contrasts two categories and assigns difficulty only to one, then infer only the property tied to that category, not both.
Error pattern: Overgeneralizing a predicate across contrasted groups instead of preserving the asymmetry signaled by the wording.
Diagnostic check: Mark each subject term and its linked property; ask whether any answer extends a property to a different term without explicit support.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic items using contrasts like feeling vs fact, but, while, whereas, or separate clauses about different subjects.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the text explicitly groups the subjects together or states the property applies equally to both.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts a change in an average after expansion, then choose the premise linking the new entrants’ quality to being lower than the retained group.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the conclusion about average performance by comparing incoming members with the current selected survivors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option directly explain why adding people changes the average in the stated direction?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/completion questions about averages, hiring, growth, survivor groups, or composition effects after a downturn.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns totals, causation unrelated to group composition, or no claim compares newcomers with the existing group.

Transfer rule: If premises say all members of a category have a property, then any option claiming some members lack that property must be false.
Error pattern: I focused on a causal/explanatory statement instead of testing each option against the universal conditions.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite premises as set rules; for each option, ask whether it directly contradicts, could fit, or is irrelevant to those rules.
Use when: Relevant in must-be-false questions with universal claims, conditionals, and options about subsets, exceptions, or explanatory language.
Boundary: Ignore this when premises are probabilistic, comparative, or define sufficiency/necessity in ways not expressible as simple category-property rules.

Transfer rule: If a rebuttal infers objectivity from the detection of bias, then test whether the detectors could also be biased; if so, the rebuttal fails.
Error pattern: Treated evidence of bias-recognition as proof of unbiased judgment, ignoring self-reference and higher-order bias.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the response answer the original universal claim, or does it assume an exception without ruling out the same flaw in the exception?”
Use when: Arguments concern whether observers, critics, evaluators, or investigators can be objective while assessing others’ bias.
Boundary: Ignore when the rebuttal independently establishes a reliable neutrality mechanism or the original claim is only about some biased cases, not all evaluators.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both attitude and active, habitual behavior, then choose the option showing self-initiated, repeated physical participation, not mere intent, supervision, or spectatorship.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking every necessary clause and rejecting choices that satisfy only motive, exposure, or interest without sustained action.
Diagnostic check: Underline each required element; for each option, mark evidence for internal willingness, actual participation, and ongoing habit—accept only if all are explicit.
Use when: Apply to definitional multiple-choice items distinguishing doing an activity from watching it, being encouraged, or just starting once.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept includes passive involvement, one-time attempts, or externally directed participation as sufficient.

Transfer rule: If a claim is about how common and important a cause is in a specific country, then prefer evidence giving direct local accident-cause proportions over indirect risk or foreign data.
Error pattern: I overvalued vivid or large statistics while ignoring scope match between the claim and the evidence.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare each option on jurisdiction, outcome type, and measure; rank highest the one matching country, accidents, and relative share/importance.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions where the conclusion asserts prevalence or significance of a causal factor within a defined population.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the conclusion is about mechanism, individual risk increase, or cross-country generalization.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a promoted benefit with research-based limits and ends with a negative analogy, then choose the option stating the author’s main evaluative claim about that method.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the central thesis instead of getting distracted by background context or broader industry claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 7-word summary of the author’s verdict; verify each paragraph detail supports that same verdict.
Use when: Apply this to main-idea questions where examples, slogans, and analogies all point toward judging one practice’s effectiveness.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, tone, or the author’s view of a larger field rather than one method.

Transfer rule: If evidence shows only one source of a trace or exposure, then do not infer the actual cause was absent; instead test whether an unobserved intermediary could explain the missing trace.
Error pattern: Confusing lack of direct evidence for a cause with evidence that the cause did not occur, by assuming traces would necessarily remain.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could the event have happened while preventing, removing, or masking the expected evidence?” If yes, the conclusion is unsupported.
Use when: Arguments infer from observed traces, contamination, fingerprints, residues, or exposure records to what could not have happened.
Boundary: Ignore when a stated rule guarantees the cause would always leave unavoidable evidence.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires tailoring by subgroup differences plus exemplar-based persuasion toward a targeted outcome, then choose the option showing matched audiences receiving relevant model cases.
Error pattern: I focused on vivid promotional examples and emotional impact while neglecting the audience-specific matching and goal alignment required by the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark three elements in each option—typical case, differentiated audience, specific intended effect—and reject any option missing one.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions involving education, propaganda, outreach, or publicity methods with several partially fitting examples.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept does not require audience segmentation or exemplar-based influence, or when the question asks about outcomes only.

Transfer rule: If asked which choice cannot weaken an argument, then prefer an option that supports the conclusion or is irrelevant, not one that merely pauses the predicted effect.
Error pattern: I treated a short-term slowdown as non-weakening, confusing delay/attenuation with support or neutrality.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it reduce the likelihood of the premise, break the causal link, or undercut the conclusion? If yes, it weakens; if it adds an independent reason for the conclusion, it cannot weaken.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions built on causal chains, forecasts, and policy-to-market predictions.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for an assumption, explains the mechanism, or uses except/not wording tied to factual consistency instead of argument force.

Transfer rule: If an argument condemns a debating tactic, then check whether the argument itself uses that same tactic against its target.
Error pattern: I mistook criticism of reasoning style for a personal attack and missed a self-undermining inconsistency.
Diagnostic check: Underline each accusation the speaker makes; ask whether any accusation attributes bad motives or character in the same way the speaker says is improper.
Use when: The stimulus evaluates rhetoric, civility, persuasion, hypocrisy, or motive-based attacks in political or argumentative contexts.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument only describes chronology, causal direction, or external effects without mirroring the criticized method.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a specific cause or activity from an observed effect/behavior, then test whether the evidence could occur for many other reasons before matching it.
Error pattern: Mistaking a one-way conditional or common accompaniment for a reversible indicator; affirming the consequent.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “If target activity, then observed sign”; then ask “Does the sign alone guarantee the activity, or could non-target cases also show it?”
Use when: The stimulus features travel, locations, habits, or other behaviors presented as proof of a hidden goal, role, or intention.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument gives a biconditional, exclusivity claim, or independent evidence ruling out alternative explanations.

Transfer rule: If a report contrasts a subgroup average rising with an overall hardship measure worsening, then prefer an inference about distribution differences, not a causal prediction.
Error pattern: Mistook offered explanations as sufficient conditions and converted “possible reasons” into a guaranteed if-then claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each statement as trend, cause, or coexistence; reject any option that strengthens possibility into certainty or projects into the future.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items with subgroup-vs-population statistics, aggregate paradoxes, and hedged language like “possible,” “may,” or “however.”
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus provides explicit causal laws, quantified necessity, or direct forecasts rather than descriptive census-style summaries.

Transfer rule: If a tax question asks for neutrality, then choose the policy that minimizes behavior-changing incentives and avoids targeting sectors, firms, or thresholds.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the abstract principle to broad non-distortion, not to tax cuts or increases that selectively steer decisions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would this make some taxpayers change investment, hiring, location, or reporting more than others? Eliminate any yes.
Use when: Relevant for questions about tax design principles, market distortion, resource allocation, and government influence on economic choices.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the goal is redistribution, industrial policy, correcting externalities, or explicitly favoring particular groups or activities.

Transfer rule: If a passage states several premises and then gives a “therefore” conclusion, then choose the option that restates the conclusion, not a supporting premise.
Error pattern: I selected a true earlier statement instead of the author’s main inferred claim.
Diagnostic check: Mark premise indicators and conclusion indicators; paraphrase the sentence after the conclusion cue, then compare options for the closest full restatement.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea, best-summary, or “meaning of the passage” questions with multiple factual statements and one inferential wrap-up.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, an example, or a statement explicitly supported rather than the overall conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage catalogs how people reframe wrongdoing as justified, accidental, or temporary, then choose the completion that restates “by their own characterization, it isn’t really wrongdoing.”
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting multiple examples into one shared self-exculpating theme instead of chasing stronger moral or legal consequences.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, paraphrase each example in neutral terms and ask, “What single claim do all these rationalizations imply about the act itself?”
Use when: Relevant in completion questions built from examples of excuses, denial, minimization, or justification.
Boundary: Ignore this when the examples support external reactions, punishment levels, victim status, or policy claims rather than the actor’s self-description.

Transfer rule: If a purchase is tied to a construction/renovation project, then classify it under project procurement rather than as a standalone goods purchase.
Error pattern: I matched “government use” too loosely and ignored the legal category triggered by the procurement’s attachment to an engineering project.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the item being bought independently for operations, or is it an embedded component of a build/renovation contract? If embedded, treat it differently.
Use when: Relevant for questions defining public procurement by categories such as goods, services, and projects, especially with equipment installed during construction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the issue is about buyer identity, funding source, or explicit exclusions unrelated to project-versus-goods classification.

Transfer rule: If a position is fixed in an ordering puzzle, then reapply every rule to each remaining slot and eliminate options by contradiction before choosing.
Error pattern: Prematurely forced a slot from one condition and ignored cross-checking all constraints jointly; local fit was mistaken for necessity.
Diagnostic check: Make a six-slot sketch, mark fixed positions and segment limits, then test each answer choice in the target slot; reject any choice that violates any rule or leaves no legal completion.
Use when: Scheduling/sequencing problems with fixed positions, before/after groups, adjacency or spacing rules, and multiple answer choices for one slot.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not a constrained ordering problem or when a full valid arrangement is already explicitly given.

Transfer rule: If a claim explains an outcome by an internal cause, then treat choices giving external causes as challengers and the choice unrelated to that outcome as the non-challenger.
Error pattern: Success came from separating alternative explanations from statements that do not bear on the proposed causal link.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could this, if true, explain the observed advantage without the proposed internal cause?” If yes, it questions; if no, it does not.
Use when: Apply to weaken/except questions about causal speculation, especially when several options introduce lifestyle, screening, or treatment differences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for support, assumes multiple causes are compatible, or the option directly measures the claimed internal mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives background, traits, and later influence, then choose the option capturing its overall significance, not just one consequence.
Error pattern: I narrowed a multi-point main idea to a single highlighted effect and ignored broader evaluative framing.
Diagnostic check: List the passage’s functions by sentence; if the answer matches only one function, reject it as too narrow.
Use when: The question asks for the best summary/main idea and the passage mixes description, influence, and historical assessment.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a specific effect, cause, detail, or inference rather than the general idea.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires inferior outcomes displacing superior ones, then choose the case showing worse quality gaining wider market/selection advantage over better quality.
Error pattern: I matched a superficial “good loses out” story instead of checking for direct replacement by an inferior alternative in the same arena.
Diagnostic check: Ask: (1) Which item is better by the stated criterion? (2) Which item actually prevails or gets chosen more? (3) Is the winner worse?
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about淘汰, crowding out, market share, promotion, selection, or competition between higher- and lower-quality options.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the outcome is explained by unrelated fit, cost tradeoffs, different criteria, or no clear inferior-vs-superior comparison exists.

Transfer rule: If a set of methods is split into “does X” or “at least does Y,” then infer only what holds for each branch, not for the whole set.
Error pattern: Treated a disjunction as if all acceptable methods shared the strongest property from one branch.
Diagnostic check: List each method category separately and test the claim against both; reject any claim that fails for even one allowed category.
Use when: The stimulus classifies processes into alternative types and asks what must be true for all acceptable cases.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement gives a universal condition without branching alternatives or when the answer is explicitly limited to one branch.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a work is going abroad or entering the world, then infer export, translation, or overseas publication rights—not audience motivation unless stated.
Error pattern: I overreached from distribution facts to a trend in foreign interest, replacing a direct publishing implication with a speculative demand claim.
Diagnostic check: Underline each option’s key verb and ask: “Is this explicitly supported by the sentence, or does it require an extra causal/trend assumption?”
Use when: The text is brief, reports circulation or international spread, and asks what can be derived from publication or distribution wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage directly gives survey data, foreign reception evidence, or explicit reasons about readers’ interests.

Transfer rule: If person-to-person “knowing” counts produce an impossible mutual-network total, then reinterpret “know” as possibly one-directional recognition before judging conclusions.
Error pattern: I assumed ordinary mutual acquaintance and jumped to a narrative explanation unsupported by the count structure.
Diagnostic check: Convert each statement into degree counts; if the total is odd or violates undirected-graph constraints, reject mutual-friendship assumptions and prefer asymmetric recognition interpretations.
Use when: A word problem gives how many people each member knows and asks for the best inference from those statistics.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem explicitly states all knowing is mutual, reciprocal, or forms confirmed friendships.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which full ordering fits several floor/position constraints, then test every stated relation on the chosen option one by one before committing.
Error pattern: I checked the chain-order constraints but failed to verify the separate non-adjacency condition against the final arrangement.
Diagnostic check: Write each rule as symbols (e.g., X<Y, Y<Z<W, A not next to B) and mark pass/fail for the candidate in order.
Use when: Use this on seating, floors, rankings, schedules, or any multiple-constraint ordering problem with at least one adjacency restriction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is pure calculation, definition recall, or when all options are partial statements rather than complete arrangements.

Transfer rule: If two speakers give different reasons but both argue about one policy’s bottom-line outcome, then choose the issue as that shared outcome, not a supporting premise.
Error pattern: Mistaking a rebuttal premise or side effect for the main point of disagreement.
Diagnostic check: State each speaker’s conclusion in one clause; if they answer the same yes/no policy question, select that question as the issue.
Use when: Argument-summary, point-at-issue, or debate questions where each side offers evidence about speed, customer preference, quality, or similar factors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for an assumption, flaw, or when speakers actually dispute a factual premise rather than the policy outcome.

Transfer rule: If a definition centers on converting waste into reusable resources/products, then exclude choices focused mainly on raw-resource extraction or broad sustainability without a waste-to-resource loop.
Error pattern: Confusing general circular-economy or environmental practices with the narrower category defined by waste recovery and reuse operations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it start with discarded material and end with collection, sorting, recycling, remanufacture, or reuse? If not, reject it.
Use when: Relevant in definition-matching questions about recycling, reverse logistics, producer responsibility, or turning by-products/garbage into usable inputs.
Boundary: Ignore when the target category explicitly includes upstream extraction, general eco-management, or the stem defines the industry more broadly than waste conversion.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires actually providing labor or action that benefits others, then exclude mere requests, opinions, or proposals that do not themselves deliver the benefit.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating performed assistance from communication about desired assistance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Did someone already do something for others, or did they only ask, suggest, or complain?” Eliminate anything in the second group.
Use when: Apply to definition questions contrasting service/activity/performance with statements, plans, or demands.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition explicitly includes advocacy, reporting, coordination, or requests as the target category.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires accurate targeting plus filtering/pushing information to particular users, then choose the option showing data-based real-time personalization.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every defining element, not latching onto any option with users, information, or usefulness alone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the core features and verify the candidate includes targeted users, screened content, and active delivery, not mere search, pricing, or broad marketing.
Use when: Apply this on definition-match questions about service models, recommendation systems, precision delivery, or personalized media/internet functions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept centers on user-initiated retrieval, payment tiers, generic promotions, or lacks explicit filtering for specific users.

Transfer rule: If an analogy hinges on a lexical misconception, then match both the mistaken literal reading and the reply using another food name whose words are nonliteral ingredients.
Error pattern: I matched only the reply’s surface “name need not contain thing” structure, ignoring domain, speech-act role, and parallelity of the initial misunderstanding.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map source and choice by slots: asker role, asks “why no X in Y?”, responder rebuts with “is there X in named item Z?”; accept only near-complete slot matches.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-analogy questions about puns, compound nouns, menu items, or category names mistaken for literal composition.
Boundary: Ignore when similarity depends on causal logic, factual knowledge, or broader theme rather than mirrored wording and pragmatic structure.

Transfer rule: If asked which option cannot weaken a causal claim, then keep only choices that directly support, are neutral to, or fail to address the causation.
Error pattern: I treated a scope-limiting fact as irrelevant instead of recognizing it as a direct weakening of a broad causal attribution.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this provide an alternative cause, limit the alleged effect’s reach, break timing, or show mere severity without linking source to effect?
Use when: Relevant in weaken/except questions about whether an event or project caused a large-scale outcome.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for the strongest support, sufficient assumption, or a descriptive summary rather than causal challenge.

Transfer rule: If a definition says the target object only appears to move while actually stationary, then verify the chosen object itself does not change position and any apparent motion is caused by surrounding motion.
Error pattern: I matched a familiar motion illusion without checking whether the described target was truly stationary and whether context objects generated the illusion.
Diagnostic check: Identify the perceived moving object, ask “Does it physically stay fixed here?”, then identify a separate moving frame that could make it seem to move.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching items about apparent motion, reference frames, background-induced displacement, or illusion versus real movement.
Boundary: Ignore when the object genuinely changes location, when no external moving context is specified, or when the phenomenon is not motion perception.

Transfer rule: If two speakers share a broad goal but propose different acquisition priorities, then compare their scope and resource-allocation commitments to find the disagreement.
Error pattern: Success came from separating shared premises from conflicting policies rather than chasing tempting side claims.
Diagnostic check: List each speaker’s explicit goals, limits, and priorities; mark overlap vs conflict; choose the option tied to a real conflict, not a merely possible inference.
Use when: Relevant in dialogue questions asking what two people would disagree about, especially with “therefore,” “ought,” or limited-resource language.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for agreement, unstated assumptions, or factual truth outside the speakers’ stated positions.

Transfer rule: If a pronoun phrase like “this” follows a causal summary, then map it to the nearest prior cause that directly supports the stated result.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing referents through argument structure instead of grabbing a broad topic or repeated noun.
Diagnostic check: Replace the pronoun with each candidate antecedent; keep the one that makes the sentence a clear causal claim without changing scope.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension items with pronouns, demonstratives, summaries, and several nearby abstract concepts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the pronoun points forward, is explicitly defined elsewhere, or grammar makes antecedent agreement decisive.

Transfer rule: If one species first changes behavior to avoid a predator/competitor, then a later counter-behavior by the other species to overcome that change is anti-specialized defense.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the sequence of co-evolved responses rather than picking any ordinary defense behavior.
Diagnostic check: Identify actor 1’s defensive adaptation, then ask whether actor 2’s behavior specifically neutralizes that adaptation; if yes, classify it as anti-specialized.
Use when: Definitions contrast baseline defense, specialized defense, and second-order countermeasures in predator-prey or co-evolution scenarios.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when behaviors are one-sided, generic survival traits, or lack a clear prior specialized defense being countered.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus attacks another argument’s evidence as irrelevant or misinterpreted, then make the main conclusion the denial that the cited evidence supports that argument’s claim.
Error pattern: I latched onto a supporting explanatory point and treated it as the conclusion, missing the higher-level rebuttal about evidential insufficiency.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What exact claim is being challenged, and does the author mainly reject that claim or merely explain why?” Then match the answer to the broadest statement.
Use when: The passage is a critique of someone else’s reasoning, especially where examples redefine what a sign or indicator really means.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage is primarily building its own positive thesis rather than undermining an inference from stated evidence.

Transfer rule: If a passage explains ingredients, chamber, and process as parts of something, then identify the whole referent being defined, not a component or output.
Error pattern: Success comes from resolving noun-reference at the system level instead of latching onto salient materials, locations, or effects.
Diagnostic check: List each noun phrase in the description and tag it as input, container, process, product, or overall object; choose the term matching the overall object.
Use when: A question asks what a named scientific or technical thing “is,” and the stem describes how it works using several related parts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term explicitly names a material, place, or reaction product rather than an apparatus or system.

Transfer rule: If a claim says one compliance method would save money over another, then compare total costs of the two methods directly, including operating/process costs.
Error pattern: I focused on a side comparison about one method in a different context instead of the core economic comparison between the proposed alternative and the current approach.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which choice most directly tells me whether the alternative is cheaper than the status quo for the same goal?” Eliminate options lacking that head-to-head cost link.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/evaluate arguments about savings, efficiency, feasibility, or replacing one process with another.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about legality, technical possibility, or effects unrelated to comparative cost.

Transfer rule: If a claim gives an either/or route to an outcome and one route is ruled out, then infer the remaining route as necessary.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing elimination of alternatives, not treating the argument as adding possibilities or handling exceptions.
Diagnostic check: List all stated ways the event could happen; mark any explicitly impossible; if exactly one remains and the event occurred, choose the answer describing necessity by exclusion.
Use when: Relevant in reasoning questions with a forced choice, a known outcome, and explicit denial of one option.
Boundary: Ignore when the options are not exhaustive, the “or” is nonexclusive, or hidden alternatives/exceptions are introduced.

Transfer rule: If a chain includes a necessary-condition statement like “only if,” then translate it as outcome → requirement and use contrapositive before linking it to other conditionals.
Error pattern: I overread a conditional chain and treated an unsupported converse as inferable from forward implications.
Diagnostic check: Symbolize each claim with arrows, mark any “only if” arrow direction, then test the chosen option by deriving it only via valid chaining or contraposition.
Use when: Relevant for logic questions with nested if-then claims, causal chains, and options mixing direct results with reversed or converse statements.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on everyday plausibility, quantified evidence, or definitions rather than formal conditional inference.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives premises, then ends with a normative/result claim, choose the option restating that final claim rather than a supporting contrast.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s main conclusion instead of getting distracted by intermediate short-term versus long-term discussion.
Diagnostic check: Underline the final inference cue and paraphrase the sentence after it; verify the chosen option matches that paraphrase most directly.
Use when: Relevant for argument-main-idea questions with concessions, time-horizon contrasts, and evidence leading to a summarized takeaway.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an assumption, detail, example purpose, or a specifically contrasted subpoint rather than the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If a sample comes from a new or unusual medium attracting a nonrepresentative subgroup, then infer that judging the whole field by that sample will distort the overall picture.
Error pattern: I matched on “biased evidence about a broader domain” but missed the tighter parallel: novelty of medium causing selective participation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map structure: broad domain → subset medium → why subset is selective → resulting misleading generalization; require all four elements.
Use when: The stimulus argues from who adopts a format, platform, or channel first to whether it represents the larger population.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument hinges on survival, preservation, deliberate curation, or representativeness without a novelty-driven adopter effect.

Transfer rule: If most exposed people stayed unaffected, then look for a narrower shared sub-exposure that isolates the causal source within the broader group.
Error pattern: Success pattern: resolving an apparent contradiction by distinguishing the relevant subset from the full exposed population.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the broad exposure and ask, “Does any choice identify all cases with one specific item, batch, time, or handler?”
Use when: Relevant in causation questions where investigators keep confidence despite evidence that many apparently exposed people were not affected.
Boundary: Ignore when the issue is not subset selection within exposure, but instead timing, measurement error, alternative causes, or reversed causation.

Transfer rule: If a statement says one condition implies several results, then treat it as separate implications to each result and combine with given truths by modus ponens.
Error pattern: Success came from unpacking a compound consequent instead of searching for invalid converses or unsupported effects of a false antecedent.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “premise implies X,” “premise implies Y,” etc.; then test each option by direct substitution, rejecting any that reverse or negate the original direction.
Use when: Apply this to conditional statements with one trigger and multiple required outcomes, especially in inference-style multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt includes biconditionals, quantifiers, causal uncertainty, or extra premises that change the conditional structure.

Transfer rule: If an argument assigns a group trait to one member solely because it belongs to that group, then prefer an analogy with the same class-to-individual leap.
Error pattern: Illicitly transferring an average or typical property of a category to a specific subtype or instance without checking fit.
Diagnostic check: Identify the broad class, the target subclass/instance, and ask whether the cited property must hold for that target rather than merely often holding in the class.
Use when: The premise says a kind/category generally has some feature and the conclusion asserts that feature for one member or subtype.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument provides evidence the target is representative, explicitly included, or governed by a definitional rule.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a group has traits and another group targets that group, then infer the targeter seeks those traits, not broader facts about location or method.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by following the subject–attribute link and avoiding unsupported jumps from audience description to industry distribution or replacement claims.
